questions.question: A point on a production possibilities frontier:

options.a: could indicate an optimal use of resources.
options.b: is less efficient that a point inside the production possibilities frontier
options.c: reflects an unattainable level unless technology is further developed to fully employ all resources to their optimum capacity
options.d: Implies that too much labor and not enough capital is being used

questions.explanation: Points on the production possibilities frontier show combinations where all resources are fully and efficiently used, so a point on it can show an optimal use of resources. Option B has it backwards, because points inside the frontier are the inefficient ones. Option C describes points outside the frontier, and option D has no basis in the PPC.

questions.question: What is the opportunity cost of one year at College or University?

options.b: at least one year of earnings in a paid employment

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, and for a year at university that is mainly the earnings you could have made from a paid job in that year. Options A, C and D are not alternatives you give up by choosing school; they are other situations, not the forgone next best use of your time.

questions.question: Opportunity cost is
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. Option A, implicit cost, is one kind of opportunity cost to a firm, not the definition. Options C and D are vague and not the standard meaning.

questions.question: The central problem of every society is

options.b: to prevent riots in our cities

questions.explanation: Every society faces scarcity: resources are limited while human wants are unlimited, so choices must be made. Options A and B are political or security goals, not the central economic problem, and option D has nothing to do with economics.

questions.question: The word "Economic" refers to
questions.explanation: In economics, something is economic when it is scarce or limited in supply relative to wants and therefore commands a price. Options A, B and C each describe one part of this meaning, so all of the above is the best answer.

questions.question: The fundamental questions that every society must answer because of scarcity are
questions.explanation: Because of scarcity, every society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom to produce it. These three questions together make up the basic economic problem, so picking only A, B or C leaves out the other two.

questions.question: In a free enterprise economy, the question of what, how and for whom to produce are solved by

options.b: the central problem of every society

questions.explanation: In a free enterprise (market) economy, prices signal what people want and what is profitable, so the price mechanism decides what, how and for whom to produce. Option A, a planning committee, is how a command economy works. Option B is just the problem, not the way it is solved.

questions.question: Economics studies how individuals and organizations in society engage in the
questions.explanation: Economics studies how people and organisations engage in production, exchange and consumption of goods and services. Options A, B and C each name only one of these activities, so all of the above is correct.

questions.question: A graph that describes the maximum amount of one good that can be produced for every level of production of the other good is
questions.explanation: The production possibilities curve (frontier) shows the maximum amount of one good that can be produced for each level of output of the other good, given resources and technology. Option A, opportunity cost, is shown by the slope of this curve but is not the graph itself. Options B and D are related ideas, not the name of the graph.

questions.question: Scarcity means

options.a: Resources are limited relative to wants

questions.explanation: Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with people's unlimited wants, so not every want can be satisfied. Option C mixes this up: scarcity forces people to make choices, it does not mean that choices are limited. Options B and D describe possible outcomes in an economy, not what scarcity means.

questions.question: Microeconomics is the study of
questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies how individual households and firms make choices under scarcity and how they interact in particular markets. Option B, the performance of the national economy, is macroeconomics. Options C and D are ideas used in economics, not the definition of microeconomics.

questions.question: According to marginal analysis, optimal decision-making involves:

options.a: Taking actions whenever the marginal benefit exceeds the marginal cost.
options.b: Taking actions whenever the marginal benefit is positive.
options.c: Taking actions only if the marginal cost is zero.

questions.explanation: Marginal analysis says you should take an action as long as its extra benefit is greater than its extra cost, stopping where they are equal. Option B ignores cost completely, and option C is too strict, since many worthwhile actions have positive marginal cost.

questions.question: ________ is a fundamental problem caused by shortage of land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship.
questions.explanation: Scarcity is the basic economic problem: resources such as land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship are limited compared with people's wants. Options A and B are budget ideas, and option D is a social problem, not the fundamental economic one.

questions.question: An imagined point D outside of the Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) is called
questions.explanation: Points outside the PPF cannot be produced with the economy's current resources and technology, so they are unattainable combinations. Option C describes points on or inside the frontier. Option B may be true in the sense that people would like more, but it does not describe what the point represents.

questions.question: ________ measures the cost of anything that we have chosen relative to alternatives that could have been chosen.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made, so it measures the cost of a choice relative to the alternatives. Option C, the theory of cost, deals with a firm's production costs, not the cost of choosing.

questions.question: An economy that is situated inside of its Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) can still

options.a: give out more resources as aids

questions.explanation: A point inside the PPF means some resources are idle or used inefficiently, so the economy can produce more by using what it has more efficiently, moving towards the frontier. Options A, C and D do not explain how production can rise from within the frontier.

questions.question: Common economic systems include: traditional system, command system, ________ and mixed system
questions.explanation: The main economic systems are the traditional, command, market (free enterprise) and mixed systems, so the missing one is the pure market system. Option B describes the forces of demand and supply at work in a market, not a type of economic system, and options C and D are political rather than economic systems.

questions.question: Economic agents make choices because ________

options.a: goods and services are readily available
options.b: resources at their disposal are scarce
options.d: the free market forces are active

questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce relative to wants, economic agents cannot have everything and must choose among alternatives. Option A is the opposite of scarcity, and option C alone does not explain why choice is needed.

questions.question: In a modern mixed economy, the state
questions.explanation: In a mixed economy, most economic activity is carried out by private individuals and firms, but the government intervenes in markets through regulation, taxes and public provision. Option C describes a command economy, and options A and B overstate the state's role.

questions.question: The concept of 'scarcity' can lead to the following except

options.a: Makes economic goods to command prices
options.b: Makes supply of resources readily available
options.c: Imposes the need to make choices.
options.d: Imposes the need to study economics.

questions.explanation: Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants, so it cannot make resources readily available. Scarcity is exactly what makes goods command prices (A), forces people to make choices (C) and creates the need to study economics (D).

questions.question: One of the following fails to describe a market economy

options.a: Individuals are for their own self-interest
options.d: Activities are governed by legal framework

questions.explanation: In a market economy prices are set freely by the forces of demand and supply, so prices being centrally controlled does not describe it. Self-interest (A), incentives (B) and a legal framework that protects property and contracts (D) are all features of a market economy.

questions.question: Means in economics simply means ________
questions.explanation: In economics, 'means' are the scarce resources available to satisfy human wants, such as land, labour and capital. Option B, goods and services, are what people want to end up with, and option D, money, is only one form of resource.

questions.question: The assumptions of production possibility frontier include the following except

options.a: Resources are used on just two commodities.
options.d: Resources are sufficient for all production.

questions.explanation: The PPF assumes resources are limited, fully used, and shared between just two goods, so options A, B and C are assumptions. Option D is not, because if resources were sufficient for all production there would be no scarcity and no need to choose.

questions.question: In a free market setting, anyone who provides goods and services is called
questions.explanation: Anyone who provides goods and services in the market is a producer. Option C, an entrepreneur, is the specific person who organises the factors and bears risk, so not every provider is one, and option A, an innovator, is narrower still.

questions.question: In a modern market economy, the state performs all of the following functions, except
questions.explanation: In a market economy prices are set by demand and supply, so laws controlling prices are not one of the state's basic functions. The state does provide contract law (A), property law (B) and a stable currency (D), which markets need to work well.

questions.question: There would be no economic problem if:

options.a: We were dealing with an economy consisting of one man on a desert island
options.b: Man did not live in nation - states
options.c: We were dealing with societies whose wants could be more than fully satisfied by the resources at their command

questions.explanation: The economic problem exists because wants exceed the resources available to satisfy them; if resources could more than fully satisfy all wants, there would be nothing to economise. Option A is wrong because even one person alone on an island has limited time and resources and must make choices. Option B is irrelevant, since scarcity exists with or without nation-states.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of a centrally planned economy?

options.a: Priorities in agricultural production set by farmers
options.b: State direction and ownership of the economy
options.d: Limited operation of the market mechanism

questions.explanation: In a centrally planned economy the state, not individual farmers, sets production priorities, so farmers setting their own priorities is not a feature of it. Options B, C and D, state direction and ownership, state ownership of land and limited use of the market, are all typical features of central planning.

questions.question: A command economy is one in which

options.a: The government allows the individuals to have a say in production and consumption
options.b: Prices set freely by demand and supply guide production and consumption
options.c: The government makes all the decisions about production and consumption

questions.explanation: In a command economy the government makes all the major decisions about what to produce, how to produce and for whom. Option B describes a market economy, where the price mechanism, not the state, guides these decisions. Option A describes a market or mixed system, where individuals have a say.

questions.question: A mixed economy is one in which

options.a: The government and the private sector interact in solving economic problems
options.c: The private sector is given a free hand to operate

questions.explanation: A mixed economy combines private enterprise with government participation, so both sectors work together to solve the basic economic problems. Option B describes a command economy, and option C describes a free-market economy, so D cannot be right either.

questions.question: Choices are necessary because

options.c: Human beings are difficult to please

questions.explanation: Choice is necessary because resources are scarce relative to our wants, so we cannot have everything and must decide what to give up. Option B is the opposite, since abundant resources would remove the need to choose. Option C is a personal trait, not the economic reason for choice.

questions.question: Consumption is the act of

options.a: Saving part of income for future use
options.c: Using goods and services to satisfy wants

questions.explanation: Consumption is the act of using goods and services to satisfy wants. Option B describes production, the making of goods and services, not their use. Option A describes saving, which is the part of income not spent on consumption, so D cannot be right either.

questions.question: Economics is the study of

options.b: How goods and services are produced in an economy
options.c: How society decides what, how and for whom to produce
options.d: How human beings choose between their wants and their goods

questions.explanation: Economics studies how society decides what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, given scarce resources. Options A and B each cover only one part of this, distribution or production. Option D is close, but it is vaguely worded, while C captures the full set of choices economics studies.

questions.question: The fundamental problem of economics is

options.a: The establishment of a political framework to determine the what, how and for whom of production
options.b: To establish an equitable distribution of income
options.c: The scarcity of productive resources relative to society's unlimited wants
options.d: The establishment of prices for the factors of production

questions.explanation: The fundamental economic problem is scarcity: resources are limited while human wants are unlimited. Option A describes how a society might organise its response to scarcity, not the problem itself. Options B and D are specific issues that only arise because of scarcity.

questions.question: Micro-economics is often referred to as price theory. Why?

options.a: Because it focuses on the general price level of the whole economy
options.b: Because it focuses on how relative prices of small units of economic elements are determined and various equilibria reached
options.c: Because it deals with small units

questions.explanation: Microeconomics is called price theory because it explains how the prices of individual goods and factors are determined in particular markets and how equilibrium is reached. Option A is wrong because the general price level is a macroeconomic variable. Option C mentions small units without explaining the link to price, and option D is too vague.

questions.question: Markets in which governments do not intervene are called:
questions.explanation: A free market is one where prices and quantities are set by demand and supply without government intervention. Option A, open markets, usually refers to markets open to all buyers or to central bank operations, not the absence of government. Option D refers to trade between countries.

questions.question: Economics is defined as a science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means by:
questions.explanation: Lionel Robbins defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Option A, Alfred Marshall, defined it as a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, and option B, Adam Smith, saw it as an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations.

questions.question: The opportunity cost of a free good is:
questions.explanation: A free good, such as air, is available in unlimited quantity, so using more of it means giving up nothing else, and its opportunity cost is zero. Option D, positive, applies to economic (scarce) goods. Option C is wrong because opportunity cost cannot be negative.

questions.question: The basic economic problems include:

options.a: What and how much to produce

questions.explanation: The basic economic problems every society faces are what (and how much) to produce, how to produce it, and for whom to produce it. Options A, B and C each state one of these questions, so the full answer is all of them; picking just one leaves out the other two.

questions.question: Examples of demerit goods include:
questions.explanation: Demerit goods are goods whose consumption harms the user and often other people, so society believes they are over-consumed. Alcohol, cigarettes and harmful drugs all fit this description, so 'all of the above' is correct. Choosing only A, B or C leaves out the other examples, which are just as much demerit goods.

questions.question: The PPC is also known as:
questions.explanation: The production possibility curve (PPC) is also called the production possibility frontier (PPF), the production possibility boundary (PPB) and the transformation curve, because it shows how resources can be shifted from one good to another. Since options A, B and C are all correct names, the best answer is all of the above.

questions.question: A type of good whose benefits people underestimate is called a:
questions.explanation: Merit goods, such as education and healthcare, are goods whose benefits people tend to underestimate, so they consume less of them than is good for themselves and society. Option C, demerit goods, are the opposite: goods whose harm people underestimate. Option B, luxury goods, are defined by income, not by how their benefits are judged.

questions.question: Reasons why the government intervenes in the economy include:

options.a: To redistribute income and wealth to improve equality of opportunity and equality of outcome
options.c: To overcome prolonged recessions and reduce unemployment

questions.explanation: Governments intervene in the economy to redistribute income and wealth, to correct market failures, and to fight prolonged recessions and unemployment, among other reasons. Since options A, B and C are all valid reasons, the answer is all of the above.

questions.question: The curve that shows the different combinations of two goods an economy can produce when it uses all its resources fully and efficiently is called the:
questions.explanation: The production possibility curve (PPC) traces the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with its given resources and technology. Option A is the tempting one, but an indifference curve shows combinations of goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction, which is about tastes rather than production.

questions.question: The definition of economics associated with Lionel Robbins is known as the:
questions.explanation: Robbins defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses, which is why it is called the scarcity definition. Option A belongs to Alfred Marshall, D to Adam Smith, and C to Paul Samuelson.

questions.question: In a free enterprise economy such as a market-driven Lagos trading system, the questions of what, how and for whom to produce are answered mainly by:
questions.explanation: In a free enterprise economy, buyers and sellers respond to prices: rising prices signal what to produce more of, costs guide how to produce, and incomes decide who can buy the output. Option A describes a command (planned) economy, where government rather than the market makes these choices.

questions.question: Which economist described political economy as "an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations"?
questions.explanation: Adam Smith's famous 1776 book was titled An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, which gave rise to the wealth definition of economics. Option C, Marshall, is linked with the welfare definition, and D, Keynes, is linked with macroeconomics.

questions.question: Which definition of economics brings in the idea of a scale of preference, where wants are ranked in order of importance?
questions.explanation: The scarcity definition says people have many wants but limited means with alternative uses, so they must rank their wants on a scale of preference and choose which to satisfy first. The wealth and welfare definitions (A and B) focus on wealth and material well-being rather than on ranking competing ends.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most widely accepted way of describing economics?

options.c: The study of mankind in the ordinary business of life
options.d: The science of making choices under scarcity

questions.explanation: Most modern economists see economics as the study of how people make choices when resources are scarce and have alternative uses, which grows out of Robbins's scarcity definition. Option C is Marshall's well-known phrase and A sums up his welfare view, but both have been criticised for being too narrow, while B is the older wealth view.

questions.question: The basic economic problem facing every economy is:
questions.explanation: Every economy has limited resources but people's wants keep growing, and this mismatch forces choices about how resources should be used. Options A, B and C are activities or goals that arise because of this problem, not the problem itself.

questions.question: Economics is best described as:

options.c: Neither a science nor an art
options.d: Both a science and an art, depending on how and for what purpose it is used

questions.explanation: Economics is a science because it studies cause-and-effect relationships systematically, and it is also an art because its knowledge is applied to solve practical problems such as designing policies. Option A is tempting, but economics also has normative and practical sides, so calling it only a positive science leaves out part of the picture.

questions.question: The word 'economic' is most closely linked with the word:
questions.explanation: Something is an economic good because it is scarce relative to the wants for it, so choices have to be made about how to use it. Options A, C and D describe free goods, such as air, which have no price and do not involve economic choice.

questions.question: The subject matter of economics is best described as the study of:
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, people, firms and governments must choose how to use them, and economics studies both the scarcity and the choices it forces. Option C is tempting but incomplete, since scarcity only matters because it leads to choices, while A and B reflect older, narrower definitions.

questions.question: The 'growth' definition of economics is linked with which economist?
questions.explanation: Paul Samuelson's definition focuses on how society chooses to use scarce resources to produce goods over time and distribute them, which is why it is called the growth definition. Option B, Robbins, gave the scarcity definition, and D, Marshall, gave the welfare definition.

questions.question: The growth definition of economics is mainly concerned with:
questions.explanation: The growth definition, linked with Samuelson, looks at how society uses scarce resources to produce goods over time, so it brings economic growth and development into the subject. Options B and C are the focus of the older welfare and wealth definitions.

questions.question: Studies that examine individuals' relationships with, and interactions within, society belong to:
questions.explanation: Social sciences, including economics, sociology and political science, study human behaviour and how people relate to each other in society. Options A, B and C study the natural and physical world or living organisms, not human society.

questions.question: Which social science is distinctive for its much heavier use of mathematics than the others?
questions.explanation: Economics uses mathematics more than other social sciences, for example in demand and supply equations, utility analysis and cost functions. Sociology, political science and anthropology also use data, but they rely far less on mathematical models.

questions.question: The scarcity definition of economics was given by:
questions.explanation: Lionel Robbins defined economics as the science that studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Adam Smith (B) is linked to the wealth definition, and Marshall (D) to the welfare definition.

questions.question: A market economy is also called a:
questions.explanation: In a market (capitalist) economy, resources are mostly privately owned and prices are set by demand and supply. Option A, a socialist economy, relies on state ownership and planning, and Option C, a mixed economy, combines market forces with significant government involvement.

questions.question: 'Economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life.' This definition was given by:
questions.explanation: This is Alfred Marshall's welfare definition, which focuses on how people earn and use income to promote well-being. Adam Smith (A) is linked to the wealth definition, and Robbins (B) to the scarcity definition based on ends and scarce means.

questions.question: The branch of economics that deals mainly with how scarce resources are allocated among different uses (which goods to produce and how their prices are set) is:
questions.explanation: Microeconomics studies individual decision-makers, such as households and firms, and how prices guide the allocation of scarce resources between competing uses. Macroeconomics (B) studies economy-wide aggregates like national income and inflation, and econometrics (C) is the use of statistical methods to test economic relationships.

questions.question: A point inside a production possibility curve shows that:

options.a: resources are being used beyond their capacity
options.b: some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
options.c: the economy has full employment of all resources

questions.explanation: Inside the PPC, the economy could produce more of one good without giving up any of the other, which means some resources are idle or wasted. Option A would be a point outside the curve, which is unattainable, and Option C, full employment, is shown by points on the curve itself.

questions.question: In which type of economy do consumers and producers make choices guided mainly by the market forces of demand and supply?
questions.explanation: In a market economy, prices set by demand and supply signal what to produce, how to produce and for whom. Options B and C are planned systems where the government makes these decisions, and Option A, an open economy, simply refers to a country that trades with others.

questions.question: In a free market economy, prices are:

options.b: determined by the free interaction of demand and supply

questions.explanation: In a free market, the price of each good settles where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer, through the free interaction of demand and supply. Options A and C involve government price control, which belongs to command or mixed systems, and Option D ignores the role of buyers.

questions.question: In Robbins' definition of economics, the 'means' available to satisfy wants are:
questions.explanation: Robbins described economics as the study of the relationship between unlimited ends (wants) and scarce means that have alternative uses. Option B confuses means with ends, since it is wants, not means, that are unlimited.

questions.question: At the most basic level, every economic question is about

options.a: how to make as much money as possible.
options.b: what goods a country should produce.
options.d: how to satisfy all of our wants.

questions.explanation: Every economic question, whether about prices, jobs or production, exists because resources are limited compared with our wants, so it is ultimately about coping with scarcity. Option B (what to produce) is only one of the questions scarcity forces on us, not the root of all of them. Option D is impossible, since scarcity means we can never satisfy all our wants, and Option A confuses economics with simply getting rich.

questions.question: In economics, an incentive

options.a: can be a reward but can never be a penalty.
options.b: can be a penalty but can never be a reward.
options.c: can be either a reward or a penalty.
options.d: is the opposite of a tradeoff.

questions.explanation: An incentive is anything that encourages or discourages an action, so it can be a reward (a bonus for meeting targets) or a penalty (a fine for late tax payment). Options A and B each wrongly rule out one of these two forms. Option D is wrong because an incentive and a tradeoff are different ideas, not opposites.

questions.question: A reward or penalty that encourages a person to take a particular action is called
questions.explanation: An incentive is an inducement that pushes people towards or away from an action, such as a discount that encourages customers to buy. Options A and B (marginal benefit and marginal cost) measure the gain or cost of one more unit of an activity, not the inducement itself. Option C, opportunity cost, is the best alternative given up when a choice is made.

questions.question: Economic questions arise mainly because we

options.a: want more than we can get.
options.b: want more than we actually need.
options.d: have limited wants that need to be satisfied.

questions.explanation: Economic questions exist because our wants are greater than what our limited resources can provide, so we always want more than we can get. Option B is tempting, but the problem is not wanting more than we need; even needs alone can outrun resources. Options C and D get the situation backwards, since resources are limited and wants are unlimited.

questions.question: The most fundamental economic problem facing any society is

options.d: the fact that a country imports more than it exports.

questions.explanation: Scarcity, meaning that limited resources cannot satisfy unlimited wants, is the basic problem from which all other economic questions arise. Security and health (Options A and C) are important goals, but they compete for scarce resources rather than being the root problem. Option D describes a trade deficit, which is a specific issue some countries face, not the fundamental problem of every society.

questions.question: Economists point out that scarcity is faced by

options.a: neither the poor nor the rich.
options.b: the poor but not the rich.
options.c: the rich but not the poor.
options.d: both the poor and the rich.

questions.explanation: Scarcity affects everyone, because even a very rich person has limited time and cannot have everything they want. Option B is the tempting wrong answer, since it confuses scarcity with poverty. A rich Lagos businessman still has to choose how to spend his 24 hours and his money, so the rich face scarcity too.

questions.question: Because of scarcity, people must
questions.explanation: Scarcity means we cannot have everything we want, so we are forced to choose among alternatives. Cooperation, competition and trade (Options A, B and C) are things people may do in response to scarcity, but none of them is unavoidable in the way that making choices is.

questions.question: When an economist talks about scarcity, he or she is referring to the

options.a: ability of society to employ all of its resources.
options.b: ability of society to consume all that it produces.
options.c: inability of society to satisfy all human wants because resources are limited.
options.d: ability of society to keep making technological breakthroughs and raise production.

questions.explanation: In economics, scarcity is society's inability to satisfy all human wants because the resources needed to produce goods and services are limited. Option A describes full employment, and Option D describes technological progress; both are about using resources well, not about the basic limit itself. Option B has nothing to do with the wants-versus-resources gap.

questions.question: Scarcity can be eliminated through

options.b: exploration that helps us find new resources.
options.d: none of the above, because scarcity cannot be eliminated.

questions.explanation: Scarcity can never be eliminated, because human wants keep growing while resources at any point in time remain limited. Markets (Option A), discovering new resources (Option B) and careful use of resources (Option C) can all help us get more from what we have, but they only ease scarcity rather than remove it.

questions.question: As an economic concept, scarcity applies to
questions.explanation: Scarcity applies to anything that is limited relative to the uses we would like to make of it, and both money and time fit this. A student with N10,000 and only 24 hours in a day must choose how to spend both. Options B and C each wrongly leave one of them out.

questions.question: Scarcity is common to all economic systems because resources are

options.a: unlimited because of constant technological advances.
options.b: limited, and so are human wants.
options.c: unlimited, and so are human wants.
options.d: limited, but human wants are unlimited.

questions.explanation: Every economic system faces scarcity because resources are limited while human wants are unlimited. Option B is tempting, but if wants were also limited they could eventually be fully satisfied and scarcity would disappear. Options A and C are wrong because technology raises output but does not make resources unlimited.

questions.question: The problem of scarcity applies

options.a: only to industrially developed countries, because resources there are heavily used.
options.b: only to underdeveloped countries, because they have few productive resources.
options.c: only to economies that are just beginning to develop, because specialised resources are rare.
options.d: to all economic systems, whatever their level of development.

questions.explanation: Scarcity is universal: every economy, from the richest to the poorest, has limited resources and unlimited wants. Option B is the most tempting, but even highly developed economies must choose how to use their resources. Options A and C wrongly limit scarcity to one stage of development.

questions.question: A wealthy businessman in Lagos is unable to get a ticket to a sold-out concert. He is experiencing
questions.explanation: The businessman cannot get something he wants because the tickets are limited, which is exactly what scarcity means, and it shows that even the rich face it. Option C, opportunity cost, is what he gives up when he makes a choice, but here he is not choosing between alternatives. Option D refers to wrongly assuming that what is true for one person is true for everyone.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines the subject of economics?

options.a: the science that studies unemployment, inflation and economic stability
options.c: the study of choices that businesses make to maximise profit
options.d: the study of the choices people make to cope with scarcity

questions.explanation: Economics is the study of the choices individuals, firms and governments make to cope with scarcity. Option A describes only macroeconomics, and Option C describes only part of microeconomics, so both are too narrow. Option B confuses economics with simply making money.

questions.question: When an economy produces more houses and fewer typewriters, it is answering the ________ question.
questions.explanation: Deciding which goods to produce, and in what quantities, answers the 'what' question, so shifting production towards houses and away from typewriters is a 'what' decision. Option B, 'how', is about the methods and resources used to produce. Option D, 'for whom', is about who gets the goods once they are produced.

questions.question: ________ all the objects that we value and are willing to pay for.
questions.explanation: Goods and services are the things people value and are willing to pay for: goods are physical items like bread, and services are tasks performed for people, like a haircut. Option A, resources, are the inputs used to produce goods and services. Option C, wants, are our desires for goods and services, and Option D, capital, is one type of resource.

questions.question: A Lagos fast-food chain decides to make more shawarma and fewer burgers. It is answering the ________ question.
questions.explanation: Choosing which products to make, and how much of each, answers the 'what' question, so switching from burgers towards shawarma is a 'what' decision. Option C, 'when', is not one of the basic economic questions, which are what, how and for whom. Options B and D are not among these questions either.

questions.question: A state government builds a road using very few machines and a great deal of labour. It is answering the ________ question.
questions.explanation: The 'how' question is about the method of production, meaning the combination of labour, machines and other resources used. Choosing a labour-intensive method over a machine-intensive one is a 'how' decision. Option A, 'what', would be the decision to build a road instead of something else, and Option D is about who receives the output.

questions.question: To meet increased demand for its product, a firm decides to hire a few highly skilled workers rather than many low-skilled workers. The firm is answering the ________ question.
questions.explanation: Deciding which mix of inputs to use, here a few skilled workers instead of many unskilled ones, is a choice about the method of production, which answers the 'how' question. Option C, 'what', would apply if the firm were deciding which product to make, but the product stays the same. Options B and D are not among the basic economic questions.

questions.question: To answer the 'for whom' question, economists study
questions.explanation: Who gets the goods and services an economy produces depends mainly on people's incomes, so the 'for whom' question is answered by studying income differences. Option D, technological change, relates more to the 'how' question. Options A and C are broad macroeconomic topics that do not directly explain who gets what.

questions.question: Ada, a lawyer, earns N50,000 an hour, while Musa, a mechanic, earns N5,000 an hour. This income difference is most directly an example of an economy answering the ________ question.
questions.explanation: The 'for whom' question is about who gets the goods and services produced, and that depends largely on incomes. Since Ada earns far more than Musa, she can buy far more of the economy's output. Option D, 'how', is about production methods, and Options A and B are not among the basic economic questions.

questions.question: An economist says that raising taxes on petrol would be in the social interest. What does the economist mean?

options.a: Higher taxes on petrol would benefit society as a whole.
options.b: Higher taxes on petrol would benefit most people.
options.c: Higher taxes on petrol would benefit everyone.
options.d: Higher taxes on petrol would benefit some social groups.

questions.explanation: A choice is in the social interest when it is best for society as a whole, using resources efficiently and fairly overall. Option B is tempting, but the social interest is about society's overall wellbeing, not a simple head count. Option C goes too far, since some people may lose, and Option D describes the interest of particular groups.

questions.question: In a market economy, what people do in pursuit of their self-interest

options.a: usually conflicts with the social interest.
options.d: always conflicts with the social interest.

questions.explanation: In a market economy, people pursuing their own interest usually end up promoting the social interest as well; this is Adam Smith's 'invisible hand' idea. A trader who wants profit must supply what customers want. Option C goes too far, because there are cases, such as pollution, where self-interest harms society, and Options A and D overstate the conflict.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the basic economic questions every society must answer?

options.a: What goods and services are produced?
options.b: How are goods and services produced?
options.c: For whom are goods and services produced?
options.d: Why do incentives affect only marginal costs?

questions.explanation: Every society must decide what to produce, how to produce it and for whom it is produced, so Options A, B and C are the basic economic questions. Option D is not one of them, and it is also false, because incentives can affect both the costs and the benefits of a choice.

questions.question: Tradeoffs arise in all of the following questions EXCEPT

options.a: What goods and services should be produced?
options.b: How should goods and services be produced?
options.c: For whom should goods and services be produced?
options.d: Why should goods and services be produced?

questions.explanation: Because of scarcity, every society faces tradeoffs over what to produce, how to produce it and for whom, which are the three basic economic questions in Options A, B and C. 'Why should goods and services be produced?' is not one of these questions, so it is the exception.

questions.question: In economics we learn that

options.a: sometimes there is such a thing as a "free lunch."
options.b: tradeoffs allow us to avoid opportunity cost.
options.c: opportunity cost is the total of all the alternatives given up when a choice is made.

questions.explanation: None of the statements is correct. Option A is false because every choice has an opportunity cost, so there is no free lunch, and Option B is false because tradeoffs are exactly what create opportunity cost. Option C is the most tempting, but opportunity cost is only the single highest-valued alternative given up, not all the alternatives added together.

questions.question: Because we face scarcity, every choice involves
questions.explanation: Scarcity means that choosing one thing always means giving up the next best alternative, and that sacrifice is the opportunity cost. Option A is wrong because many choices, such as how to use your time, involve no money at all. Option C is wrong because we give something up in exchange for what we choose, not for nothing.

questions.question: The loss of the highest-valued alternative given up when a choice is made is called
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice. For example, if you spend Saturday at work instead of at a study group, the study time is your opportunity cost. Option B, scarcity, is the reason choices must be made, and Option A, marginal benefit, is the gain from one more unit of an activity.

questions.question: Which of these statements are correct? I. The highest-valued alternative given up to get something is its opportunity cost. II. Rich economies do not face opportunity costs. III. Scarcity gives rise to opportunity costs.
questions.explanation: Statement I is the definition of opportunity cost, and statement III is right because scarcity forces choices, and every choice means giving something up. Statement II is false: even rich economies have limited resources compared with their wants, so they also face opportunity costs. That rules out options B and D, and option A leaves out the true statement III.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines opportunity cost?

options.a: The amount of money paid for something.
options.b: The money and time needed to consume something.
options.c: The value of the next best alternative sacrificed when a choice is made.
options.d: The sum of all the alternatives sacrificed when a choice is made.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the single next best alternative you sacrifice. Option D is the common trap: you could only have taken one of the other options anyway, so adding all of them together overstates the cost. Options A and B focus on money and time spent rather than on the alternative given up.

questions.question: Tunde can spend next week on holiday in Calabar, working at his job in Lagos, or repainting his flat. If he chooses the holiday, his opportunity cost is

options.a: both working and repainting the flat.
options.b: working or repainting the flat, whichever he would have done instead.
options.c: working, because he gives up his pay.
options.d: nothing, because he will enjoy the holiday.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative, the one Tunde would actually have chosen if he had not gone on holiday. Option A adds both alternatives together, but he could not have done both in the same week. Option C assumes work is the next best choice just because it pays, and option D is wrong because enjoying a choice does not make it free.

questions.question: The night before a test, Bisi goes to a party instead of studying and scores 60 percent. Had she studied, she would have scored 70 percent. What was the opportunity cost of the party?
questions.explanation: By going to the party Bisi gave up the extra marks that studying would have earned her: 70 - 60 = 10 percentage points. Options B and C give whole scores rather than the difference she sacrificed. Option D ignores that the evening had a better alternative use.

questions.question: On Saturday morning Chidi ranks his options in this order: go to the library, go to the gym, have breakfast with friends, sleep late. If he goes to the library, his opportunity cost is

options.a: going to the gym, having breakfast with friends and sleeping late.
options.c: zero, because using the library is free.
options.d: impossible to tell from the information given.

questions.explanation: The library is his first choice, so his opportunity cost is his second-ranked option, the gym. Option A lists every other option, but opportunity cost is only the next best one. Option C confuses a zero money price with zero cost, and option D is wrong because the ranking gives us exactly what we need.

questions.question: Femi and Ngozi are each given free tickets to the same film and both decide to go. Which statement is correct?

options.a: Both face an opportunity cost, because each could have done something else with the time.
options.b: Both face exactly the same opportunity cost, because they are doing the same thing.
options.c: Their opportunity cost cannot be worked out, because the tickets were free.
options.d: Their opportunity cost is zero, because the tickets were free.

questions.explanation: Even a free ticket uses up time that could have gone to another activity, so each person gives up something to watch the film. Option B is wrong because their next best alternatives may differ, so their opportunity costs need not be the same. Options C and D confuse a zero money price with a zero opportunity cost.

questions.question: By deciding to attend a lecture, you know you are giving up the chance to watch a film at home. You are applying the idea of
questions.explanation: Recognising what you give up when you make a choice is exactly what opportunity cost means. Option B, the fallacy of composition, is assuming what is true for one person is true for everyone. Option C, the post hoc fallacy, is assuming that because one event came first it caused the other, and option D has nothing to do with a personal choice.

questions.question: Adaeze takes a holiday that costs her N200,000. While away she misses work where she would have earned N75,000. The opportunity cost of the holiday is
questions.explanation: The full cost includes the money spent plus the earnings given up: N200,000 + N75,000 = N275,000. Option A counts only the spending and option B counts only the lost wages. Option D subtracts the two, but both are sacrifices, so they are added.

questions.question: The idea of opportunity cost emphasises that

options.a: there may be such a thing as a free lunch.
options.b: some people will not make the most of life's chances because they fail to reach their goals.
options.c: managers do not always spot profit opportunities quickly enough.
options.d: every decision about using a resource involves a costly choice.

questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, using one for any purpose means giving up its next best use, so every choice carries a cost. Option A contradicts this idea, which is often summed up as 'there is no free lunch.' Options B and C use the word 'opportunity' in an everyday sense that has nothing to do with the economic concept.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an example of opportunity cost?

options.a: By spending Thursday night preparing for an economics test, a student could not finish her accounting assignment.
options.b: Because Musa used all his leave days to renovate his house, he could not visit his family in Kano.
options.c: Because Halima now earns a higher salary, she can afford a new car even though she is moving into a bigger flat.
options.d: By choosing to study full time, Ifeanyi had to stop working as an electrician and gave up his earnings.

questions.explanation: Option C describes Halima affording more because her income rose; nothing is being given up, so no opportunity cost is shown. Options A, B and D each describe a choice where one thing was sacrificed to get another: the assignment, the trip to Kano and the electrician's earnings.

questions.question: Between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m., Amaka can watch a football match, attend a concert, or go to a book reading. She chooses the concert and decides that if she had not gone, she would have watched the match. Her opportunity cost of the concert is

options.a: watching the match and going to the book reading.

questions.explanation: Amaka tells us her next best alternative is the football match, so that is what she gives up by going to the concert. Option A wrongly adds the book reading too, which she would not have chosen anyway. Option D names the time used, but opportunity cost is measured by the best alternative use of that time, not the hours themselves.

questions.question: When the government uses resources to build a dam, those resources can no longer be used to build a highway. This illustrates
questions.explanation: Resources used for the dam are no longer available for the highway, so the highway is what is sacrificed, which is opportunity cost. Option A refers to how prices allocate resources, not to a single trade-off. Options B and D are unrelated: macroeconomics is the study of the whole economy and the fallacy of composition is a reasoning error.

questions.question: Kemi is thinking about taking holiday courses. Fees and books cost N120,000, accommodation N40,000 and food N30,000. If she skips the courses, she lives at home for free, spends only N10,000 on food and works full time earning N500,000. If she takes the courses she can still work part time, earning at most N100,000. What is her opportunity cost of taking the courses?
questions.explanation: Count only what changes because of the courses: fees and books N120,000 + accommodation N40,000 + extra food (30,000 - 10,000) = N20,000 + lost earnings (500,000 - 100,000) = N400,000, giving N580,000. Option A counts only the lost earnings and option B counts only the spending. Option C adds the full N500,000 wage and all the food, ignoring the part-time pay she keeps and the food she would buy anyway.

questions.question: After graduating, Seun accepts a job paying N4.5 million a year. His other offers were from a supermarket chain at N3.8 million and a consulting firm at N4.2 million, and of those two he preferred the consulting firm. What is his opportunity cost of the job he accepted?

options.a: The N4.5 million he will earn in the job he accepted.
options.b: The N4.2 million from the consulting firm.
options.c: The N3.8 million from the supermarket chain.
options.d: The N4.2 million from the consulting firm plus the N3.8 million from the supermarket.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, and Seun ranked the consulting job above the supermarket job, so it is the N4.2 million offer. Option A is what he gains, not what he gives up. Option D adds both offers, but he could only have taken one of them.

questions.question: On graduating, Dayo can play professional football for N200 million a year or coach for N5 million a year, and he chooses football. Eight years later, although he could keep playing for N200 million a year, he quits to act in films for N300 million a year. His opportunity cost of football at graduation was ____, and of acting eight years later was ____.
questions.explanation: At graduation the best alternative to football was coaching, worth N5 million. Eight years later the best alternative to acting is the football career he gives up, worth N200 million. Option C uses the income from the chosen activity each time, but opportunity cost is always the value of what is given up.

questions.question: Zainab has already spent 5 hours cleaning her room. When she decides whether to clean for one more hour, she is applying the principle of
questions.explanation: Deciding whether to do one more hour of an activity is a choice at the margin: she weighs the extra benefit of that hour against its extra cost. Option A, scarcity, explains why choices are needed but is not the principle being used here. Option B means 'other things being equal,' a tool for analysis, not a way of making this decision.

questions.question: Marginal benefit is the

options.a: extra gain from one more unit of an activity.
options.b: extra cost of one more unit of an activity.
options.d: opportunity that has been given up.

questions.explanation: Marginal benefit measures the additional gain from one more unit of something, like one more plate of food or one more hour of study. Option B describes marginal cost, the mirror image. Options C and D describe opportunity cost, which is a cost, not a benefit.

questions.question: Your employer asks you to work overtime and offers N1,800 for each hour beyond 40 hours a week. Each of the first 40 hours still pays the usual N1,500. In naira terms, what is the marginal benefit of each overtime hour?
questions.explanation: The marginal benefit of an overtime hour is what that extra hour pays you, which is N1,800. Option B is the difference between the two wage rates, but you receive the full N1,800 for the extra hour, not just the increase. Option C is the pay for a normal hour, not the extra one.

questions.question: A student studies for 2 hours a day and is deciding whether to add a third hour. Her marginal benefit

options.a: depends on the grade she finally gets in the exam.
options.b: is the benefit she gets from studying all 3 hours.
options.c: is the benefit she gets from the extra hour.
options.d: is greater than her marginal cost.

questions.explanation: Marginal benefit is the gain from the additional unit, so here it is the benefit of the third hour only. Option B describes the total benefit of all three hours. Option D cannot be known until she weighs it; it is true only if she actually decides the extra hour is worth it.

questions.question: You study economics for 2 hours a day and your score is 85 percent. You add an extra hour a day and your score rises to 90 percent. Your marginal benefit is the

options.a: 90 percent score that you now get.
options.b: extra hour per day spent studying.

questions.explanation: Marginal benefit is the gain from the extra hour of study, which is the rise in your score from 85 to 90 percent, or 5 points. Option A is the total score you end up with, not the extra gain that the added hour brings. Options B and D describe the time spent studying, which is the cost side, not the benefit.

questions.question: Marginal cost is the

options.a: cost of a small increase in an activity.
options.c: cost of an activity minus its benefits.
options.d: cost of all the alternatives given up.

questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the extra cost from a small increase in an activity, such as producing one more unit. Option B is total cost, the cost of everything. Option D is wrong twice: opportunity cost is only the best alternative, and marginal cost is about the extra unit.

questions.question: A production manager at a Lagos electronics firm is deciding whether to make a few more television sets. She is choosing at the margin when she compares

options.a: total revenue from all sets with the total cost of producing all of them.
options.b: the extra revenue from the additional sets with the extra cost of producing them.
options.c: the extra revenue from the additional sets with the average cost of producing them.
options.d: her firm's televisions with those of rival firms.

questions.explanation: A marginal decision compares the extra revenue from the additional units with the extra cost of making them. Option A uses totals, which do not tell her whether the next few sets are worth producing. Option C mixes a marginal benefit with an average cost, which is not the right comparison.

questions.question: Managers at a Lagos phone assembler are deciding whether to raise output by 4,000 handsets a month. Doing so will increase revenue by N10 million a month and costs by N9 million a month, and total monthly profit will be N30 million. The managers

options.a: should go ahead because the firm will make a large total profit.
options.b: should go ahead because the marginal benefit of the extra output exceeds its marginal cost.
options.c: should not go ahead because it costs too much.
options.d: cannot decide without knowing total profit before the increase.

questions.explanation: The extra revenue (N10 million) is greater than the extra cost (N9 million), so the change adds N1 million to profit and is worth doing. Option A gets the decision right for the wrong reason, because the size of total profit does not tell you whether this particular change pays. Option D is wrong because the marginal figures alone are enough to decide.

questions.question: A cleaning company is deciding whether to add one more worker to its team. The marginal cost of hiring this worker depends on the

options.a: total amount paid to the new worker.
options.b: total amount paid to all the workers already hired.
options.c: total amount paid to all workers, new and old.
options.d: extra revenue the new worker brings in.

questions.explanation: The marginal cost of hiring is the extra cost of that one additional worker, which is what the firm pays the new worker. Options B and C include wages already being paid, which do not change with this decision. Option D describes the marginal benefit of hiring, not its cost.

questions.question: A shop sells 5 pens for N150 and 6 pens for N175. What is the marginal cost of the sixth pen?
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit: N175 - N150 = N25. Option C is the total cost of all six pens and option B is the total for five. Option D wrongly adds the two totals.

questions.question: If the marginal cost of an activity is greater than its marginal benefit, then

options.a: the activity will take place because of the high marginal cost.
options.b: the costs of the alternatives given up must rise.
options.c: an alternative action will be chosen.
options.d: the person must focus on the total benefits of the activity.

questions.explanation: When the extra cost of doing more exceeds the extra benefit, a rational person will not do that extra unit and will choose something else instead. Option A gets the logic backwards, since a high cost discourages the activity. Option D is wrong because decisions at the margin depend on extra benefit and extra cost, not totals.

questions.question: To decide whether to travel to Badagry beach during the semester break, you should

options.a: compare the marginal cost with the marginal benefit of the trip.

questions.explanation: Choosing whether to take one trip is a decision at the margin, so you weigh what the trip adds against what it costs you. Options B, C and D are rules for avoiding mistakes in economic reasoning, not a method for making a personal choice.

questions.question: A shop in Yaba opens from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays. The owner is deciding whether to stay open one more hour each evening. The owner's marginal benefit

options.a: is the benefit from staying open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.
options.b: depends on the revenue earned during the day.
options.c: must be at least equal to the marginal cost if the owner decides to stay open.
options.d: is the benefit from staying open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

questions.explanation: Marginal benefit is the extra benefit from the extra hour, and a sensible owner stays open that hour only if its benefit is at least as large as its cost. Option A describes the benefit of the whole day from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., which is a total, not a marginal, benefit. Option D is also a total for an even longer day, and option B ignores that only the extra hour matters.

questions.question: If the marginal cost of an activity falls or its marginal benefit rises, a person will

options.c: not change how much of the activity they do.

questions.explanation: A fall in marginal cost or a rise in marginal benefit makes extra units of the activity more worthwhile, so people do more of it. This is how incentives work. Option A is the response to the opposite changes, and option D would only happen if the activity stopped being worth doing at all.

questions.question: Suppose Lagos State promises a tax cut to a firm if it stays in Lagos rather than moving to another state. This policy is ____, designed to make the ____ of the firm staying in Lagos.

options.a: an incentive; marginal benefit exceed the marginal cost
options.b: an incentive; marginal cost exceed the marginal benefit
options.c: a command; marginal benefit exceed the marginal cost
options.d: a command; marginal cost exceed the marginal benefit

questions.explanation: A tax cut is an incentive, a reward that changes the firm's choice, and it raises the benefit of staying so that it outweighs the cost. Options C and D call it a command, but the state is not ordering the firm to stay. Option B gets the direction wrong, because a firm stays only when benefit exceeds cost.

questions.question: Obinna scored 50 percent in a test. An extra-credit task would raise his score by 20 percentage points but would take 10 hours. Obinna will do the task if he values

options.a: the 20 percentage points more than the 10 hours of his time.
options.b: the 10 hours of his time more than the 20 percentage points.
options.c: the 70 percentage points more than the 10 hours of his time.

questions.explanation: The marginal benefit of the task is the extra 20 points and its marginal cost is the 10 hours, so he does it only if the points are worth more to him than the time. Option C uses his total score of 70, but the first 50 points are already his and are not affected by this decision. Option B describes when he would skip the task.

questions.question: When the government spends its tax revenue on national security, this choice

options.a: involves giving up other goods and services, such as education, for more security.
options.b: shows that scarcity does not always exist.
options.c: involves no trade-off, because security is necessary.
options.d: mainly affects who gets the goods and services produced.

questions.explanation: Tax revenue is limited, so naira spent on security cannot also be spent on schools or hospitals, which is a trade-off. Option C is wrong because even a necessary item still has an opportunity cost. Option B gets it backwards, since the trade-off exists only because of scarcity.

questions.question: Making a choice at the margin means

options.a: letting someone else decide for you.
options.b: waiting until the last minute to decide.
options.c: deciding whether to do a little more or a little less of an activity.
options.d: deciding by comparing total benefit with total cost.

questions.explanation: A marginal choice is about one more or one less unit, such as one extra hour of study. Option D is the tempting one, but margin decisions compare the extra benefit with the extra cost of that small change, not the totals. Options A and B use 'margin' in an everyday sense that has nothing to do with economics.

questions.question: For two months you studied economics one hour a day. You now decide to study two hours a day. During those two months,

options.a: the marginal cost of an hour of economics study must have been greater than its marginal benefit.
options.b: the marginal cost of studying economics must have fallen.
options.c: the marginal benefit of an hour of economics study must have been greater than its marginal cost.
options.d: the opportunity cost of studying economics must have risen.

questions.explanation: You chose to study one hour a day, which you would only do if that hour was worth more to you than it cost. Option A describes a case in which you would not have studied at all. Options B and D talk about changes that may explain your new decision, but nothing in the question tells us they happened.

questions.question: The Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria must choose whether to spend an afternoon meeting the Minister of Finance or a committee of the National Assembly. This reflects the fact that the Governor
questions.explanation: The Governor has limited time and cannot do both meetings at once, so he faces scarcity and must choose. Option C is about reacting to rewards or penalties, which the question does not describe. Options B and D refer to factors of production, not the problem of limited time.

questions.question: A TV station decides to produce another season of a reality show instead of a new drama series. The station is

options.b: facing no trade-off, because air time is unlimited.
options.d: facing no scarcity, because many actors are looking for work.

questions.explanation: Picking which programme to make is a 'what to produce' decision. Option B is wrong because air time is limited, so choosing one show means giving up another. Option C would apply to how the show is produced, and option D is wrong because the station still has limited money and time.

questions.question: When an airline encourages customers to book tickets online instead of by phone, it is

options.c: making a choice only in the social interest.

questions.explanation: Switching from phone bookings to online bookings changes the method used to provide the service, which is the 'how to produce' question. Option A would apply if the airline were changing which services it offers. Option C is wrong because the airline is mainly acting in its own interest, for example to cut costs.

questions.question: When a football club pays a new player a N100 million signing bonus, it is answering
questions.explanation: Paying a player a bonus decides who receives income and therefore who gets to enjoy goods and services, which is the 'for whom' question. Options A and B deal with which goods are produced and how, which the bonus does not decide.

questions.question: One political party wants higher income tax on the highest earners, while another wants to keep the current tax structure. The parties are answering the ____ question.
questions.explanation: Income tax affects how much income different groups keep, and therefore who gets the goods and services produced, which is the 'for whom' question. Options B and C are about which goods are made and how they are made, which the tax debate does not decide directly.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about scarcity is correct?

options.a: Scarcity affects only people who are in need.
options.b: Scarcity affects both the rich and the poor.
options.c: Rich people do not face scarcity because they can buy whatever they want.

questions.explanation: Scarcity means wants are greater than the resources available to satisfy them, and that is true for everyone, rich or poor. Options D, C and A confuse scarcity with poverty; even a very rich person has limited time and must choose how to use it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the link between scarcity and opportunity cost?

options.a: Scarcity and opportunity cost are unrelated ideas.
options.b: Opportunity cost exists only when there is no scarcity.
options.c: Scarcity arises because of opportunity costs.
options.d: Opportunity costs arise because of scarcity.

questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce we must choose, and every choice means giving up the next best alternative, which is opportunity cost. Option C reverses the cause and effect, which is the most common mistake. Options A and B ignore that scarcity is the very reason opportunity costs exist.

questions.question: Macroeconomics is the study of

options.a: aggregate variables such as national output and unemployment.
options.b: the price of a single good in one market.
options.c: how one firm decides how many workers to hire.
options.d: the choices of individual households and firms.

questions.explanation: Macroeconomics looks at the economy as a whole, using aggregates such as total output, unemployment and the general price level. Options D, B and C describe individual decision makers or single markets, which belong to microeconomics.

questions.question: A country that builds a dam using mainly labour rather than mainly machines is answering which basic economic question?
questions.explanation: Choosing between labour and machines is a choice of production method, which is the 'how' question. Option A would apply if the country were deciding whether to build the dam at all, and option D is about who receives the output. Option B is not one of the basic economic questions.

questions.question: Ada buys a N2,000 cinema ticket instead of two novels that would have cost the same amount. What is her opportunity cost of going to the cinema?

options.a: Nothing, since she enjoyed the film.
options.b: The film plus the two novels.
options.c: The two novels she did not buy.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, and here that is the two novels the money could have bought. Option D names what she chose rather than what she gave up. Option A is wrong because enjoying a choice does not make it free, and option B adds in the thing she actually chose.

questions.question: Which of the following is a normative economics statement?

options.a: Next year inflation rate will be under 4%
options.b: Consumers will buy more kerosene over Christmas holiday even if its price is 10 naira higher than it was during the Independence holiday.
options.c: The government cuts in welfare spending impose an unfair hardship on the poor.
options.d: The current agricultural output surplus is the result of federal policies.

questions.explanation: A normative statement is a value judgement about what ought to be, and calling welfare cuts an 'unfair hardship' is a matter of opinion. Options A, B and D are positive statements: they are claims about what will happen or what caused something, which can be checked against facts.

questions.question: How people should behave is
questions.explanation: Normative economics deals with how people or society ought or should behave, so it involves value judgements. Options A and B, micro and macroeconomics, describe the level of study (individual units versus the whole economy), and both can be either positive or normative.

questions.question: Positive economic principle predicts
questions.explanation: Positive economics describes and predicts how people will actually behave, using statements that can be checked against facts. Option B, how people should behave, is normative economics. Options C and D are not what positive economics predicts.

questions.question: Constant (or parameter) is

options.a: a quantity that is fixed in value

questions.explanation: A constant (or parameter) is a quantity whose value is fixed within a given model, such as the 50 in Q = 50 - 2P. Options B and C are variables whose values change, and option D is also a variable, not a fixed value.

questions.question: Ceteris paribus means
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus is Latin for 'other things being equal', meaning all other factors are held constant while we study the effect of one variable. Option C, technology being given, is just one example of something held constant, not the full meaning. Options A and B do not express the idea at all.

questions.question: The steps involved in constructing economic models are:
questions.explanation: Building an economic model starts with abstraction (simplifying reality by keeping only key variables), then deduction (working out logical predictions from the assumptions), and finally testing (checking the predictions against real data). Options A, B and D put these steps in the wrong order.

questions.question: The aspect of economics that deals with aggregate variables is refer to ________
questions.explanation: Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole, using aggregate variables such as national income, inflation and unemployment. Option D, microeconomics, studies individual consumers, firms and markets. Options A and C are about whether statements are factual or value-based, not about the scale of study.

questions.question: The branch of economics that studies individual markets, consumers and firms is called
questions.explanation: Microeconomics focuses on small units of the economy, such as how one market sets the price of rice or how a single firm decides its output. Option A, macroeconomics, studies the economy as a whole instead. Option D measures total output for the whole country, so it belongs to macroeconomics.

questions.question: An economic hypothesis is best tested by:

options.c: Whether it can accurately predict outcomes that follow logically from its assumptions

questions.explanation: A hypothesis is judged by checking its predictions against real-world evidence: if the outcomes it predicts actually happen, it is supported. Option A is tempting, but all models simplify reality, so realistic assumptions alone do not prove a hypothesis right, and agreement among economists (D) is not a test at all.

questions.question: Which school of thought emphasised the normative (ethical) side of economics?
questions.explanation: The German historical school argued that economics should be concerned with ethics and what ought to be, and should be studied through history rather than pure abstract reasoning. Option B is wrong because Robbins insisted that economics is a positive science that should stay neutral between ends, and the classical economists (A) also stressed a mainly positive, deductive approach.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about methods of economic analysis is correct?

options.a: The deductive method moves from general principles to particular conclusions
options.b: The inductive method moves from general principles to particular conclusions
options.c: The classical economists mainly used the inductive method
options.d: The deductive method depends mainly on experimentation

questions.explanation: Deduction starts from general assumptions, such as people seeking to maximise satisfaction, and reasons down to specific conclusions. Option B swaps the two methods, since induction moves from particular facts to general conclusions, and the classical economists actually favoured deduction, which rules out C.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of the deductive method?

options.c: It assumes economic conditions are always changing
options.d: It was strongly supported by the historical school

questions.explanation: The deductive method reasons logically from simplified assumptions, so its conclusions are abstract and may be far from real-life conditions. Option B is the opposite of this, and D is wrong because the historical school favoured the inductive method and criticised deduction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of the inductive method?
questions.explanation: The inductive method collects and studies real facts and data before arriving at general conclusions, which makes it empirical. Option A better describes the deductive method, which works from assumed premises, and C is wrong because induction relies on observation and testing.

questions.question: Which statement about economic models is correct?

options.a: The predictions of economic models cannot be tested against evidence
options.b: Models turn verbal statements into more precise, scientific forms
options.c: Models do not rely on any assumptions
options.d: Economic models cover every aspect of the economy at once

questions.explanation: A model expresses an economic idea in a precise form, such as an equation like Qd = 100 - 2P or a graph, so it can be analysed and tested. Option A is wrong because predictions can be checked against data, C is wrong because every model rests on simplifying assumptions, and D is wrong because models deliberately focus on a few variables.

questions.question: Microeconomic theory studies how a free enterprise economy determines:

options.c: The prices of resources (factors of production)

questions.explanation: Microeconomics covers price theory in full: product pricing, which includes both goods and services, and factor pricing, such as wages, rent and interest. Option A is true but incomplete, so it is not the best answer when D includes it along with services and resources.

questions.question: Which aspect of a tax is a question of normative economics?

options.a: Who finally bears the burden of the tax
options.c: How the tax affects people's incentive to work

questions.explanation: Normative economics deals with value judgements about what ought to be, and whether a tax is fair depends on opinions about justice. Options A and C are positive questions because they can be checked with evidence, which also rules out D.

questions.question: Microeconomics deals mainly with:

options.a: Comparative statics, general equilibrium and positive economics
options.b: Comparative statics, partial equilibrium and normative economics
options.c: Dynamics, partial equilibrium and positive economics
