questions.explanation: The Coase theorem says private bargaining leads to efficient outcomes provided property rights are clearly defined and transaction costs are low. A corrective tax is a government remedy for externalities, which is the alternative to private bargaining rather than its condition.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: A cement factory in Ewekoro pollutes nearby farms. Which of the following would NOT help internalize this externality?

options.a: A subsidy for cleaner production methods
options.b: A tax on each tonne of pollution
options.c: A system of tradable emissions permits

questions.explanation: A price ceiling on cement controls its selling price but does nothing to make the factory bear the cost of its pollution. Taxes, subsidies and emissions trading are the tools used to internalize externalities such as pollution.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: A policy that sets a limit on total carbon emissions and allows firms to buy and sell emission permits is called
questions.explanation: Cap-and-trade sets a ceiling on total emissions and lets firms trade permits, and it is one of the climate-change policies studied in energy and environmental economics. A tariff is a tax on imports and has nothing to do with emission permits.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a renewable resource?
questions.explanation: Renewable resources such as forests and fisheries can regenerate if managed well. Tin ore, limestone and gold are minerals, which are non-renewable because once extracted they are not replaced.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of transaction cost studied in institutional economics?
questions.explanation: Depreciation is the wearing out of capital equipment in production, not a cost of carrying out an exchange. Transaction costs are the costs of searching for partners, negotiating deals and enforcing agreements.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: In institutional economics, which of the following is an example of an informal institution?

options.b: Cultural norms about how traders settle debts
options.c: A Central Bank of Nigeria regulation
options.d: The Companies and Allied Matters Act

questions.explanation: Informal institutions are unwritten rules such as norms and culture, so customs about settling debts among traders fit this category. An Act, a regulation or a tax law are formal rules backed by the state.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: Path dependence, the idea that past choices shape how institutions develop, belongs to
questions.explanation: Theories of institutional change, including path dependence, explain how institutions evolve and why past decisions constrain present ones. The Heckscher-Ohlin theory is about trade and factor endowments, not institutions.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: An economist studies how corruption, weak property rights and information asymmetry affect how markets work in Nigeria. She is working mainly in
questions.explanation: Property rights, market functioning (including information asymmetry), and governance and corruption are key areas of institutional economics. Development economics is also concerned with poor countries, but these specific topics are the core of the institutional field.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: A Lagos company automatically enrols new staff in a savings scheme unless they choose to opt out, which raises saving. This is an example of

options.d: a Pigovian tax in welfare economics

questions.explanation: Behavioural economics combines psychology and economics, and nudging, such as automatic enrolment in savings, gently steers choices without forcing them. A Pigovian tax changes behaviour by raising costs on harmful activities, which is quite different from changing the default option.

questions.topic: Major Areas of Specialization in Economics
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the behavioural biases studied in behavioural economics?
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage is a principle of international trade about lower opportunity cost, not a psychological bias. Loss aversion, the endowment effect, present bias and herd behaviour are the biases behavioural economics examines.

questions.question: Diamond is non essential to life and yet command a great price while air is essential to life but has no economic price to a great extent, this is
questions.explanation: The paradox of value (the diamond-water paradox) is the puzzle that essential things like air or water are cheap while non-essentials like diamonds are expensive. It is explained by scarcity and marginal utility: diamonds are scarce, so the last unit is highly valued. Options A and C are not recognised names for this idea.

questions.question: The following are the early classical theories of income distribution except
questions.explanation: Marginal productivity theory came later, from the neoclassical economists, who explained factor payments by the value of what the last unit of a factor adds to output. Option B (subsistence theory) and option C (wages fund theory) are early classical theories of wages. Option D, the residual claimant theory, is also an older theory than marginal productivity.

questions.question: A resource allocation from which it is impossible to move to another allocation that makes some people better off without making anybody worse off is termed
questions.explanation: Pareto optimality is a situation where it is impossible to make someone better off without making someone else worse off. Option B, Arrow's impossibility theorem, is about combining individual preferences into social choices. Option C, equity, is about fairness, not efficiency.

questions.question: When there is an optimal distribution of goods and services, taking into account consumers' preferences, this is known as:
questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency occurs when resources produce the mix of goods and services that consumers value most, so output matches consumer preferences (where price equals marginal cost). Option A, full utilisation, only means all resources are employed, which can still produce the wrong mix of goods. Option B, effectiveness, is a general word, so option D, all of the above, is also wrong.

questions.question: The book 'Principles of Economics' (1890) was written by:
questions.explanation: Alfred Marshall wrote Principles of Economics, which introduced ideas such as partial equilibrium and gave the welfare definition of economics. Option A, Keynes, wrote The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, and D, Pigou, was Marshall's student.

questions.question: Who is widely known as the father of economics?
questions.explanation: Adam Smith is called the father of economics because his book The Wealth of Nations (1776) laid the foundation of economics as a separate discipline. Ricardo (B) and Marshall (A) built on classical ideas later, and Keynes (D) is regarded as the father of modern macroeconomics.

questions.question: The Wealth of Nations was written by:
questions.explanation: Adam Smith wrote An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, the classic work that explained the division of labour and the 'invisible hand' of the market. Marshall (A) is known for Principles of Economics, and Robbins (D) for the scarcity definition of economics.

questions.question: Classical economics developed in the late 18th and early 19th centuries largely as a reaction to
questions.explanation: Classical economics arose in the late 18th and early 19th centuries as a reaction to mercantilism and feudal systems. Neoclassical marginalism came later, in the late 19th century, as a refinement of classical ideas, so classical thought could not have been reacting to it.

questions.question: Which of the following economists is NOT usually grouped with the classical school?
questions.explanation: Leon Walras was a neoclassical economist of the late 19th century, best known for general equilibrium theory. Adam Smith, David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus are the leading classical economists.

questions.question: Which of the following did classical economists emphasise?

options.a: Extensive state control of prices and output
options.b: Marginal utility as the only basis of value
options.d: Free markets that regulate themselves with limited government

questions.explanation: Classical economists stressed free markets, self-regulation, a natural tendency towards equilibrium and limited government. Simultaneous equilibrium across all markets is Walras's general equilibrium idea from the neoclassical period.

questions.question: The classical idea that the value of a good is determined by the amount of labour required to produce it is the
questions.explanation: The labour theory of value holds that a good's value is set by the labour needed to produce it, and it is a core classical idea. Marginal utility theory came later with the neoclassical school, which located value in the extra satisfaction from the last unit.

questions.question: The idea that individuals pursuing their own self-interest in free markets are guided, as if by an unseen force, to promote the good of society is the

options.a: invisible hand, associated with Adam Smith
options.b: general equilibrium theory of Leon Walras
options.c: invisible hand, associated with David Ricardo
options.d: greatest happiness principle of Jeremy Bentham

questions.explanation: The invisible hand is Adam Smith's idea that self-interested behaviour in free markets ends up serving society. Bentham's greatest happiness principle is a utilitarian rule about maximizing happiness for the greatest number, not about market coordination.

questions.question: A shoe factory in Ikeja splits production so that one worker cuts leather, another stitches and a third fixes soles, and output per worker rises sharply. This illustrates Adam Smith's idea of
questions.explanation: Division of labour, emphasised by Adam Smith, means breaking production into specialised tasks so that productivity rises. Comparative advantage is Ricardo's idea about specialization between countries according to opportunity cost, not between workers within a factory.

questions.question: In what year was Adam Smith's An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations published?
questions.explanation: The Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776. The year 1817 is when Ricardo published Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, and 1798 is the year of Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population.

questions.question: Under Adam Smith's idea of laissez-faire, the role of government should be

options.a: expanded to owning the major industries
options.b: limited to functions such as defence and infrastructure
options.c: focused on redistributing all income equally
options.d: extended to fixing the prices of all goods

questions.explanation: Laissez-faire means leaving markets largely free, with government limited to tasks like defence and infrastructure. Fixing prices or owning major industries would be heavy state intervention, the opposite of laissez-faire.

questions.question: Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) was written by
questions.explanation: David Ricardo wrote Principles of Political Economy and Taxation in 1817. Alfred Marshall wrote a book with a similar-sounding title, Principles of Economics, but that appeared in 1890.

questions.question: David Ricardo argued that two countries can both gain from trade by specializing in what they produce relatively more efficiently

options.a: only if the government fixes the exchange rate
options.b: only if both countries have identical factor endowments
options.c: even if one country is less efficient in producing all goods
options.d: only if each country is more efficient in at least one good

questions.explanation: Ricardo's comparative advantage shows that trade benefits both countries even when one is less efficient at producing everything, because what matters is relative efficiency. Requiring each country to be more efficient in at least one good confuses comparative advantage with absolute advantage.

questions.question: David Ricardo's theory of rent predicts that as population rises,

options.b: food output grows faster than population

questions.explanation: Ricardo's theory of rent holds that landowners gain as population grows and the demand for land increases. Saying rent falls towards zero gets the direction wrong, since rising population pushes rents up.

questions.question: An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798) was written by
questions.explanation: Thomas Malthus published An Essay on the Principle of Population in 1798. David Ricardo was a fellow classical economist, but his main work is Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817).

questions.question: Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow

options.a: geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically
options.b: at the same rate as food supply
options.c: arithmetically while food supply grows geometrically
options.d: geometrically while food supply stays constant

questions.explanation: Malthus held that population grows geometrically while food grows only arithmetically, leading to poverty and famine unless population is checked. Reversing the two rates removes the very gap that drives his gloomy conclusion.

questions.question: In Malthus's population theory, which of the following is an example of moral restraint?

options.b: Delaying marriage and having fewer births
options.d: War reducing the number of people

questions.explanation: Moral restraint is the voluntary check of delaying marriage and having fewer children. Famine, disease and war are natural checks that reduce population after it has outgrown food supply.

questions.question: Which of the following is a natural check on population in Malthus's theory?
questions.explanation: Malthus's natural checks are famine, disease and war, which raise deaths when population outgrows food. Delayed marriage and fewer births by choice are forms of moral restraint, the voluntary check.

questions.question: Neoclassical economics emerged in the late 19th century as

options.c: the first school to study population
options.d: a rejection of all market analysis

questions.explanation: Neoclassical economics developed in the late 19th century as a refinement of classical economics, with leading figures such as Alfred Marshall and Leon Walras. The reaction to feudal systems describes classical economics, which came about a century earlier.

questions.question: The neoclassical approach that focuses on the value of an additional unit rather than on total value is called
questions.explanation: Marginalism focuses on marginal rather than total value, and it is a core neoclassical idea. The labour theory of value is a classical idea that ties value to the labour needed to make a good.

questions.question: A student lists the core ideas of the school led by Alfred Marshall and Leon Walras. Which entry on the list is wrong?
questions.explanation: The labour theory of value belongs to classical economics, not to the neoclassical school. Marginalism, utility theory, general equilibrium, market equilibrium and price theory are the neoclassical core ideas.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a core idea of classical economics?
questions.explanation: Marginalism, the focus on marginal rather than total value, is a neoclassical idea. Division of labour, the invisible hand and the labour theory of value are all core classical ideas, alongside comparative advantage and Malthus's population theory.

questions.question: The idea that consumers seek to maximize utility and that each additional unit of a good gives less satisfaction than the one before is part of
questions.explanation: Neoclassical utility theory assumes people maximize utility and that marginal utility diminishes as more is consumed. The classical labour theory of value explains value by labour input, not by consumers' satisfaction.

questions.question: Which economist developed general equilibrium theory, showing how all markets in an economy adjust simultaneously?
questions.explanation: Leon Walras developed general equilibrium theory, in which all markets adjust at the same time. Alfred Marshall is better known for price theory and analysing one market at a time, which is partial rather than general equilibrium.

questions.question: Elements of Pure Economics (1874), which used mathematical modelling to present general equilibrium theory, was written by
questions.explanation: Leon Walras wrote Elements of Pure Economics in 1874, presenting general equilibrium with mathematical models. Alfred Marshall's major work was Principles of Economics, published in 1890.

questions.question: Alfred Marshall argued that the price of a good is determined by

options.a: supply and cost of production alone
options.b: both demand, based on utility, and supply, based on cost
options.c: the amount of labour required alone

questions.explanation: Marshall held that demand (reflecting utility) and supply (reflecting cost) together determine price. Pointing to labour alone is the classical labour theory of value, which Marshall moved beyond.

questions.question: Which economist is associated with developing price elasticity of demand, supply curves and the distinction between short-run and long-run costs?
questions.explanation: Alfred Marshall's price theory introduced price elasticity of demand, supply curves and the short-run versus long-run cost distinction. Leon Walras is known for general equilibrium across all markets rather than these single-market tools.

questions.question: Utilitarianism, the view that the best actions and policies are those that maximize happiness for the greatest number, is associated with

options.a: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill

questions.explanation: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill are the leading utilitarians, holding that policies should maximize happiness for the greatest number. Pigou and Pareto are associated with welfare economics, which builds on similar concerns but is a separate school.

questions.question: Jeremy Bentham's principle of utility holds that human behaviour is driven by

options.a: the need to keep population below food supply
options.b: the labour required to produce goods
options.c: the desire to make others better off first
options.d: the pursuit of pleasure and the avoidance of pain

questions.explanation: Bentham's principle of utility says people act to pursue pleasure and avoid pain, which leads to the greatest happiness principle. Labour required to produce goods relates to the classical labour theory of value, not to Bentham's theory of behaviour.

questions.question: The Lagos State Government approves a new bridge only after showing that its total benefits to society exceed its total costs. This approach reflects the utilitarian idea of
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis, a utilitarian idea, justifies a policy when its benefits exceed its costs. Pareto efficiency is a stricter test that requires no one be made worse off, which a project that simply has net benefits need not satisfy.

questions.question: How did John Stuart Mill's view on the distribution of wealth differ from Jeremy Bentham's?

options.a: Both rejected any concern with the well-being of society
options.b: Both held that wealth should be shared only by landowners
options.c: Bentham argued for reducing inequality, while Mill showed little concern for distribution
options.d: Mill argued for reducing inequality, while Bentham showed little concern for distribution

questions.explanation: Mill extended Bentham's ideas to society's well-being and individual freedom and argued for reducing inequality, while Bentham paid little attention to how wealth was distributed. Swapping the two thinkers reverses their actual positions.

questions.question: Welfare economics, which combines efficiency with fairness in studying how resources can be allocated to improve social welfare, is associated with

options.b: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill

questions.explanation: Welfare economics is linked with Arthur Pigou and Vilfredo Pareto, and it combines efficiency with fairness. Bentham and Mill are the utilitarians, whose ideas on happiness influenced welfare economics but who form a separate school.

questions.question: A corrective tax placed on a harmful activity, such as pollution from a factory in Agbara, so that the producer bears the full social cost, is called a
questions.explanation: A Pigovian tax, named after Arthur Pigou, is a corrective tax on harmful activities that makes producers internalize the social cost. A tariff is a tax on imports, which has nothing to do with correcting pollution.

questions.question: Arthur Pigou identified market failures such as

options.a: externalities such as pollution, and public goods
options.b: the division of labour and specialization
options.c: diminishing marginal utility and consumer surplus

questions.explanation: Pigou identified externalities such as pollution, and public goods, as market failures that government can correct with taxes and subsidies. Geometric population growth and famine belong to Malthus's population theory, not to Pigou.

questions.question: In welfare economics, a social welfare function is used to

options.a: measure the labour required to produce each good
options.b: calculate the geometric growth rate of population
options.c: aggregate individual utilities while considering distribution and equity
options.d: set the exchange rate between two currencies

questions.explanation: A social welfare function combines individual utilities into a measure of society's welfare and takes distribution and equity into account. Measuring the labour required to produce goods is the classical labour theory of value, not a welfare tool.

questions.question: Two students share a fixed stock of textbooks. Any change in the allocation that helps Ada would make Bola worse off. This allocation is

options.a: Pareto inefficient, since Ada could gain

questions.explanation: An allocation is Pareto efficient when no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off, which is exactly the situation described. Calling it inefficient because Ada could gain ignores that her gain would come at Bola's expense.

questions.question: Use Table 1 (Demand and Supply Schedule: Price / Quantity Demand (Qd) / Quantity Supply (Qs): 2.00 / 70 / 10; 3.50 / 60 / 20; 4.00 / 50 / 30; 4.50 / 40 / 40; 5.00 / 30 / 50; 5.50 / 20 / 60; 6.00 / 10 / 70). Equilibrium price is
questions.explanation: Equilibrium price is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and in the table that happens at a price of 4.50, where Qd = Qs = 40. At 2.00 (option A) demand is 70 but supply is only 10, a big shortage, while at 5.50 (option B) supply of 60 is far above demand of 20. Option D (1.50) is not even in the table.

questions.question: Use Table 1 (Demand and Supply Schedule: Price / Quantity Demand (Qd) / Quantity Supply (Qs): 2.00 / 70 / 10; 3.50 / 60 / 20; 4.00 / 50 / 30; 4.50 / 40 / 40; 5.00 / 30 / 50; 5.50 / 20 / 60; 6.00 / 10 / 70). Equilibrium quantity is
questions.explanation: At the equilibrium price of 4.50, buyers want 40 units and sellers offer 40 units, so the equilibrium quantity is 40. Options B (20) and C (30) are quantities found at other prices, where the market is not clearing, and option D (0) has no basis in the table.

questions.question: Use Table 1 (Demand and Supply Schedule: Price / Quantity Demand (Qd) / Quantity Supply (Qs): 2.00 / 70 / 10; 3.50 / 60 / 20; 4.00 / 50 / 30; 4.50 / 40 / 40; 5.00 / 30 / 50; 5.50 / 20 / 60; 6.00 / 10 / 70). At price = 5.00
questions.explanation: At a price of 5.00 the table shows Qd = 30 and Qs = 50, so supply exceeds demand by 50 - 30 = 20, which is a surplus. Option A is wrong because supply equals demand only at 4.50, and option B gets the size of the gap wrong. Option C reverses the gap; excess demand happens at prices below 4.50, not above it.

questions.question: A movement along the demand curve indicates that a different quantity is demanded because there has been a change in:
questions.explanation: A movement along a demand curve happens only when the good's own price changes, all other things held constant. Changes in income, taste or population (options A, B and D) are non-price determinants, and they shift the whole demand curve instead of moving along it.

questions.question: A bodily shift in demand can be caused by a
questions.explanation: A bodily shift of the whole demand curve is caused by non-price factors such as income, taste and population. Option A is wrong because a change in the good's own price only causes a movement along the demand curve. Option C is about sellers, not buyers, and option D is a concept from indifference analysis, not a cause of demand shifts.

questions.question: A rise in the demand for a commodity can be represented by a bodily shift of the demand curve to

options.c: a point higher up the same curve
options.d: a point lower down the same curve

questions.explanation: An increase in demand means buyers want more at every price, so the entire demand curve moves to the right. Option B, a shift to the left, shows a fall in demand. Options C and D describe movements along the same curve, which come from a change in the good's own price, not a shift.

questions.question: A leftward shift of the demand curve means a
questions.explanation: When the demand curve shifts to the left, buyers want less at every price, which is a fall (decrease) in demand. Option B describes a rightward shift. Option C is wrong because a movement along the curve comes from a change in the good's own price, not a shift, and option D has nothing to do with the direction of a shift.

questions.question: A table that shows the price and quantity of a commodity demanded per unit of time is referred to as
questions.explanation: A demand schedule is a table listing different prices and the quantity demanded at each price per period of time. Option D, the demand curve, shows the same information as a graph rather than a table. Option A, a time series, is data recorded over time, and option B, the slope, is a property of the curve.

questions.question: The quantity of a good offered in a market at all possible prices per unit of time is referred to as
questions.explanation: Supply is the quantity of a good that sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at all possible prices per period of time. Option D, quantity demanded, refers to buyers, not sellers. Option A, price elasticity, measures responsiveness, and option B, market offer, is not a standard economic term.

questions.question: If a negatively sloped demand curve remains unchanged, a leftward shift of the supply curve causes

options.a: rise in equilibrium quantity and no change in price
options.b: fall in equilibrium quantity and a fall in price
options.c: fall in price and a rise in quantity
options.d: decrease in equilibrium quantity bought and sold, and an increase in equilibrium price

questions.explanation: A leftward shift of supply with demand unchanged creates a shortage at the old price, so the price rises and the equilibrium quantity falls. Option B gets the quantity right but the price wrong, since a cut in supply pushes price up, not down. Options A and C get the direction of quantity wrong.

questions.question: A leftward shift of the demand curve when supply remains unchanged, results in

options.a: a fall in price, quantity remaining constant
options.b: a rise in price and a decrease in the equilibrium quantity bought and sold
options.c: a fall in equilibrium price and a decrease in equilibrium quantity bought and sold
options.d: a fall in quantity and a rise in price

questions.explanation: A leftward shift of demand with supply unchanged leaves a surplus at the old price, so the price falls and less is bought and sold. Option C gives both effects. Options B and D wrongly say price rises, and option A wrongly says quantity stays constant.

questions.question: Goods that are produced together are said to be (in)
questions.explanation: Goods in joint supply are produced together from the same source, so producing one automatically yields the other, as with beef and leather from cattle. Option A, competitive supply, refers to different commodities supplied to satisfy the same want, such as butter and margarine. Option C, complementarity, refers to goods demanded together, not produced together, and option D is not a standard term.

questions.question: The following goods are said to be complementary
questions.explanation: Complementary goods are used together, so demand for one goes with demand for the other, and tea and sugar fit this well. The pairs in options B, C and D are not normally consumed together, so a change in the price of one would hardly affect demand for the other.

questions.question: Goods that are demanded for several purposes are said to be in
questions.explanation: Composite demand arises when one good is wanted for several different uses, such as electricity for lighting, cooking and running machines. Option A, joint demand, is when two goods are wanted together. Option B describes how responsive demand is to price, and option D is an excess of supply over demand.

questions.question: Examples of goods in joint supply include
questions.explanation: Palm oil and palm kernel both come from the same oil palm fruit, so producing one gives you the other; that is joint supply. Option D, milk and tea, are consumed together, which makes them complements (joint demand). Options B and C are also not pairs that are produced together.

questions.question: The following are substitute goods
questions.explanation: Substitutes can be used in place of each other, and butter and margarine serve the same purpose as spreads. Option C, pen and paper, are used together, so they are complements. The pairs in options B and D are unrelated goods.

questions.question: The responsiveness of the quantities demanded of a commodity to changes in the prices of other commodities is called
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand measures how quantity demanded of one good responds to a change in the price of another good. Option B, price elasticity, looks at the good's own price. Option D, income elasticity, looks at changes in income, and option A is just the general term.

questions.question: Income elasticity of demand is defined as

options.a: the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded of a commodity to a percentage change in income
options.b: the percentage change in quantity demanded to a percentage change in prices
options.c: the percentage change in income to a percentage change in quantity demanded
options.d: the ratio of price changes to income change

questions.explanation: Income elasticity of demand = (%change in quantity demanded)/(%change in income). Option B is price elasticity, not income elasticity. Option C turns the ratio upside down, and option D does not involve quantity demanded at all.

questions.question: The cross elasticity of two goods that are substitutes is
questions.explanation: For substitutes, a rise in the price of one good makes people buy more of the other, so both percentage changes move in the same direction and cross elasticity is positive. Option C, a negative value, is what you get for complements. Option A, zero, means the goods are unrelated.

questions.question: Supply curves are usually positively sloped. This shows that

options.a: more is supplied at lower prices
options.b: the same quantity is supplied regardless of the price
options.c: more is supplied as price increases
options.d: more is supplied as price falls

questions.explanation: An upward (positive) slope means price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, so sellers offer more as price rises. Options A and D describe the opposite relationship. Option B describes a perfectly inelastic (vertical) supply curve, which is not the usual case.

questions.question: When the demand curve is parallel to the price axis, demand is said to be
questions.explanation: A demand curve parallel to the price (vertical) axis is a vertical line, meaning quantity demanded stays the same whatever the price; this is perfectly inelastic demand. Option A, perfectly elastic demand, is a horizontal line parallel to the quantity axis. Option C, unit elasticity, gives a curved shape called a rectangular hyperbola.

questions.question: If the price elasticity of demand for good X equals to Zero, then

options.a: Demand can be said to be perfectly elastic; a tiny change in price leads to an infinite change in quantity demanded.
options.b: Demand can be said to be relatively elastic; a given % change in price leads to a larger % change in quantity demanded.
options.c: Demand can be said to be unit elastic; a given % change in price leads to an equal % change in quantity demanded.
options.d: demand can be said to be perfectly inelastic

questions.explanation: A price elasticity of zero means quantity demanded does not change at all when price changes, which is perfectly inelastic demand shown by a vertical demand curve. Option A describes the opposite extreme, an elasticity of infinity. Option B describes elasticity greater than 1, and option C describes elasticity exactly equal to 1.

questions.question: If the price elasticity of demand for good x is perfectly inelastic, then an increase in price of the good will

options.d: first increase demand and their reduce it successively

questions.explanation: Perfectly inelastic demand means the quantity demanded does not respond to price at all, so a price rise leaves it unchanged. Option A would be true for a normal downward-sloping demand curve, not this one. Options C and D describe responses that perfectly inelastic demand rules out.

questions.question: Bayo drinks only Pepsi and Coke. After three bottles of Pepsi, he switches to Coke, indicating that:

options.a: the marginal utility of Pepsi falls below zero after three bottles
options.b: the marginal utility of the additional Coke exceeds the average utility of the three bottles of Pepsi
options.c: total utility will start to fall after three bottles of Pepsi
options.d: the marginal utility per Naira of Coke is higher than the marginal utility per Naira of Pepsi after three bottles

questions.explanation: A rational consumer spends where the marginal utility per naira is highest, so switching to Coke after three Pepsis shows that MU/P for Coke has become higher than MU/P for Pepsi. Option A goes too far, because Bayo can switch even while Pepsi still gives positive marginal utility. Option C is also not implied, since total utility only falls once marginal utility is negative, and option B compares marginal with average utility, which is not the switching rule.

questions.question: If the MRS of Meat for Chicken is higher than Pm/Pc for a consumer at a point on the budget line, the consumer should consume:

options.c: More Meat and the same amount of Chicken
options.d: Less Meat and the same amount of Chicken

questions.explanation: The MRS of meat for chicken shows how much chicken the consumer is willing to give up for one more unit of meat, and it equals MUm/MUc. If this is higher than Pm/Pc, the consumer values meat more than the market charges for it, so they gain by buying more meat and less chicken until the two ratios are equal. Option B moves in the wrong direction, and options C and D would take the consumer off the budget line or leave the gain unused.

questions.question: Sets of indifference curves drawn in the commodity space is called.....
questions.explanation: An indifference map is a set of indifference curves drawn on the same graph, each showing a higher or lower level of satisfaction. Option A is a description of what the curves do, not their name. Options B and D are not standard terms.

questions.question: Consumer of a goods will maximize utility where

options.a: the ratio of marginal utility to the price are all equal for all the commodities in the consumption basket
options.b: Marginal social benefits equals marginal social cost
options.c: Marginal social cost exceeds marginal social benefit

questions.explanation: A consumer maximises utility when the marginal utility per naira is the same for every good bought, that is MUx/Px = MUy/Py and so on. Options B, C and D are conditions about social welfare and market efficiency, not about an individual consumer's choice.

questions.question: A consumer of Chicken and Chips is willing to pay N600, but he paid N500.00. The difference gained is called
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between the most a buyer is willing to pay and what they actually pay, here N600 - N500 = N100. Option A, profit, is a gain earned by sellers, not buyers. Options B and C are not the standard names for this gain.

questions.question: ________ defines the slope of the indifference curve at a point.
questions.explanation: The slope of an indifference curve at a point is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS), the rate at which a consumer is willing to swap one good for another while staying equally satisfied. Option C, the marginal rate of technical substitution, is the slope of an isoquant in production, not an indifference curve.

questions.question: The line that joins quantity of goods bought with level of income is called
questions.explanation: The Engel curve shows how the quantity of a good bought changes as the consumer's income changes. Option A is a misspelling of the same idea, not the correct term. Option C is not a standard curve, and option D is not the name used for this relationship.

questions.question: A change in people's expectation will result in

options.c: a movement along the demand curve

questions.explanation: Expectations are a non-price determinant of demand; if people expect prices to rise, for example, they buy more now at every price, so the demand curve shifts. Options B and C describe the effect of a change in the good's own price. Option D is wrong because expectations clearly affect buying decisions.

questions.question: For demand to be effective in the market

options.a: seller must make goods and service available in sufficient amounts
options.b: people must be willing to pay the same price as others for good and service
options.c: the relationship between price and quantity must be known
options.d: consumer must have both the ability and willingness to pay for goods and services

questions.explanation: Effective demand is a desire backed by both the ability and willingness to pay. Option A is about supply, not demand. Options B and C are not conditions that make demand effective.

questions.question: A change in the firm's technology will always result in

options.b: a movement along the supply curve

questions.explanation: Technology is a non-price determinant of supply, so a change in it shifts the whole supply curve, which is a change in supply. Option A is wrong because better technology usually increases supply. Options B and C describe the effect of a change in the good's own price.

questions.question: An increase income will cause an increase in demand in
questions.explanation: A normal good is one people buy more of when their income rises. Option D, an inferior good, is the opposite: people buy less of it as income rises. Options A and B are not defined by how they respond to income.

questions.question: An outward shift of the demand curve will lead to

options.a: an increase in both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.b: a decrease in both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.c: a fall in equilibrium price but an increase in equilibrium quantity
options.d: no change in either equilibrium price or quantity

questions.explanation: An outward (rightward) shift of demand with supply unchanged creates a shortage at the old price, so price rises and sellers supply more; both equilibrium price and quantity increase. Option B describes a fall in demand, and option C describes an increase in supply. Option D is wrong because both price and quantity change.

questions.question: An outward shift of the supply curve will lead to

options.a: a fall in equilibrium price but a rise in equilibrium quantity
options.b: an increase in both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.c: a decrease in both the equilibrium price and quantity
options.d: a rise in equilibrium price but a fall in equilibrium quantity

questions.explanation: An outward (rightward) shift of supply with demand unchanged creates a surplus at the old price, so price falls and more is bought and sold. Option B describes an increase in demand. Option C describes a fall in demand, and option D describes a fall in supply.

questions.question: The law of supply states that

options.a: an increase in supply is always accompanied by an increase in demand
options.b: firms will offer more for sale at higher prices than at lower prices
options.c: firms will maintain higher prices, even if they cannot sell all of the goods they want
options.d: an increase in supply must drive prices down

questions.explanation: The law of supply says that, other things equal, firms offer more for sale at higher prices than at lower prices. Options A and D mix up supply and demand. Option C describes firms refusing to cut prices, which is not what the law says.

questions.question: The demand for labour as a factor of production is
questions.explanation: Labour is demanded not for itself but for the goods and services it helps produce, so its demand is derived demand. Option B, joint demand, is goods wanted together. Option D, composite demand, is one good wanted for several uses.

questions.question: The law of demand states that

options.a: quantity demanded is positively related to price
options.b: quantity demanded is inversely related to price
options.c: quantity demanded is absolutely related to price
options.d: quantity demanded is equally related to price

questions.explanation: The law of demand says that, other things equal, quantity demanded rises when price falls and falls when price rises, so the two are inversely related. Option A describes the law of supply. Options C and D are not meaningful relationships.

questions.question: When there is no tendency for a system to change, then there is
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is a state of rest where the forces acting on a system balance, so there is no tendency for it to change. Option B, efficiency, is about making the best use of resources, which is a different idea. Options A and C do not describe a state of rest.

questions.question: A movement along the demand curve is a
questions.explanation: A movement along the demand curve is caused by a change in the good's own price, and it is called a change in quantity demanded. Options A and B are only one direction each, while C covers both. Option D, a change in demand, is a shift of the whole curve.

questions.question: A shift of the entire supply curve is a

options.b: change in price of goods supplied

questions.explanation: A shift of the whole supply curve is caused by non-price factors such as technology or input costs, and it is called a change in supply. Options A and D describe movements along the curve caused by the good's own price. Option B is a cause of movement along the curve, not a shift.

questions.question: Complements are

options.a: two goods with the same price
options.b: two goods serving the same purpose
options.d: two goods that are not related

questions.explanation: Complements are goods that are jointly demanded, so they are used together, like tea and sugar. Option B describes substitutes, which serve the same purpose. Option A has nothing to do with how goods are related, and option D describes unrelated goods.

questions.question: Inferior goods depend on
questions.explanation: Inferior goods are defined by how their demand responds to income: people buy less of them as their income rises. Option A is wrong because price affects the demand for every good, so it does not set inferior goods apart. Options C and D are not what defines the category.

questions.question: ________ is the practice of buying at a low price in one location and selling at a higher price in another location
questions.explanation: Arbitrage is buying a good where its price is low and selling it where its price is higher, making a profit from the price difference. Options B and C, haggling and bargaining, are ways of negotiating a price in one place. Option D is not the economic term for this.

questions.question: Price of copper in the world market may decline or remain constant for a long time because

options.d: copper now have very close substitute such as aluminium and fiber optics used in telecommunication infrastructure

questions.explanation: When close substitutes such as aluminium and fibre optics become available, demand for copper falls or stops growing, so its price may decline or stay flat. Option B would push the price up, not down, and option C, lower output, would also raise the price. Option A is true of copper but does not explain the price trend.

questions.question: Two goods for which the marginal rate of substitution of one for the other is constant are said to be
questions.explanation: Perfect substitutes can be swapped at a fixed rate, so the MRS between them is constant and their indifference curves are straight lines. Option D, perfect complements, are used in fixed proportions and have L-shaped indifference curves. Options A and B have MRS values that change along the curve.

questions.question: If less of a good is preferred to more, then the good is
questions.explanation: A 'bad' is something a consumer prefers less of, such as pollution or garbage. Option B, an economic good, is something people want more of and that is scarce. Options C and D do not describe goods people prefer less of.

questions.question: ________ relates quantity of goods consumed to income of the consumer
questions.explanation: The Engel curve relates the quantity of a good consumed to the consumer's income. Option B is just a misspelling, and option C, the Lorenz curve, shows how income is distributed across a population.

questions.question: The difference between what a consumer is willing to pay for a commodity rather than do without the good and the amount actually paid is
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the gap between the most a consumer would be willing to pay for a good and the price actually paid; it is the extra benefit the buyer enjoys. Options A and D sound similar but are not economic terms for this gap, and option B (price differentials) refers to differences between prices, not to the buyer's gain.

questions.question: The aspiration to buy because others are buying is ________ effect
questions.explanation: The bandwagon effect happens when people buy a good simply because others are buying it, so demand rises with the number of buyers. Option C, the snob effect, is the opposite: some consumers buy less of a good once it becomes popular. Spendthrift and frugal describe spending habits, not this effect.

questions.question: Marginal rate of substitution represents

options.a: the arc of the indifference curve
options.b: the slope of the indifference curve
options.d: the total utility of the consumer

questions.explanation: The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) is the rate at which a consumer gives up one good for another while staying equally satisfied, which is exactly the slope of the indifference curve. Option A (an arc) is a section of the curve, not the rate, and option C (indifference maps) is a whole set of curves. Total utility (option D) is the satisfaction level itself, not a rate of exchange.

questions.question: The slope of the total utility curve is
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one more unit, so it is the slope of the total utility curve. Option A is only true while marginal utility is positive; once MU becomes negative the TU curve slopes downward. Option C is wrong because diminishing MU means the slope keeps changing.

questions.question: When total utility is maximum, marginal utility will be
questions.explanation: Total utility keeps rising as long as each extra unit adds positive satisfaction, so it reaches its peak exactly where marginal utility falls to zero. Option A describes the stage where TU is still rising, and option B describes the stage after the peak, when TU is falling.

questions.question: Consumer is assumed to maximize satisfaction subject to

options.c: number of sellers in the market

questions.explanation: A rational consumer tries to get the highest satisfaction possible, but only with the income available at given prices, which is the budget constraint. Option D is wrong because insatiable wants are the reason choice is needed, not the limit on it. Options A and C may affect the market but are not the constraint in consumer theory.

questions.question: Use the information: Suppose consumer utility is given as U = XY. The price of X and Y are #4 and #8 respectively. And the consumer's income is #240. What is the quantity of X the consumer should purchase at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: At equilibrium MUx/Px = MUy/Py, so Y/4 = X/8, giving X = 2Y. Putting this in the budget 4X + 8Y = 240 gives 4(2Y) + 8Y = 240, so Y = 15 and X = 30. Option C (25) or B (40) come from slips in substituting into the budget, and 20 ignores the equilibrium condition.

questions.question: Use the information: Suppose consumer utility is given as U = XY. The price of X and Y are #4 and #8 respectively. And the consumer's income is #240. What is the quantity of Y the consumer should purchase at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: With U = XY, equilibrium needs Y/4 = X/8, so X = 2Y. Substituting into 4X + 8Y = 240 gives 16Y = 240, so Y = 15 (and X = 30). Option D (30) is the quantity of X, not Y, which is the most common mix-up here.

questions.question: Use the information: Suppose consumer utility is given as U = XY. The price of X and Y are #4 and #8 respectively. And the consumer's income is #240. What is the value of lambda (the marginal utility of money) at equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Lambda is the marginal utility of money, equal to MUx/Px = MUy/Py at the optimum. With X = 30 and Y = 15, MUx = Y = 15, so lambda = 15/4 = 3.75 (check: MUy/Py = 30/8 = 3.75). Options B and D are rounding-style guesses that do not match this exact value.

questions.question: Use the information: Suppose consumer utility is given as U = XY. The price of X and Y are #4 and #8 respectively. And the consumer's income is #240. What is the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) of X for Y at the consumer's equilibrium?
questions.explanation: For U = XY, the MRS of X for Y is MUx/MUy = Y/X. Spending half of the #240 income on each good gives X = 120/4 = 30 and Y = 120/8 = 15, so MRS = 15/30 = 1/2, which matches the price ratio Px/Py = 4/8. Option A (2) is the ratio turned upside down, X/Y.

questions.question: The total effect of price change can be divided into.
questions.explanation: When the price of a good changes, the total effect on quantity demanded can be split into the substitution effect (the good becomes relatively cheaper or dearer than others) and the income effect (the change in real purchasing power). Option B mixes up the cause, the price change, with one of its effects.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains Engel curve for luxury goods

options.a: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first increase rapidly but become less proportional to the increase in income
options.b: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first increase slowly but become less proportional to the increase in income
options.c: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first decrease rapidly but become less proportional to the increase in income
options.d: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first increase slowly but later increase more rapidly than the increase in income

questions.explanation: For a luxury good, spending rises more than proportionally as income keeps rising, so the Engel curve starts slowly and then climbs faster than income. Options A and B describe spending that becomes less proportional to income, which is the pattern for necessities, and option C wrongly has spending falling.

questions.question: Why does the demand curve traditionally slope downward from left to right? The reason is
questions.explanation: Because each extra unit gives less additional satisfaction (diminishing marginal utility), a consumer will only buy more units if the price falls, which gives the downward-sloping demand curve. Options A and D describe the result of the consumer's decision, not the reason demand slopes down, so option B, which combines them, is also wrong.

questions.question: For a normal commodity, the substitution effect of a price change is ----
questions.explanation: The substitution effect always moves quantity demanded in the opposite direction to the price change: when a good becomes dearer relative to others, people buy less of it. This inverse relationship is called a negative substitution effect, so option B is wrong. Options A and C would mean price changes have no effect on choice, which is not the case.

questions.question: Perfect complements will have indifference curves that are
questions.explanation: Perfect complements are goods used in fixed proportions, like left and right shoes, so extra units of one without the other add no satisfaction. This makes the indifference curves L-shaped. Option D, straight lines, describes perfect substitutes instead.

questions.question: A producer's price elasticity of demand is greater than 1. What will happen to his total revenue if the price of his product is reduced by 5 percent?

options.c: It will fall by more than 5 percent

questions.explanation: When demand is elastic (Ed > 1), a 5 percent price cut raises quantity demanded by more than 5 percent, so total revenue rises. Option A is the unit-elastic case, where the two percentage changes cancel out. Option C cannot happen here: even with inelastic demand, a 5 percent price cut makes revenue fall by less than 5 percent, because quantity still rises a little.

questions.question: Diminishing marginal rate of substitution necessarily implies that the marginal rate of substitution

options.a: falls as one travels down (eastward) along an indifference curve.
options.b: decreases as the quantities of both goods increase
options.c: stays the same as one travels up (westward) along an indifference curve.
options.d: falls as one travels up (westward) along an indifference curve.

questions.explanation: Diminishing MRS means that as a consumer moves down an indifference curve, getting more of the good on the horizontal axis, she is willing to give up less and less of the other good for each extra unit, so the MRS falls. Option D gets the direction wrong, and option C would mean a constant MRS, as with perfect substitutes.

questions.question: In the ordinal approach to the theory of consumer behavior, which among the following are objective factors
questions.explanation: In indifference curve analysis, prices and income are objective, measurable facts that define the budget line, while tastes and preferences are subjective and are shown by the indifference curves. Options B, C and D all include preferences, which are subjective.

questions.question: If the demand for electricity is inelastic, then when the price of electricity increases, revenues will:

options.a: decrease, because consumers will switch to substitutes

questions.explanation: When demand is inelastic, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises, so total revenue increases after a price rise. Option A gets this backwards, since inelastic demand means buyers do not switch away much. Option C is the result for elastic demand, and option D is the unit-elastic case.

questions.question: The consumer surplus can be defined as

options.a: The difference between the total amount paid and the total utility gained
options.b: The total amount consumers paid and total utility gained
options.c: The sum of the total prices paid by the consumers
options.d: The difference between the amount consumers would be willing to pay and the amount paid

questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a good and what they actually pay. Options A and B compare money paid with utility, which are not measured in the same units, and option C is simply total spending.

questions.question: Ugo and Idowu live in the same town where they both face the same prices. Ugo has preferences that can be represented by the utility function U(X,Y)=X+Y. Idowu has preferences that can be represented by the utility function V(X,Y)=3X+3Y. Which of the following statement is true?

options.a: The quantity of X purchased by Ugo PLUS the quantity of X purchased by Idowu will equal the total quantity of Y they purchase.
options.b: Idowu gets greater satisfaction from her consumption than Ugo
options.c: A tax on X would have a greater welfare effect on Idowu than on Ugo
options.d: Idowu and Ugo have identical preferences, ranking every bundle of X and Y in the same order

questions.explanation: V = 3X + 3Y is just U = X + Y multiplied by 3, so Ugo and Idowu rank every bundle in exactly the same order, meaning they have the same preferences. Option B is wrong because utility numbers cannot be compared between people, and option C has no basis because their preferences are identical. Option A has no economic reason to hold.

questions.question: Which of the following shifts the supply curve leftward?

options.a: An improvement in technology that decreases the cost of production.
options.b: An anticipated drought that will make inputs more expensive.
options.c: A decrease in the wage rate.
options.d: An increase in the number of suppliers.

questions.explanation: Supply shifts left when producing becomes more costly, and an expected drought that pushes up input prices does exactly that. Options A, C and D all lower costs or add more sellers, which shift supply to the right.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains Engel curve for necessities?

options.a: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first decrease rapidly but become less proportional to the increase in income
options.b: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first increase rapidly but become less proportional to the increase in income
options.c: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first decrease rapidly but later increase more than the income
options.d: Continuous increases in income make expenditure to first increase rapidly but later increase more than the income

questions.explanation: For a necessity, spending rises with income but by a smaller proportion, so the Engel curve rises quickly at first and then flattens out. Option D describes a luxury, where spending eventually grows faster than income, and options A and C wrongly have spending falling.

questions.question: A rightward shift of the demand curve occurs (and demand increases) when:

options.b: the price of an input used in its production falls
options.c: the price of a complementary good falls.

questions.explanation: When a complementary good becomes cheaper, people buy more of it and so want more of the good used with it, shifting its demand curve to the right. Option B is wrong because a cheaper input lowers production costs, which shifts supply, not demand. Option A causes a movement along the curve, and option D shifts demand left for a normal good.

questions.question: If markets for some addictive drugs are found to have a higher price-elasticity of demand than was often thought, and if many addicts have difficulty holding down steady, well-paying jobs, we might speculate that the most likely reason for the surprising elasticity estimates is that:

options.a: the substitution effect is smaller than expected.
options.b: the income effect is larger than expected.
options.c: the income and substitution effects work in opposite directions.

questions.explanation: If addicts have low and unstable incomes, the drug takes a large share of their budget, so a price rise cuts their real income a lot and they buy noticeably less. This bigger-than-expected income effect makes demand more elastic. Option A would make demand less elastic, not more, and option D is not supported by the facts given.

questions.question: When total utility is declining, marginal utility is -----:
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the change in total utility from one more unit, so when total utility is falling, each extra unit is reducing satisfaction and MU is negative. Option A applies only at the exact peak of total utility, and option C applies while total utility is still rising.

questions.question: Given that the demand for a commodity is Q= 200 - 4.5P, where Q is quantity demanded and P is price, find own price elasticity of demand when price is N10:
questions.explanation: At P = 10, Q = 200 - 4.5(10) = 155. Price elasticity is Ed = (dQ/dP) x (P/Q) = 4.5 x 10/155 = 0.29 in absolute value. Option D (0.28) is a rounding slip, and option A (0.20) would come from using the wrong quantity.

questions.question: The cross elasticity of two goods X and Y is zero. This means that X and Y are:

options.c: X and Y are NOT strongly related

questions.explanation: A cross elasticity of zero means a change in the price of one good has no effect on demand for the other, so the goods are unrelated (independent). Option B needs a positive cross elasticity, and option A needs a negative one.

questions.question: Paul likes two scoop of vanilla ice cream for every chocolate scoop. He gets no extra utility for an additional chocolate scoop if He doesn't have two additional vanilla scoops and no extra utility for extra vanilla scoops without the appropriate amount of chocolate. His utility function can be represented by:
questions.explanation: Paul wants vanilla and chocolate in a fixed ratio of 2 vanilla to 1 chocolate, so they are perfect complements and utility is a min function. With U = min{2c, v}, one chocolate and two vanilla give 2c = v = 2, and extra units of either alone add nothing. Option A gets the ratio backwards, and options B and C are perfect-substitute functions.

questions.question: The income effect of a change in price shows that

options.a: As price increases, real income increases as quantity increases
options.b: As price increases, real income increases as quantity decreases
options.c: As price decreases, real income decreases as quantity increases
options.d: As price decreases, real income increases as quantity increases

questions.explanation: When price falls, the consumer's money income buys more, so her real income rises and she can afford more of the good (for a normal good). Option A wrongly says real income rises when price increases, and option C wrongly says it falls when price decreases.

questions.question: Along a given indifference curve:

options.a: Both the combination of goods and the consumer's income remain constant
options.b: The combination of goods remains constant but the level of utility varies
options.c: The combination of goods remains constant
options.d: The combination of goods varies but the level of utility remains constant

questions.explanation: An indifference curve joins different combinations of two goods that all give the consumer the same satisfaction, so the bundles change but utility stays constant. Option B has this backwards, and options A and C wrongly suggest the combination of goods is fixed.

questions.question: Change in supply can be caused by

options.d: Change in price of the good

questions.explanation: A change in supply means the whole supply curve shifts, and this is caused by non-price factors such as technology and production costs, so both A and B are correct. Option D is wrong because a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the curve, called a change in quantity supplied.

questions.question: A decrease in supply when demand remains the same will make the equilibrium

options.a: P to fall while Q rise
options.b: P and Q to both fall
options.c: P to rise while Q fall
options.d: P and Q to both rise

questions.explanation: A decrease in supply shifts the supply curve to the left along an unchanged demand curve, so the new equilibrium has a higher price and a lower quantity. Option A describes an increase in supply, and option B describes a fall in demand.

questions.question: ________ is a positively sloped curve while ________ is a negatively sloped curve
questions.explanation: The supply curve slopes upward (positively) because higher prices encourage more production, while the demand curve slopes downward (negatively) because people buy more at lower prices. Option A reverses the two, and options B and C are not standard curves.

questions.question: ________ is the quantity of goods and services a consumer is willing and able to purchase at given price in given period of time.
questions.explanation: Demand is the quantity of a good or service consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price over a given period. Options A and C, needs and desires, lack the 'able to pay' part, and option B describes the sellers' side.

questions.question: Any price below the equilibrium price will lead to ________ which is also referred to as ________
questions.explanation: Below the equilibrium price, buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is excess demand, also called a shortage. Option C describes a price above equilibrium, and options B and D mix up the two terms.

questions.question: For a single commodity, consumer equilibrium is where
questions.explanation: With a single commodity and the marginal utility of money taken as one, the consumer keeps buying until the satisfaction from the last unit equals its price, so MUx = Px. Option A applies when comparing two goods, and options C and D wrongly match one good's utility with another good's price.

questions.question: All of the following have a negative slope, except
questions.explanation: The supply curve slopes upward because sellers offer more at higher prices. The demand curve, the aggregate demand curve and the production possibility curve all slope downward, so options A, B and D do have a negative slope.

questions.question: A shift in demand curve is the same as
questions.explanation: A shift of the whole demand curve is called a change in demand and is caused by factors other than the good's own price, such as income or tastes. Option D, a change in price, causes a movement along the curve, and option C is about supply.

questions.question: The first law of demand assumes that

options.a: Price can influence demand while other determinants are held constant.
options.b: Price is the only determinant of demand.
options.c: Price is held constant while other determinants of demand are allowed to influence demand.
options.d: Price and other factors influence demand.

questions.explanation: The law of demand looks at how price affects quantity demanded while assuming other determinants, like income and tastes, stay constant (ceteris paribus). Option B is wrong because price is not the only determinant; the others are only held fixed. Option C reverses the assumption.

questions.question: One of the following is not a property of an indifference curve

options.a: It gives the same level of satisfaction at all points on the curve
options.b: It slopes downward from left to the right
options.c: It has no shape for some commodities
options.d: Two indifference curves do not intersect

questions.explanation: An indifference curve shows equal satisfaction at every point, slopes downward, and two indifference curves never cross, so options A, B and D are genuine properties. Option C is not a property, since every indifference curve has a definite shape, usually convex to the origin.

questions.question: The school of thought that is of the opinion that utility is measurable is referred to as?
questions.explanation: The cardinalists, associated with Marshall, held that utility can be measured in units (utils). Option A, the ordinalists, argued that utility can only be ranked, not measured, which is the basis of indifference curve analysis.

questions.question: These are all properties of indifference curve (IC) except

options.a: IC is convex to the origin
options.b: Higher IC signifies a higher level of satisfaction
options.c: The slope of IC is marginal rate of technical substitution
options.d: The slope of IC is marginal rate of substitution

questions.explanation: The slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution between two goods, not the marginal rate of technical substitution, which is the slope of an isoquant in production. Options A, B and D are true properties: indifference curves are convex, higher curves mean more satisfaction, and the slope is the MRS.

questions.question: Suppose that marginal utility of good X=100, the price of X=N10 per unit and the price of good Y=N5. Assuming that the consumer is in equilibrium by consuming both good X and Y, what will the marginal utility of Y be?
questions.explanation: In equilibrium the consumer sets MUx/Px = MUy/Py, so 100/10 = MUy/5. That gives 10 = MUy/5, so MUy = 10 x 5 = 50. Option B (10) is only the ratio MU per naira, and option C (200) comes from inverting the price ratio.

questions.question: Suppose a rational consumer earns the income of N200 per month and he spends N60 on food which is a necessity and the remaining on other goods and services. Assuming the price of food now increases, what will happen to the consumer's allocation of funds, considering that the demand for food is price inelastic?

options.a: The consumer will spend a larger part of his income on food and less on other goods
options.b: The consumer will reduce his quantity of food consumption but increase consumption of other goods
options.c: The consumer will spend less on food because he buys much less of it
options.d: The consumer will increase the quantity of his consumption

questions.explanation: With price-inelastic demand, quantity bought falls by a smaller percentage than the price rises, so total spending on food goes up. Out of a fixed N200 income, that leaves less for other goods and services. Option C would only happen if demand for food were elastic, and option B is wrong for the same reason, since spending on food rises rather than falls.

questions.question: The law of demand states that

options.a: The quantity demand is directly related to the commodity's price
options.b: At lower prices a lower quantity will be demanded and vice versa
options.c: At higher prices, lower quantities will be demanded and vice versa
options.d: At higher prices, a higher quantity will be demanded and vice versa

questions.explanation: The law of demand states that, other things being equal, the higher the price the lower the quantity demanded, and the lower the price the higher the quantity demanded. Options A and D describe a direct relationship, which is the law of supply, and option B wrongly links lower prices with lower quantities.

questions.question: A movement down a demand curve is called

options.d: An increase in the quantity demanded

questions.explanation: Moving down along a demand curve means the price has fallen and buyers respond with a larger quantity, which is an increase in quantity demanded. Option A is tempting, but an increase in demand means the whole curve shifts to the right, not a movement along it. Option C is the opposite, a movement up the curve.

questions.question: Supply curve will shift downwards if

options.a: Prices of factor inputs fall on the average
options.c: Price of other commodities fall on the average

questions.explanation: A supply curve shifts downward (to the right) when it becomes cheaper or more attractive to produce the good at each price. Cheaper inputs (A) and better technology (B) both cut costs, and falling prices of other goods (C) make producers switch resources into this good, so any of these would shift supply.

questions.question: Demand curve would shift outward definitely if

options.b: Average price of substitute good falls

questions.explanation: For a normal good, a general rise in household income increases demand at every price, shifting the demand curve outward. Option B is wrong because a cheaper substitute pulls buyers away, shifting demand inward. Option C is also wrong because a dearer complement reduces demand, so D cannot be right.

questions.question: The marginal utility theory assumes
questions.explanation: Marginal utility theory assumes the consumer has a limited budget (A), that each extra unit gives less satisfaction (B), and that the consumer aims to maximise total utility (C). Since all three are assumptions of the theory, D is correct.

questions.question: One of the following does not belong to the group. Which is it?
questions.explanation: The income-consumption line, the price-consumption line and the budget line are all lines drawn in indifference curve analysis, so utility is the odd one out. Utility is a general concept of satisfaction rather than a line on the indifference diagram. Option D, the budget line, is tempting, but it belongs with the other two.

questions.question: The purpose of indifference curve analysis is:

options.a: To prove the law of diminishing utility
options.b: To derive a theory of producer behaviour
options.c: To prove that the demand curve for all commodities is negatively sloped
options.d: To derive a theory of consumer behaviour without requiring cardinal utility measurement

questions.explanation: Indifference curve analysis explains consumer behaviour using only the ranking of preferences (ordinal utility), so it does not need utility to be measured in numbers. Option A is wrong because the approach avoids measuring utility, and option B is wrong because it is about consumers, not producers. Option C is wrong because the analysis allows exceptions such as Giffen goods.

questions.question: The market price of a commodity is determined by
questions.explanation: Market price adjusts through excess demand (qd - qs): when it is positive, buyers bid the price up, and when it is negative, sellers cut prices until qd = qs at equilibrium. Option A is only half the story, since household demand alone ignores supply. Options B and D can affect demand or supply, but they do not set the market price directly.

questions.question: One of the most important determinants of elasticity is:

options.a: The degree of availability of close substitute
options.b: The degree of specificity of various commodities
options.c: The cost of production of various commodities

questions.explanation: The more close substitutes a good has, the more elastic its demand, because buyers can easily switch when its price rises. Option C, cost of production, affects supply rather than how buyers respond to price. Options B and D are not standard determinants of elasticity.

questions.question: The normal demand curve is:
questions.explanation: The demand curve slopes downward from left to right (negatively sloped), because more is bought at lower prices. Option B, positively sloped, is the shape of a normal supply curve. Options A and C describe skewness, which is a statistics term, not the slope of a demand curve.

questions.question: The responsiveness of supply to changes in price is known as:
questions.explanation: Elasticity of supply measures how much the quantity supplied responds to a change in the good's price. Option D, elasticity of demand, measures the response of buyers rather than sellers. Options B and C measure responses to other prices and to income.

questions.question: What does positive cross-elasticity of demand imply?
questions.explanation: A positive cross elasticity means that when the price of one good rises, demand for the other rises too, which happens with substitutes such as Coke and Pepsi. Options B and C, jointly demanded goods and complements, have a negative cross elasticity. Option A is not a standard term in this context.

questions.question: If the price of a given item is substantial in relation to the consumer's income, demand for it tends to be:
questions.explanation: When a good takes a large share of the consumer's income, a price rise hurts a lot, so buyers cut back noticeably and demand is elastic. Option D is the case for cheap items like salt or matches that take a tiny share of income. Options A and B are extreme cases that do not follow from this.

questions.question: The relation between the changes in demand for one product with respect to changes in the price of another is termed:
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand measures how the demand for one product responds to a change in the price of another. Option D, demand elasticity, usually means the response to the good's own price. Option C, income elasticity, is the response to a change in income.

questions.question: If a good is considered "inferior" then

options.a: As its price falls, more of it will be purchased
options.b: As the consumer's income increases, less of the good will be purchased
options.c: As its price rises, less of it will be bought
options.d: If price or income changes, no change will be induced in its consumption

questions.explanation: An inferior good is one whose demand falls as income rises, because consumers switch to better alternatives, for example from garri to rice. Options A and C simply describe the normal law of demand, which applies to most goods, so they do not define an inferior good. Option D describes something unrelated.

questions.question: Mention one of the basic assumptions of the Cardinalist approach
questions.explanation: The cardinalist (marginal utility) approach assumes the consumer is rational and aims to maximise utility from their income. Option D is wrong because the theory assumes diminishing, not increasing, marginal utility. Option B is wrong because it assumes the marginal utility of money is constant.

questions.question: What does additivity imply?

options.a: Independent utilities of the various commodities
options.c: Related utilities of the various commodities in the bunch
options.d: Dependent utilities of the various commodities

questions.explanation: Additivity means the total utility from a bundle is the sum of the separate utilities from each good, which assumes the utilities of the goods are independent of one another. Options C and D are the opposite, since related or dependent utilities could not simply be added. Option B just repeats the word without explaining it.

questions.question: The slope of the indifference curve is known as

options.d: The marginal rate of substitution of the commodity
