questions.explanation: The slope of an indifference curve is the marginal rate of substitution, the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up one good for another while staying equally satisfied. Option B, the indifference map, is the whole set of indifference curves, not the slope of one. Option A, the isoquant, is the producer's equal-output curve.

questions.question: What does the assumption of convexity of the indifference curve imply?
questions.explanation: A convex indifference curve reflects a diminishing marginal rate of substitution, meaning the consumer gives up less and less of one good for each extra unit of the other. This is the idea of substitution between goods. Options C and D, preference and choice, are too general and are not what convexity specifically tells us.

questions.question: When total utility is at a maximum, marginal utility is
questions.explanation: Total utility is at its maximum when one more unit adds nothing, so marginal utility is zero at that point. Option A is wrong because a positive marginal utility means total utility is still rising. Options C and D also describe total utility still increasing.

questions.question: A concept that shows all the indifference curves which rank a consumer's preferences is known as
questions.explanation: An indifference map is a set of indifference curves, with higher curves showing higher levels of satisfaction, so it ranks the consumer's preferences. Option C, a single indifference curve, shows only one level of satisfaction. Option A, the isoquant, belongs to production theory.

questions.question: If the commodities are perfect substitutes, what will be the shape of the indifference curve?

options.c: A straight line with negative slope
options.d: A straight line with positive slope.

questions.explanation: Perfect substitutes can be swapped at a constant rate, so the marginal rate of substitution never changes and the indifference curve is a straight, downward-sloping line. Option A, a convex curve, is the normal case for imperfect substitutes. Option D is wrong because indifference curves slope downward, since more of one good must make up for less of the other.

questions.question: In the utility theory what is important to the consumer's equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Consumer equilibrium in utility theory is reached where the marginal utility per naira is equal across goods (MUx/Px = MUy/Py), so marginal utility is what matters. Option D, total utility, is what the consumer wants to maximise, but the decision rule uses marginal utility. Options A and C describe how utility changes, not the equilibrium condition.

questions.question: A curve that shows how consumption bundles changes as price of one of the commodities changes while the price of other commodities and income remain constant is called:
questions.explanation: The price-consumption curve traces the consumer's best bundle as the price of one good changes, with income and other prices held constant. Option A, the income-consumption line, traces the best bundle as income changes instead. Option C, a revenue curve, belongs to the theory of the firm.

questions.question: A measure of the difference between the value that consumers place on their total consumption of a commodity and the amount they must pay for it is known as:
questions.explanation: Consumer surplus is the difference between what consumers are willing to pay for a commodity, the value they place on it, and what they actually pay. Option B, consumer's benefit, is a loose term rather than the name of this measure. Option D, income, is what the consumer has to spend.

questions.question: Whenever real choices concern a little more or a little less, they are influenced by:
questions.explanation: Most real choices are about a little more or a little less of something, so they depend on the extra satisfaction from one more unit, which is marginal utility. Option C, total utility, measures overall satisfaction rather than the gain from a small change. Options A and B are not what such decisions are weighed against.

questions.question: A consumer that chooses the consumption bundle at which the highest attainable indifference curve is just tangent to the budget line is known as:
questions.explanation: A consumer who picks the bundle where the highest attainable indifference curve just touches the budget line is maximising utility, since no affordable bundle gives more satisfaction. Option B is the opposite. Options C and D are not standard terms.

questions.question: A utility-maximising household will consume a commodity only up to the point where its consumer's surplus on the last unit purchased is:
questions.explanation: A utility-maximising household keeps buying until the value of the last unit equals the price paid, so the consumer surplus on that last unit is zero. Option D, negative, would mean the household paid more than the unit was worth, so it would stop before that. Option A is wrong because surplus on the last unit is not one.

questions.question: Ostentatious goods are also known as
questions.explanation: Ostentatious goods are luxury items bought largely to show off status, and they are called Veblen goods; demand for them can rise as their price rises. Option A, Giffen goods, also have upward-sloping demand, but they are inferior necessities consumed by poor households, not status symbols. Option B, inferior goods, are goods whose demand falls as income rises.

questions.question: Demand backed by the ability to pay for goods and services is:
questions.explanation: Effective demand is the desire for a good backed by the ability and willingness to pay for it. Option A, ineffective demand, is the opposite: a wish without the money to pay. Option D, opportunity cost, is the next best alternative given up, which is a different idea.

questions.question: The market equilibrium price of a commodity is determined by:

options.a: Market demand for the commodity alone
options.b: Market supply of the commodity alone
options.c: The interaction of market demand and supply for the commodity

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is reached where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer, so it depends on demand and supply working together. Options A and B each take only one side of the market, which is like trying to cut paper with one blade of a pair of scissors.

questions.question: The theory of demand mainly studies the behaviour of the:
questions.explanation: Demand theory explains how consumers decide how much of a good to buy, given prices, income and tastes. Options B, C and D relate to the supply side, which is studied under the theory of production and the firm.

questions.question: The want-satisfying power of a commodity is called:
questions.explanation: Utility is the capacity of a good or service to satisfy a human want, such as the ability of bottled water to quench thirst. Option A, satisfaction, is the feeling obtained after consumption, and Option D, marginal utility, is only the extra utility from one more unit.

questions.question: Utility is best described as:

options.b: subjective, differing from person to person
options.c: measurable in physical units such as kilograms

questions.explanation: Utility is subjective: it depends on each consumer's tastes and needs, so the same plate of food can give a hungry student far more satisfaction than someone who has just eaten. Option A is wrong because utility is not fixed across people, and Option C is wrong because utility cannot be measured in physical units.

questions.question: The change in total utility that results from consuming one more unit of a good is called:
questions.explanation: Marginal utility is the addition to total utility from consuming one extra unit: MU = (change in TU)/(change in quantity). Option A is the overall satisfaction from all units consumed, and Option D is total utility divided by the number of units.

questions.question: When marginal utility becomes negative, total utility:
questions.explanation: Negative marginal utility means the extra unit actually reduces satisfaction, like being made to eat a fifth plate of rice, so total utility falls. Option B applies when MU is positive, and Option C applies only at the exact point where MU is zero.

questions.question: The saturation point in consumption is the point where:
questions.explanation: At the saturation point one more unit adds no extra satisfaction, so MU = 0 and total utility is at its maximum. Option A is wrong because total utility is at its highest there, not zero, and Option C describes the stage before saturation is reached.

questions.question: The idea that utility can be measured in cardinal numbers (units) is a postulate of the:
questions.explanation: Neo-classical economists such as Alfred Marshall assumed that utility could be measured in units (utils) or in money, which is the cardinal approach. Option B, the ordinalist school associated with Hicks and Allen, held that consumers can only rank combinations, not measure utility, and Option C, the Keynesians, focused on macroeconomics rather than utility measurement.

questions.question: Gossen's first law is another name for the law of:
questions.explanation: Gossen's first law states that as a person consumes more of a good, the extra satisfaction from each additional unit falls, which is the law of diminishing marginal utility. Option B, the law of equi-marginal utility, is known as Gossen's second law, and Option D, diminishing returns, is a law of production rather than consumption.

questions.question: For a free good (one with a zero price), a consumer is in equilibrium when:
questions.explanation: A consumer buys up to the point where MU = P, and since the price of a free good is zero, they keep consuming until MU = 0. Option C is wrong because total utility is at its maximum, not zero, at that point, and Option A is wrong because MU is highest at the very first unit consumed.

questions.question: A change in the demand for a good caused by a change in the price of a related good is called:
questions.explanation: Cross demand links the quantity demanded of one good to the price of another, related good, such as the demand for bread changing when the price of butter changes. Option B, price demand, relates demand to the good's own price, and Option C, income demand, relates it to the consumer's income.

questions.question: For an ordinary inferior good (one that is not a Giffen good), the relationship between its price and its quantity demanded is:
questions.explanation: Even for an inferior good, the substitution effect usually outweighs the negative income effect, so quantity demanded still rises when price falls and the price-quantity relationship is inverse. Option A, a direct relationship, applies only to the special case of a Giffen good, where the income effect is strong enough to dominate.

questions.question: For a normal good, quantity demanded varies inversely with:

options.d: the price of a substitute good

questions.explanation: By the law of demand, a higher price of a normal good leads to a lower quantity demanded, so the relationship with its own price is inverse. Option B is wrong because demand for a normal good rises with income, and Option D is also a direct relationship, since a dearer substitute makes consumers buy more of this good.

questions.question: Which of these is a cardinal approach to demand analysis?
questions.explanation: Marshall's utility analysis assumes utility can be measured in units or in money, which makes it the cardinal approach. Option B, indifference curve analysis, is ordinal because it only ranks combinations, and Option C, revealed preference, is based on observed choices rather than measured utility.

questions.question: Which of these is a property of a standard indifference curve?

options.a: It is convex to the origin.
options.b: It is concave to the origin.
options.c: It slopes upward from left to right.
options.d: Two indifference curves can cross each other.

questions.explanation: A standard indifference curve is convex to the origin because of a diminishing marginal rate of substitution. Option C is wrong because indifference curves slope downward (to keep satisfaction the same, more of one good means less of the other), and Option D is wrong because crossing curves would mean the same bundle gives two different levels of satisfaction.

questions.question: The convexity of an indifference curve reflects:

options.a: a diminishing marginal rate of substitution
options.b: an increasing marginal rate of substitution
options.c: a constant marginal rate of substitution
options.d: a zero marginal rate of substitution everywhere

questions.explanation: As a consumer gets more of good X, they are willing to give up less and less of good Y for each extra unit of X, so the MRS diminishes and the curve bows in toward the origin. Option C, a constant MRS, would give a straight-line indifference curve (perfect substitutes), and Option B would make the curve concave.

questions.question: Moving from one point to another along the same indifference curve leaves the consumer's satisfaction:
questions.explanation: Every point on an indifference curve gives the same level of satisfaction, which is why the consumer is 'indifferent' between them. Options A and B would require moving to a higher or lower indifference curve, not along the same one.

questions.question: Compared with combinations on a lower indifference curve, combinations on a higher indifference curve (further from the origin) are:

options.b: preferred, because they give more satisfaction

questions.explanation: A higher indifference curve contains bundles with more of at least one good and no less of the other, so, assuming more is better, they give greater satisfaction and are preferred. Option A applies only to points on the same curve, and Option D is wrong because indifference curve analysis is built on the consumer's ability to rank bundles.

questions.question: As a consumer moves down an indifference curve from left to right, the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y:
questions.explanation: Moving down the curve, the consumer has more X and less Y, so they are willing to give up fewer units of Y for each extra unit of X, and the MRS of X for Y decreases. Option B would only hold for perfect substitutes, whose indifference curves are straight lines.

questions.question: The slope of an indifference curve measures the:

options.a: ratio of the prices of goods X and Y
options.b: marginal rate of technical substitution between labour and capital
options.c: marginal rate of substitution of X for Y (MRSxy)
options.d: marginal rate of transformation along the production possibility curve

questions.explanation: The slope of an indifference curve shows how much Y the consumer will give up for one more unit of X while staying equally satisfied, which is MRSxy. Option A is the slope of the budget line, Option B is the slope of an isoquant in production, and Option D is the slope of the production possibility curve.

questions.question: A consumer spends income on goods X and Y, with X on the horizontal axis. If only the price of Y changes, the X-intercept of the budget line will:

options.d: move parallel with the whole budget line

questions.explanation: The X-intercept equals income divided by the price of X (M/Px), and neither of these changes, so it stays fixed while the budget line pivots around it. Only the Y-intercept (M/Py) moves, which rules out A and B, and Option D, a parallel shift, happens when income changes rather than one price.

questions.question: At the point where an indifference curve is tangent to the budget line:
questions.explanation: At the tangency the two slopes are equal: the consumer's willingness to swap Y for X (MRSxy) equals the market rate of exchange (Px/Py), which is the condition for consumer equilibrium. Options B and C describe points where the consumer could still gain by buying more X or more Y, and Option D turns the price ratio upside down.

questions.question: Goods that consumers buy more of when their income rises are called:
questions.explanation: Normal goods have a positive income elasticity of demand: as income rises, demand for them rises too. Options B and C are goods whose demand falls as income rises, with a Giffen good being a special kind of inferior good.

questions.question: The curve showing the quantity of a good a consumer would buy at different levels of income is the:
questions.explanation: The Engel curve plots the quantity of a good bought against the consumer's income, showing directly how purchases change as income changes. Option A, the demand curve, relates quantity to the good's own price rather than income, and Option B traces the best bundles as the price of one good changes.

questions.question: The change in quantity demanded caused only by a change in relative prices, with real income held constant, is the:
questions.explanation: The substitution effect isolates the response to a change in relative prices alone, as consumers switch toward the good that has become relatively cheaper while real income is held constant. Option A is the response to the change in purchasing power, and Option C, the price effect, is the combined total of the substitution and income effects.

questions.question: The substitution effect of a price change on quantity demanded is:

options.a: always negative (quantity moves opposite to price)

questions.explanation: When a good becomes relatively cheaper, the substitution effect always leads the consumer to buy more of it, and when it becomes dearer, less of it, so the effect moves opposite to price and is described as negative. It is the income effect, not the substitution effect, that can go either way, which is why Options B and C are wrong.

questions.question: If the income effect of a price change works in the same direction as the substitution effect, the good is:
questions.explanation: For a normal good, a price fall makes the good relatively cheaper (substitution effect) and also raises real income, which increases demand further (income effect), so both effects push quantity demanded the same way. For inferior and Giffen goods, Options B and C, the income effect works against the substitution effect.

questions.question: If the income effect works in the opposite direction to the substitution effect, the good cannot be a:

options.d: good with a negative income elasticity

questions.explanation: Opposite income and substitution effects happen only when the income effect is negative, which is the case for inferior goods, including Giffen goods. A normal good has an income effect that reinforces the substitution effect, so it cannot be the good described, while Options A, B and D are all types of inferior goods.

questions.question: Which theory of consumer demand is based on observing consumers' actual market behaviour?
questions.explanation: Revealed preference theory, developed by Paul Samuelson, infers preferences from the bundles consumers actually choose at given prices and incomes. Options A and D rest on the assumption that utility can be measured, and Option B relies on the consumer's own ranking of bundles, so none of them is built on observed behaviour.

questions.question: The indifference curve approach to consumer behaviour is associated with:
questions.explanation: J.R. Hicks, working with R.G.D. Allen, popularised the indifference curve (ordinal) approach to consumer demand. Marshall (A) is linked to the cardinal utility approach, and Samuelson (C) to revealed preference theory.

questions.question: Which pair of goods are close substitutes?
questions.explanation: Tea and coffee serve the same purpose for many consumers, so if the price of one rises, people switch to the other, which makes them close substitutes. Options B, C and D are complements, goods used together, so a rise in the price of one reduces demand for the other.

questions.question: Other things remaining equal, the quantity demanded of a product increases when its price:
questions.explanation: The law of demand states that, other things equal, price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so quantity demanded rises when price falls. Option A would be true only for special cases like Giffen goods, and Option C gives no reason for quantity demanded to change.

questions.question: For complementary goods, such as cars and petrol, the cross elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: When the price of petrol rises, people buy fewer cars, so the quantity demanded of one good moves opposite to the price of the other and cross elasticity is negative. Option A, a positive cross elasticity, is the mark of substitutes, and Option C, zero, indicates unrelated goods.

questions.question: The responsiveness of demand for one commodity to a change in the price of another commodity is measured by:
questions.explanation: Cross elasticity of demand = (%change in Qd of good X)/(%change in price of good Y), so it links one good's demand to another good's price. Option A uses the good's own price, and Option B uses the consumer's income.

questions.question: The demand curve for a Giffen good:
questions.explanation: For a Giffen good, a strong negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so a price rise leads consumers to buy more of it, giving an upward-sloping demand curve. Option C is the normal case under the law of demand, which the Giffen good is an exception to.

questions.question: When Q = f(P), the price elasticity of demand is measured by:
questions.explanation: Price elasticity is (%change in Q)/(%change in P) = (change in Q/Q)/(change in P/P), which rearranges to (change in Q/change in P) x (P/Q). Option B uses the inverse slope and gives the reciprocal of elasticity, and Option A divides by P/Q instead of multiplying by it.

questions.question: The income elasticity of demand for inferior goods is:
questions.explanation: For an inferior good, demand falls as income rises (people switch to better alternatives), so the percentage change in quantity has the opposite sign to the percentage change in income and income elasticity is negative. Option B, a positive income elasticity, belongs to normal goods.

questions.question: For luxury goods, the income elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Demand for a luxury rises more than proportionately with income, so (%change in Qd)/(%change in income) is greater than one. Option A, positive but less than one, describes a necessity, and Option D describes an inferior good.

questions.question: Income elasticity of demand is positive but less than one for:
questions.explanation: Demand for necessities, such as salt or basic foodstuffs, rises with income but by a smaller percentage, giving an income elasticity between 0 and 1. Option B, luxuries, have income elasticity above one, and Option C, inferior goods, have a negative income elasticity.

questions.question: A movement along a demand curve (a change in quantity demanded) is caused by a change in:
questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves the consumer along an existing demand curve, which economists call a change in quantity demanded. Options A, C and D are other determinants of demand, and a change in any of them shifts the whole demand curve instead.

questions.question: A normal supply curve shows a ______ relationship between price and quantity supplied.
questions.explanation: By the law of supply, producers offer more at higher prices because production becomes more profitable, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction. Option B describes the demand curve, not the supply curve.

questions.question: When drawing an individual's demand curve for a good, all of the following are held constant EXCEPT:

options.c: the price of the good itself

questions.explanation: A demand curve shows how quantity demanded responds to the good's own price, so that price must be allowed to vary along the curve. Income, prices of related goods and tastes (A, B and D) are held constant, and a change in any of them shifts the curve.

questions.question: A fall in the price of a good, with all other things held constant, leads to:
questions.explanation: A change in a good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, and a lower price raises the quantity demanded. Option A, an increase in demand, is a rightward shift of the whole curve caused by things like higher income, not by the good's own price.

questions.question: When a consumer's income rises, with everything else constant, their demand for a normal good:
questions.explanation: A normal good is defined by a positive link between income and demand, so higher income shifts its demand curve to the right. Option B describes an inferior good, and Option D is wrong because the direction for a normal good is not in doubt.

questions.question: When a consumer's income falls, with everything else constant, their demand for an inferior good:
questions.explanation: With less income, consumers switch from dearer options to cheaper, lower-quality ones, so demand for an inferior good increases when income falls. Option B is what happens to a normal good when income falls.

questions.question: When the price of a substitute for good X falls, the demand for X:
questions.explanation: If a substitute becomes cheaper, some consumers switch to it, so demand for X falls; for example, cheaper tea would reduce the demand for coffee. Option A would apply if the price of the substitute rose, or if the price of a complement fell.

questions.question: If the price of a substitute for good X and the price of a complement of X both rise at the same time, the demand for X will:

options.d: rise, fall or stay the same, depending on which effect is stronger

questions.explanation: A dearer substitute pushes demand for X up, while a dearer complement pulls demand for X down, so the two effects work in opposite directions. The final result depends on which change is stronger, so none of the definite outcomes in A, B or C can be guaranteed.

questions.question: With an upward-sloping supply curve, a rise in the good's own price leads to:
questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price moves producers along the existing supply curve, and a higher price raises quantity supplied. Option A, an increase in supply, is a rightward shift of the whole curve caused by factors such as lower input costs or better technology.

questions.question: Starting from a stable equilibrium, if market supply decreases while demand is unchanged:

options.c: both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity fall
options.d: equilibrium price rises but equilibrium quantity falls

questions.explanation: A decrease in supply shifts the supply curve to the left, creating a shortage at the old price, so price rises and the quantity traded falls. Options A and B are results of an increase in supply, and Option C is what happens when demand falls.

questions.question: If the percentage rise in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage fall in price, the price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Ed = (%change in Qd)/(%change in P); when the top is smaller than the bottom, the ratio is less than one and demand is inelastic. Option A would require quantity to respond more than price, and Option D would mean quantity does not respond at all.

questions.question: If a good's demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, a fall in its price will make total expenditure on the good:
questions.explanation: Along a rectangular hyperbola, P x Q is the same at every point, so price elasticity is one everywhere and total expenditure does not change when price changes. Option A would hold for elastic demand, and Option B for inelastic demand.

questions.question: If the quantity demanded stays exactly the same when the price of a good falls, the price elasticity of demand is:

options.c: less than one but above zero

questions.explanation: With no change in quantity demanded, the top of Ed = (%change in Qd)/(%change in P) is zero, so elasticity is zero and demand is perfectly inelastic. Option C describes demand that responds a little, not demand that does not respond at all.

questions.question: When demand for a good is inelastic, a rise in its price causes consumers' total expenditure on it to:
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so P x Q goes up; for example, if price rises 10% and quantity bought falls only 4%, spending becomes 1.10 x 0.96 = 1.056 times its old level. Option C is true only for unit elastic demand, and Option B applies when demand is elastic.

questions.question: A negative income elasticity of demand for a good means that as income falls, the quantity of the good purchased:
questions.explanation: A negative income elasticity means quantity and income move in opposite directions, so a fall in income leads to more of the good being bought, which is the case for inferior goods. Option B describes a normal good with positive income elasticity.

questions.question: If the income elasticity of demand for a good is greater than one, the good is a:
questions.explanation: An income elasticity above one means demand rises by a bigger percentage than income, which is the mark of a luxury. Option A, a necessity, has income elasticity between 0 and 1, and Option C, an inferior good, has a negative income elasticity.

questions.question: If the quantity bought of one good stays unchanged when the price of another good changes, the cross elasticity of demand between them is:
questions.explanation: If the quantity of one good does not respond at all to the other good's price, the top of the cross elasticity formula is zero, so cross elasticity is zero and the goods are unrelated. Option A would indicate substitutes and Option B complements.

questions.question: If the income elasticity of demand for a good is 0.4, the good is a:
questions.explanation: An income elasticity of 0.4 is positive but less than one, so demand rises with income but less than proportionately, which is the mark of a necessity. A luxury (A) has income elasticity above one, and a Giffen good (C) is an inferior good with negative income elasticity.

questions.question: For a straight-line, upward-sloping supply curve that cuts the price axis above the origin, the elasticity of supply is:
questions.explanation: Such a supply curve can be written Q = c(P - k), where k is the positive price intercept, so Es = (change in Q/change in P) x (P/Q) = P/(P - k), which is always greater than one. Option B applies to a line through the origin, and Option D to a line that cuts the quantity axis.

questions.question: If an upward-sloping, straight-line supply curve cuts the quantity axis, supply is:
questions.explanation: Such a curve can be written Q = k + cP with k positive, so Es = cP/(k + cP), which is always less than one, meaning supply is inelastic. Option B applies to a line cutting the price axis, and Option C to a line passing through the origin.

questions.question: If an upward-sloping, straight-line supply curve passes through the origin, supply is:
questions.explanation: A line through the origin is Q = cP, so Es = (change in Q/change in P) x (P/Q) = c x P/(cP) = 1 at every point, which is unit elastic. Options A and B apply to lines that cut the quantity axis and the price axis respectively.

questions.question: A horizontal supply curve (parallel to the quantity axis) represents:
questions.explanation: A horizontal supply curve means producers will supply any quantity at one price but nothing below it, so elasticity of supply is infinite: perfectly elastic. Option D, perfectly inelastic supply, is shown by a vertical supply curve.

questions.question: For an inferior good, a fall in consumers' income, other things being equal, causes:
questions.explanation: Consumers buy more of an inferior good when their income falls, because they switch away from dearer alternatives, so the whole demand curve shifts right: an increase in demand. Option B would apply to a normal good, and Options C and D describe movements along the curve, which only a change in the good's own price can cause.

questions.question: Which of the following causes an increase in the supply of a good?

options.a: A fall in the price of inputs
options.b: An increase in the number of producers
options.c: A fall in the price of another good the firms could produce instead

questions.explanation: Cheaper inputs lower production costs, more producers add to market output, and a fall in the price of an alternative product makes producing this good relatively more attractive, so each shifts the supply curve to the right. Since A, B and C are all correct, D is the best answer.

questions.question: Which of these elasticities measures a movement along a demand curve rather than a shift of it?
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand measures the response of quantity demanded to the good's own price, which is a movement along the demand curve. Income elasticity (B) and cross elasticity (C) measure responses to income and to other goods' prices, which shift the demand curve.

questions.question: The cross elasticity of demand between substitutes is:
questions.explanation: When the price of one substitute rises, consumers buy more of the other, so the quantity of one good moves in the same direction as the price of the other and cross elasticity is positive. Option B, a negative cross elasticity, is the mark of complements, and Option A indicates unrelated goods.

questions.question: A movement down along a given demand curve is known as:
questions.explanation: Moving down along the same demand curve means a lower price and a larger quantity demanded, which is called an extension of demand. Option D, a contraction, is a movement up the curve as price rises, while A and B refer to shifts of the whole curve.

questions.question: For a normal good, which of the following would cause an increase in demand?

options.a: A fall in the price of a substitute
options.b: A rise in the price of a complement

questions.explanation: Each listed change actually reduces demand for a normal good: a cheaper substitute draws buyers away (A), a dearer complement makes the pair costlier to use (B), and lower income cuts purchases of normal goods (C). Since none of them raises demand, D is correct.

questions.question: A change in the quantity supplied of a product (a movement along its supply curve) results from a change in:
questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price moves producers along the existing supply curve. Changes in production costs, technology or prices of related products (B, C and D) shift the whole supply curve, which is a change in supply rather than in quantity supplied.

questions.question: An increase in supply means:

options.a: a movement down along a given supply curve
options.b: a movement up along a given supply curve
options.c: a leftward shift of the supply curve
options.d: a rightward shift of the supply curve

questions.explanation: An increase in supply means producers are willing to sell more at every price, which is shown by the whole supply curve shifting to the right. Options A and B are movements along the curve caused by a change in the good's own price, and Option C is a decrease in supply.

questions.question: At any price above the equilibrium price:
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy, creating a surplus (excess supply) that tends to push the price down. Options B and C describe the situation below the equilibrium price, where there is a shortage.

questions.question: An increase in market supply, with demand unchanged, causes:

options.c: a fall in equilibrium price and a rise in equilibrium quantity
options.d: a rise in both equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of supply creates a surplus at the old price, so price falls and, moving along the demand curve, more is bought. Option D is what happens when demand increases, not supply.

questions.question: An increase in market demand, with supply unchanged, results in:

options.c: a fall in equilibrium price and a rise in equilibrium quantity
options.d: a rise in both equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand creates a shortage at the old price, so price rises and producers respond by supplying more, raising both equilibrium price and quantity. Option C describes the effect of an increase in supply instead.

questions.question: A fall in market demand, with supply unchanged, results in:

options.c: a rise in equilibrium price and a fall in equilibrium quantity
options.d: a fall in both equilibrium price and quantity

questions.explanation: A leftward shift of demand creates a surplus at the old price, so price falls and producers move down their supply curve, cutting quantity, so both equilibrium price and quantity fall. Option C describes a decrease in supply, which raises price while cutting quantity.

questions.question: Which elasticity measure uses the average of the two prices and the two quantities?
questions.explanation: Arc elasticity measures elasticity between two points on a demand curve using averages: Ed = (change in Q/average Q)/(change in P/average P), so the answer is the same whichever direction the price moves. Option A, point elasticity, measures elasticity at a single point and needs no averages.

questions.question: If a fall in price leads to a fall in total expenditure on a good, the price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: Spending falls after a price cut only if quantity rises by a smaller percentage than price falls, which means demand is inelastic (Ed less than one). With elastic demand (B) spending would rise, and with unit elasticity (A) it would stay the same.

questions.question: If a tiny change in price leads to an infinitely large change in quantity demanded, demand is:
questions.explanation: Perfectly elastic demand has an elasticity of infinity and is drawn as a horizontal demand curve: even a small price rise makes quantity demanded fall to zero. Option B, perfectly inelastic demand, is the opposite case where quantity does not respond to price at all, and Option C is a milder case with elasticity merely above one.

questions.question: When the demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, the price elasticity of demand is:
questions.explanation: A rectangular hyperbola has P x Q constant, so any percentage fall in price is matched by an equal percentage rise in quantity and elasticity is one at every point. Option C would mean spending rises as price falls, and Option D describes a horizontal demand curve.

questions.question: On a straight-line demand curve, at the point where price elasticity of demand equals one, marginal revenue is:
questions.explanation: MR = P(1 - 1/Ed), using the absolute value of elasticity, so when Ed = 1, MR = P(1 - 1) = 0; this is the midpoint of the linear demand curve where total revenue is at its maximum. MR is positive on the elastic upper half (A) and negative on the inelastic lower half (C).

questions.question: In a free market, when consumers increase their purchases of a good so that ______ exceeds ______, prices tend to rise.
questions.explanation: When demand exceeds supply at the current price, there is a shortage, and buyers competing for the limited goods bid the price up. Option B describes a surplus, which pushes prices down instead.

questions.question: A relative price is:

options.a: the ratio of one price to another
options.b: the difference between one price and another
options.c: the slope of the supply curve
options.d: the slope of the demand curve

questions.explanation: A relative price compares two money prices by dividing one by the other, showing how many units of one good must be given up to get one unit of another. Option B uses subtraction instead of a ratio, which gives a naira amount rather than a rate of exchange between goods.

questions.question: If a chocolate bar costs N200 and a plate of jollof rice costs N1,000, then:

options.a: the money price of a plate of rice is N200
options.b: the relative price of a plate of rice is 1/5 of a chocolate bar
options.c: the relative price of a plate of rice is 5 chocolate bars
options.d: the relative price of a chocolate bar is 5 plates of rice

questions.explanation: Relative price of rice = price of rice / price of chocolate = N1,000/N200 = 5, so one plate of rice costs as much as 5 chocolate bars. Option B turns the ratio upside down, Option D is wrong because a chocolate bar is only 1/5 of a plate of rice, and Option A gives the chocolate bar's money price, not the rice's.

questions.question: If a meat pie costs N500 and a shawarma costs N1,000, then:

options.a: the money price of a shawarma is N500
options.b: the relative price of a meat pie is 2 shawarmas
options.c: the relative price of a meat pie is 1/2 of a shawarma
options.d: the relative price of a shawarma is 1/2 of a meat pie

questions.explanation: Relative price of a meat pie = N500/N1,000 = 1/2, so a meat pie costs half a shawarma (and a shawarma costs 2 meat pies). Options B and D flip the ratio, and Option A is wrong because the money price of a shawarma is N1,000.

questions.question: The opportunity cost of good A in terms of good B equals the:

options.a: ratio of the price of B to the price of A
options.b: ratio of the price of A to the price of B
options.c: price of A minus the price of B
options.d: price of B minus the price of A

questions.explanation: To buy one unit of A you give up PA/PB units of B, so the opportunity cost of A in terms of B is the relative price PA/PB. Option A is the opportunity cost of B in terms of A, and C and D use differences, which are naira amounts rather than quantities of a good forgone.

questions.question: The opportunity cost of a meat pie in terms of shawarma is:

options.a: the price of a meat pie minus the price of a shawarma
options.b: the ratio of the slope of the meat pie supply curve to the slope of the shawarma supply curve
options.c: the ratio of the slope of the meat pie demand curve to the slope of the shawarma demand curve
options.d: the ratio of the price of a meat pie to the price of a shawarma

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost of a meat pie is the number of shawarmas you give up to buy it, which equals the price of a meat pie divided by the price of a shawarma, its relative price. Option A uses a difference, which is a naira amount rather than a number of shawarmas, and B and C use curve slopes, which have nothing to do with this trade-off.

questions.question: Unlike demands, wants are:

options.b: the goods a consumer plans to buy
options.c: the unlimited desires of the consumer
options.d: the goods a consumer has already bought

questions.explanation: Wants are the unlimited desires people have for goods and services, whether or not they can afford them. Demands, by contrast, depend on price and reflect plans to buy, so Options A and B describe demand rather than wants.

questions.question: Demands differ from wants because:

options.a: wants need a plan to buy a good, but demands do not
options.b: demands are unlimited, while wants are limited by income
options.c: wants involve deciding which demands to satisfy, while demands involve no plan to buy
options.d: demands reflect a decision about which wants to satisfy and a plan to buy, while wants are unlimited and involve no plan to buy

questions.explanation: A demand is a want backed by a decision and a plan to buy at a given price with limited income, while wants are unlimited wishes with no buying plan attached. Options A, B and C all reverse the roles of wants and demands.

questions.question: Scarcity guarantees that:
questions.explanation: Scarcity means people's wants are unlimited while their incomes and resources are limited, so they can only turn some of their wants into demands they are able to pay for. That is why wants always exceed demands. Option B would mean scarcity did not exist, option C is impossible because demands come from wants, and option D is not guaranteed by scarcity.

questions.question: The quantity demanded of a good is:

options.a: the amount consumers plan to buy at a particular price
options.d: always equal to the equilibrium quantity

questions.explanation: Quantity demanded is the amount buyers plan to purchase at one particular price, which is a single point on the demand curve. Option B is wrong because quantity demanded changes with price, and Option D is wrong because at prices other than equilibrium, quantity demanded differs from quantity supplied.

questions.question: The law of demand states that, other things equal, the higher the price of a good, the:

options.a: smaller the demand for the good
options.b: smaller the quantity of the good demanded
options.c: larger the quantity of the good demanded
options.d: larger the demand for the good

questions.explanation: The law of demand is about a movement along a demand curve: a higher price reduces the quantity demanded. Option A is tempting, but a 'smaller demand' means the whole curve shifts left, which is caused by factors other than the good's own price.

questions.question: The law of demand implies that, other things equal:

options.a: as the demand for suya rises, its price will fall
options.b: as the price of suya rises, the quantity of suya demanded falls
options.c: as income rises, the quantity of suya demanded rises
options.d: as the price of suya rises, the quantity of suya demanded rises

questions.explanation: The law of demand links a good's own price to its quantity demanded in opposite directions, so a higher price of suya means less suya is demanded. Option C is about income, which shifts demand rather than being part of the law of demand, and Option A is wrong because a rise in demand tends to raise price, not lower it.

questions.question: The law of demand states that the quantity demanded of a good varies:

options.d: inversely with the price of substitute goods

questions.explanation: The law of demand is specifically about the good's own price: as it rises, quantity demanded falls, an inverse relationship. Options B and C are other determinants of demand rather than the law itself, and Option D is wrong because a dearer substitute actually raises demand for the good.

questions.question: Which of these is consistent with the law of demand?

options.a: A fall in the price of sachet water reduces the quantity of sachet water demanded.
options.b: A rise in the price of a soft drink reduces the quantity of soft drinks demanded.
options.c: A rise in the price of a phone charger increases the quantity of chargers demanded.
options.d: A fall in the price of juice leaves the quantity of juice demanded unchanged.

questions.explanation: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so a dearer soft drink leading to fewer being bought fits it exactly. Options A and C show price and quantity moving in the same direction, and Option D shows no response at all, so none of them follows the law.

questions.question: The law of demand implies that, other things equal, the relationship between a good's price and its quantity demanded is:
questions.explanation: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so the relationship is negative and the demand curve slopes downward. Option B would mean quantity rises with price, and the law says nothing about the curve's exact shape, so A and D are not implied.

questions.question: Which of the following affects how much of a good people plan to buy AND changes as we move along that good's demand curve?

options.b: The price of the good itself

questions.explanation: A demand curve plots quantity demanded against the good's own price, so moving along it means only that price is changing. Options A, C and D also affect buying plans, but a change in any of them shifts the whole demand curve instead of moving us along it.

questions.question: Which statement correctly expresses the law of demand?

options.a: A fall in the price of a good shifts its demand curve to the left.
options.b: Holding other things constant, the higher the price of a good, the smaller the quantity demanded.
options.c: Holding other things constant, the higher the price of a good, the larger the quantity demanded.
options.d: A rise in the price of a good shifts its demand curve to the left.

questions.explanation: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, ceteris paribus. Option C reverses this relationship, and Options A and D are wrong because a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the demand curve, not a shift.

questions.question: Because of the law of demand, demand curves

options.a: shift to the left whenever price rises.
options.b: shift to the right whenever price rises.
options.c: slope downward from left to right.
options.d: slope upward from left to right.

questions.explanation: If a higher price means a smaller quantity demanded, then plotting price against quantity gives a downward-sloping curve. Options A and B confuse a price change with a shift, and Option D describes the usual shape of a supply curve.

questions.question: Each point on a demand curve shows

options.a: the highest price consumers are willing and able to pay for that particular unit of the good.
options.b: the highest price sellers will accept for all the units they produce.
options.c: the cheapest technology available for producing the good.
options.d: every want of a given household.

questions.explanation: Read upward from any quantity, the demand curve tells us the maximum price buyers would pay for that last unit, which reflects its marginal benefit to them. Option B mixes in sellers, who are described by the supply curve, and Option D ignores that demand requires both willingness and ability to pay.

questions.question: A fall in the price of Bluetooth earbuds shifts the demand curve for wired earphones to the left. This tells you that Bluetooth earbuds and wired earphones are
questions.explanation: When one good becomes cheaper, people switch to it and buy less of a good that does the same job, so demand for the other good falls. That is the definition of substitutes. If they were complements (Option D), a cheaper earbud would raise demand for earphones, not reduce it.

questions.question: A substitute is a good that

options.a: is of higher quality than another good.
options.b: is not used in place of another good.
options.c: can be used in place of another good.
options.d: is of lower quality than another good.

questions.explanation: Substitutes satisfy the same want, so one can be used instead of the other, like bread and yam for breakfast. Quality has nothing to do with the definition, which rules out Options A and D, and Option B is the opposite of the idea.

questions.question: People buy more of good X when the price of good Y rises. Goods X and Y are
questions.explanation: When Y becomes more expensive, buyers switch towards X, which can take Y's place, so X and Y are substitutes. Complements (Option B) behave the other way: a rise in Y's price would reduce demand for X. Options A and D describe how demand responds to income, not to another good's price.

questions.question: Which pair of goods is most likely to be substitutes?

options.c: Cola drinks and lemon-lime soft drinks

questions.explanation: Two soft drinks satisfy the same want, so a buyer can easily choose one instead of the other. Options A and B are complements, since they are consumed together, while Option D is a pair of unrelated goods.

questions.question: The demand for a good increases when the price of a substitute ________ and also increases when the price of a complement ________.
questions.explanation: A dearer substitute pushes buyers towards our good, and a cheaper complement makes using our good less costly, so both raise its demand. Option C gets the complement wrong, because a dearer complement reduces demand for the good it goes with.

questions.question: A complement is a good that is

options.c: of lower quality than another good.
options.d: of higher quality than another good.

questions.explanation: Complements are consumed jointly, like a car and petrol or a phone and airtime. Option B describes a substitute, and Options C and D bring in quality, which is not part of either definition.

questions.question: People buy more of good X when the price of good Y falls. These goods are
questions.explanation: A cheaper Y leads people to use more Y, and if X is used along with Y they buy more X too, so the goods are complements. With substitutes (Option A), a cheaper Y would cause people to buy less X.

questions.question: As the opportunity cost of a good falls, people buy

options.a: more of that good but less of its complements.
options.b: less of that good and less of its complements.
options.c: less of that good but more of its complements.
options.d: more of that good and more of its complements.

questions.explanation: A good's price is its opportunity cost, so a lower opportunity cost means people buy more of it, and because complements are used together with it, they buy more of those as well. Option A is wrong because complements rise with the good rather than move against it.

questions.question: Motorists come to expect that the price of a litre of petrol will rise next week. As a result,

options.a: next week's supply of petrol decreases.
options.b: the price of petrol falls today.

questions.explanation: Buyers who expect a higher price later try to fill their tanks now, so today's demand curve shifts right. Option C is wrong because sellers expecting higher prices next week would rather hold stock back today, and Option B ignores that higher demand pushes today's price up, not down.

questions.question: The demand curve for a normal good shifts to the left if income ________ or the expected future price ________.
questions.explanation: Lower income reduces demand for a normal good, and if buyers expect the price to fall later they postpone purchases, so demand today falls as well. Option D gets the expectation wrong, because an expected price rise makes people buy more now.

questions.question: If income increases or the price of a complement falls,

options.a: the supply curve of a normal good shifts to the left.
options.b: the supply curve of a normal good shifts to the right.
options.c: the demand curve for a normal good shifts to the right.
options.d: the demand curve for a normal good shifts to the left.

questions.explanation: Both changes make buyers want more of a normal good at every price, so its demand curve shifts right. Options A and B are wrong because income and complement prices affect buyers, not the supply curve.

questions.question: If income decreases or the price of a complement rises,

options.a: there is an upward movement along the good's demand curve.
options.b: there is a downward movement along the good's demand curve.
options.c: the demand curve for a normal good shifts to the left.
options.d: the demand curve for a normal good shifts to the right.

questions.explanation: Lower income and a dearer complement both reduce the amount of a normal good people want at each price, so the whole demand curve shifts left. Options A and B describe movements along the curve, which happen only when the good's own price changes.

questions.question: For a normal good, demand decreases when

options.a: the price of a substitute rises.
options.b: the price of a complement falls.

questions.explanation: A normal good is defined by its link to income, so when income decreases, demand for it falls and the whole demand curve shifts left. Option C is tempting, but a rise in the good's own price only reduces the quantity demanded, a movement along the curve, while a dearer substitute or a cheaper complement (Options A and B) would raise demand.

questions.question: A normal good is a good for which
questions.explanation: Normal goods are bought more as people become richer, so demand moves in the same direction as income. Option B is the definition of an inferior good, and Options A and D have nothing to do with how a good responds to income.

questions.question: Most goods
questions.explanation: For most things people buy, demand rises as income rises, which makes them normal goods. Demand curves usually slope downward and supply curves upward, so Options A and B are wrong, and most pairs of goods are not used together, so Option D fails.

questions.question: Inferior goods are those for which demand increases as

options.c: the price of a complement rises.
options.d: the price of a substitute falls.

questions.explanation: With an inferior good, people buy more when they become poorer and switch away from it as they become richer, so demand rises as income decreases. Option B describes a normal good, and Options C and D would actually reduce demand, since a dearer complement and a cheaper substitute both draw buyers away.

questions.question: By definition, an inferior good is a

options.a: normal good that is also a substitute.
options.b: good for which demand decreases when its own price rises.
options.c: want that is not backed by demand.
options.d: good for which demand decreases when income increases.

questions.explanation: An inferior good is one people buy less of as their income rises, often because they can now afford a preferred alternative. Option B confuses the law of demand, which applies to almost all goods, with the income-based definition of an inferior good.

questions.question: If a good is inferior, purchases of it will decrease when

options.d: the price of a substitute rises.

questions.explanation: Demand for an inferior good moves opposite to income, so higher income means people buy less of it. Options A, B and D would all increase purchases rather than decrease them.

questions.question: When economists say that preferences influence demand, they mean

options.a: whether a good is available to all income groups.
options.b: directly observable changes in prices and incomes.
options.c: the excess of wants over the available supply.
options.d: an individual's attitudes and tastes towards goods and services.

questions.explanation: Preferences are people's likes and dislikes, which shape how much they want of a good at any price. Option B lists prices and incomes, which are separate determinants of demand, and Option C describes scarcity rather than preferences.

questions.question: In one year, 200,000 gas cookers were demanded at a price of N150,000 each. The next year, more than 200,000 were demanded at the same price. This increase could be caused by any of the following EXCEPT

options.a: an increase in the supply of gas cookers.
options.c: an increase in income, if gas cookers are a normal good.
options.d: a fall in the price of cooking gas, a complement of gas cookers.

questions.explanation: More cookers demanded at an unchanged price means the demand curve has shifted right, and a change in supply does not shift demand. Options B, C and D are all genuine causes of higher demand: more buyers, more income for a normal good, and a cheaper complement.

questions.question: A change in the price of a good

options.a: shifts its demand curve but does not cause a movement along it.
options.b: does not shift its demand curve but does cause a movement along it.
options.c: shifts its demand curve and also causes a movement along it.
options.d: neither shifts its demand curve nor causes a movement along it.

questions.explanation: The good's own price is on the axis of the demand curve, so a change in it moves us to a different point on the same curve. Options A and C are wrong because only changes in other factors, such as income or related prices, shift the curve.

questions.question: A fall in the price of a good

options.a: shifts its demand curve to the left and decreases the quantity demanded.
options.b: shifts its demand curve to the left but leaves the quantity demanded unchanged.
options.c: does not shift its demand curve but decreases the quantity demanded.
options.d: does not shift its demand curve but increases the quantity demanded.

questions.explanation: A lower price moves buyers down along the same demand curve to a larger quantity demanded. Option C gets the direction wrong, since cheaper goods are bought in larger amounts, and Options A and B are wrong because a change in the good's own price never shifts its demand curve.

questions.question: A decrease in quantity demanded caused by a rise in price is shown by a

options.a: movement up and to the left along the demand curve.
options.b: movement down and to the right along the demand curve.
options.c: leftward shift of the demand curve.
options.d: rightward shift of the demand curve.

questions.explanation: A higher price puts us higher up the curve, and the smaller quantity puts us further left, so we slide up and to the left. Option C is tempting, but a leftward shift is a decrease in demand caused by something other than the good's own price.

questions.question: A change in which of the following alters people's buying plans for cars but does NOT shift the demand curve for cars?

options.a: A 10 percent fall in the price of car insurance
options.b: A 20 percent rise in the price of a car
options.c: A 5 percent rise in people's incomes
options.d: A growing preference for walking instead of driving

questions.explanation: The price of the car itself causes a movement along the demand curve for cars rather than a shift. Insurance is a complement (Option A), income is a demand determinant (Option C) and tastes (Option D) also matter, and all of these shift the demand curve.

questions.question: Which of the following would NOT shift the demand curve for chicken?

options.a: A change in consumers' taste for chicken
options.b: A fall in the price of beef
options.d: A change in the price of chicken

questions.explanation: A change in chicken's own price moves buyers along the existing demand curve for chicken. Tastes, the price of a substitute such as beef, and income (Options A, B and C) are all factors that shift the curve.

questions.question: When we say demand has increased, we mean there is a

options.a: movement to the right along the demand curve.
options.b: movement to the left along the demand curve.
options.c: leftward shift of the demand curve.
options.d: rightward shift of the demand curve.

questions.explanation: An increase in demand means buyers want more at every price, so the whole curve moves to the right. Option A is an increase in quantity demanded caused by a lower price, which is a different idea.

questions.question: The quantity supplied of a good is

options.a: the difference between the quantity available and the quantity desired by all buyers and sellers.
options.b: the same as the quantity demanded at each price.
options.c: the amount producers plan to sell at a particular price during a given period.
options.d: the amount a firm would sell if it faced no resource constraints.

questions.explanation: Quantity supplied is a planned amount linked to a specific price and time period. Option B confuses it with quantity demanded, which equals quantity supplied only at equilibrium, and Option D ignores that real firms always face limited resources.

questions.question: The quantity supplied of a good or service is the amount that a producer

options.a: actually sells at a particular price in a given period.
options.b: ought to sell at a particular price in a given period.
options.c: is willing to sell at a particular price in a given period.
options.d: needs to sell at a particular price in a given period.

questions.explanation: Quantity supplied describes producers' plans: how much they are willing to offer at a given price. Option A is tempting, but actual sales may differ from plans if there is a shortage or surplus.

questions.question: A fall in the price of a good leads producers to reduce the quantity of it they are willing to offer. This illustrates

options.c: the nature of an inferior good.

questions.explanation: The law of supply says that, other things equal, a higher price raises quantity supplied and a lower price reduces it. Option A is wrong because a price-driven change is a change in quantity supplied, not a shift in supply, and Option B is about buyers rather than producers.

questions.question: Each point on a supply curve shows

options.a: the highest price sellers can get for each unit over time.
options.b: the lowest price buyers will accept for each unit of the good.
options.c: the lowest price at which a supplier is willing to sell one more unit.
options.d: the highest price buyers will pay for the good.

questions.explanation: Read upward from a quantity, the supply curve gives the minimum price that covers the cost of producing that extra unit. Options B and D are about buyers, which the demand curve describes, and Option A turns a minimum into a maximum.

questions.question: Because marginal cost rises as output increases, most supply curves
questions.explanation: If each extra unit costs more to produce, producers need a higher price to offer more, so the supply curve slopes upward. A downward slope (Option B) is the typical shape of a demand curve.

questions.question: A supply curve shows the relationship between the quantity supplied of a good and

options.a: the price of the good, and it usually slopes downward.
options.b: income, and it usually slopes upward.
options.c: income, and it usually slopes downward.
options.d: the price of the good, and it usually slopes upward.

questions.explanation: Supply links quantity supplied to the good's own price, and because higher prices encourage more output, the curve slopes upward. Option A has the right variable but the wrong slope, and income (Options B and C) is a demand factor, not what the supply curve plots.

questions.question: A supply curve differs from a supply schedule because a supply curve

options.a: is a graph, while a supply schedule is a table.
options.b: holds the number of sellers constant, while the schedule lets it vary.
options.c: holds input prices constant, while the schedule lets them vary.
options.d: represents one firm, while the schedule represents the whole market.

questions.explanation: A supply schedule and a supply curve carry the same information, one as a table of prices and quantities and the other as a graph. Both hold all other factors constant, so Options B and C are wrong, and either can describe a single firm or a whole market, so Option D is wrong too.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT held constant as we move along a supply curve?

options.a: Prices of the inputs used in production
options.d: The price of the good itself

questions.explanation: Moving along a supply curve means the good's own price is changing, so that is the one thing allowed to vary. Input prices, expectations and the number of sellers (Options A, B and C) are held constant, and a change in any of them shifts the curve.

questions.question: If a producer can use the same resources to produce either good X or good Y, then X and Y are
questions.explanation: When resources used for one good must be taken away from the other, the goods compete for those resources, which makes them substitutes in production. Complements in production (Option C) come out together from one process, like beef and hides, and Options A and B describe buyers, not producers.

questions.question: Goods X and Y are substitutes in production. The demand for X increases, so the price of X rises. This rise in the price of X shifts the

options.a: demand curve for Y to the right.
options.b: demand curve for Y to the left.
options.c: supply curve of Y to the right.
options.d: supply curve of Y to the left.

questions.explanation: A higher price for X makes it more profitable, so producers move resources from Y into X and the supply of Y decreases. Options A and B are wrong because the link here runs through production, not through buyers of Y.

questions.question: A Lagos bakery can use its ovens to bake either bread or meat pies, so the two are substitutes in production. A rise in the price of meat pies will cause

options.a: a decrease in the supply of bread.
options.b: an increase in the quantity of bread supplied but not in the supply of bread.
options.c: a decrease in the quantity of bread supplied but not in the supply of bread.
options.d: an increase in the supply of bread.

questions.explanation: Dearer meat pies draw oven time away from bread, so the bakery offers less bread at every bread price, which is a decrease in supply. Option C is wrong because the price of bread itself has not changed, so this is a shift of the bread supply curve rather than a movement along it.

questions.question: Goods X and Y are substitutes in production. The demand for X decreases, lowering the price of X. The fall in the price of X
questions.explanation: With X less profitable, producers shift resources into Y, so the supply of Y increases. Options A and B are tempting but wrong because substitutes in production are linked through sellers' choices, not buyers'.

questions.question: An increase in the number of fast-food restaurants

options.a: increases the demand for substitutes for fast-food meals.
options.b: raises the price of fast-food meals.
options.c: increases the supply of fast-food meals.
options.d: increases the demand for fast-food meals.

questions.explanation: More sellers means more meals are offered at every price, so the supply curve shifts right. Option D confuses sellers with buyers, and Option B gets the price effect backwards, since higher supply tends to lower price.

questions.question: Technological improvements that lower the cost of producing cars have increased

options.a: the demand for cars but not the supply.
options.b: both the supply of and the demand for cars.
options.c: the supply of cars but not the demand.
options.d: neither the supply of nor the demand for cars.

questions.explanation: Lower production costs let producers offer more cars at each price, which shifts supply to the right. Demand is unaffected because buyers' incomes, tastes and related prices have not changed, which rules out Options A and B.

questions.question: Which of the following will shift the supply curve of good X to the left?

options.b: A rise in the cost of the machinery used to produce X
options.c: A fall in the wages of workers who produce X
options.d: A technological improvement in producing X

questions.explanation: Higher input costs make production less profitable, so producers offer less at every price and supply shifts left. Options C and D lower costs and shift supply right, and Option A is a shortage, which changes price rather than shifting supply.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT shift the supply curve?

options.a: A rise in the price of the good
options.b: A fall in the price of a substitute in production
options.c: A fall in the wages of labour used to produce the good

questions.explanation: A change in the good's own price moves producers along the existing supply curve. Options B, C and D change production costs or profitability, so each of them shifts the curve.

questions.question: If the price of a good changes but everything else affecting sellers' plans stays the same, there is a

options.a: rotation of the supply curve around the initial price.
options.b: new supply curve to the right of the original one.
options.c: new supply curve to the left of the original one.

questions.explanation: When only the good's own price changes, sellers move to a different point on the same supply curve. Options B and C would need a change in some other factor such as costs, technology or the number of sellers.

questions.question: A decrease in the quantity supplied is shown by a

options.a: rightward shift of the supply curve.
options.b: movement down along the supply curve.
options.c: leftward shift of the supply curve.
options.d: movement up along the supply curve.

questions.explanation: Quantity supplied falls when the good's price falls, which moves sellers down and to the left along the upward-sloping supply curve. Option C is tempting, but a leftward shift is a decrease in supply caused by something other than the good's own price.

questions.question: Which of the following increases the quantity supplied of good X but NOT the supply of good X?

options.a: A rise in the price of X
options.b: A rise in the price of Y, a complement in production of X
options.c: An improvement in the technology for producing X
options.d: A fall in the price of resources used to produce X

questions.explanation: Only a change in the good's own price causes a movement along the supply curve, which is a change in quantity supplied. Options B, C and D each shift the supply curve of X to the right, which is an increase in supply.

questions.question: The interaction of demand and supply determines

options.a: both the prices and the quantities of goods and services.
options.b: the quantities of goods and services but not their prices.
options.c: the prices of goods and services but not their quantities.
options.d: neither the prices nor the quantities of goods and services.

questions.explanation: Where the demand and supply curves cross we read off both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity. Options B and C each leave out one half of what the market determines.

questions.question: When the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied,

options.a: the government must be intervening in the market.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium is the price at which buyers' plans and sellers' plans match exactly, so nothing pushes the price to change. A shortage or surplus (Options B and C) needs the two quantities to differ, and markets reach equilibrium without government action, so Option A is wrong.

questions.question: When the price is below the equilibrium price, the quantity demanded

options.a: is less than the equilibrium quantity, and the quantity supplied is greater than it.
options.b: is greater than the equilibrium quantity, and the quantity supplied is less than it.
options.c: is greater than the equilibrium quantity, and so is the quantity supplied.
options.d: is less than the equilibrium quantity, and so is the quantity supplied.

questions.explanation: A lower price moves buyers down their demand curve to a larger quantity and moves sellers down their supply curve to a smaller quantity. Option A describes a price above equilibrium, and Options C and D ignore that demand and supply respond to price in opposite directions.

questions.question: A price below the equilibrium price results in
questions.explanation: Below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers offer, so quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, which is a shortage. Options C and D mean the same thing, a surplus, which happens when price is above equilibrium, and a shortage pushes price up, not down as Option A says.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes how price changes eliminate a shortage?

options.a: As the price falls, quantity demanded increases and quantity supplied decreases.
options.b: As the price rises, quantity demanded decreases and quantity supplied increases.
options.c: As the price falls, quantity demanded decreases and quantity supplied increases.
options.d: As the price rises, quantity demanded increases and quantity supplied decreases.

questions.explanation: In a shortage, buyers compete for the limited goods and bid the price up; the higher price cuts quantity demanded and encourages more supply until the gap closes. Option A would make the shortage worse, and Option D gets both responses backwards.

questions.question: A shortage causes the

options.a: supply curve to shift to the right.
options.d: demand curve to shift to the left.

questions.explanation: When quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, frustrated buyers offer more and sellers raise their prices. Options A and D are wrong because a shortage leads to movements along the curves as price adjusts, not shifts of the curves.

questions.question: If the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied, there is

options.a: a shortage, and the price is above the equilibrium price.
options.b: a surplus, and the price is below the equilibrium price.
options.c: a shortage, and the price is below the equilibrium price.
options.d: a surplus, and the price is above the equilibrium price.

questions.explanation: Excess quantity demanded is a shortage, and it only happens when the price is too low to clear the market. Option A names the shortage correctly but puts the price on the wrong side of equilibrium.

questions.question: A surplus occurs when the price is

options.d: at any level, because a surplus does not depend on price.

questions.explanation: Above equilibrium, sellers offer more than buyers want, leaving unsold stock. Option C describes the condition for a shortage, and Option A is where neither a surplus nor a shortage exists.

questions.question: If the quantity supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, there is

options.a: a shortage, and the price is below the equilibrium price.
options.b: a surplus, and the price is below the equilibrium price.
options.c: a surplus, and the price is above the equilibrium price.
options.d: a shortage, and the price is above the equilibrium price.

questions.explanation: Excess quantity supplied is a surplus, which arises when the price is set too high for the market to clear. Option B names the surplus correctly but places the price below equilibrium, where a shortage would occur instead.

questions.question: The price of a good will fall if

options.a: the price of a complement falls.
options.b: there is a surplus at the current price.
options.c: the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied.
options.d: the current price is below the equilibrium price.

questions.explanation: With unsold goods piling up, sellers cut their prices to clear their stock. Options C and D describe a shortage, which pushes the price up, and Option A raises demand for the good, which also tends to raise its price.

questions.question: A market analyst records the following schedules for the market for honey beans in Lagos. Price (N per kg): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. Quantity demanded (millions of kg per year) - Demand 1: 15, 12, 9, 6, 3; Demand 2: 10, 8, 6, 3, 2; Demand 3: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Quantity supplied (millions of kg per year) - Supply A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Supply B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Supply C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. In a normal year, demand is Demand 2 and supply is Supply B. In a normal year, the price of honey beans will be
questions.explanation: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: with Demand 2 and Supply B, both equal 6 million kg at N300. At N200 (Option C) buyers want 8 million kg but sellers offer only 4 million, a shortage, and at N400 (Option B) sellers offer 8 million while buyers want 3 million, a surplus.

questions.question: A market analyst records the following schedules for the market for honey beans in Lagos. Price (N per kg): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. Quantity demanded (millions of kg per year) - Demand 1: 15, 12, 9, 6, 3; Demand 2: 10, 8, 6, 3, 2; Demand 3: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1.
