Quantity supplied (millions of kg per year) - Supply A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Supply B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Supply C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. In a normal year, demand is Demand 2 and supply is Supply B. In a normal year, the equilibrium quantity of honey beans will be
questions.explanation: Under Demand 2 and Supply B, the only price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is N300, and the quantity there is 6 million kg. Options A and B are the quantities demanded and supplied at N200, where the market is in shortage rather than equilibrium.

questions.question: A market analyst records the following schedules for the market for honey beans in Lagos. Price (N per kg): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. Quantity demanded (millions of kg per year) - Demand 1: 15, 12, 9, 6, 3; Demand 2: 10, 8, 6, 3, 2; Demand 3: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Quantity supplied (millions of kg per year) - Supply A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Supply B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Supply C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. In a normal year, demand is Demand 2 and supply is Supply B. If a drought hits the bean-growing areas, supply will ________ and demand will ________.

options.a: stay at Supply B; become Demand 3
options.b: stay at Supply B; become Demand 1
options.d: become Supply A; stay at Demand 2

questions.explanation: A drought reduces the harvest, so sellers offer less at every price, which is the move from Supply B to the smaller Supply A. Nothing has changed for buyers, so demand stays at Demand 2; Options A and B wrongly treat the drought as a change in demand.

questions.question: A market analyst records the following schedules for the market for honey beans in Lagos. Price (N per kg): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. Quantity demanded (millions of kg per year) - Demand 1: 15, 12, 9, 6, 3; Demand 2: 10, 8, 6, 3, 2; Demand 3: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Quantity supplied (millions of kg per year) - Supply A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Supply B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Supply C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. In a normal year, demand is Demand 2 and supply is Supply B. If the bean-growing areas enjoy exceptionally good weather, supply will ________ and demand will ________.

options.a: stay at Supply B; become Demand 1
options.b: become Supply C; stay at Demand 2

questions.explanation: Good weather increases the harvest, so the market moves to Supply C, which offers more beans at every price. Buyers' incomes, tastes and other factors are unchanged, so demand remains Demand 2, which rules out Options C and D.

questions.question: A market analyst records the following schedules for the market for honey beans in Lagos. Price (N per kg): 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. Quantity demanded (millions of kg per year) - Demand 1: 15, 12, 9, 6, 3; Demand 2: 10, 8, 6, 3, 2; Demand 3: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Quantity supplied (millions of kg per year) - Supply A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Supply B: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10; Supply C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. In a normal year, demand is Demand 2 and supply is Supply B. If it is discovered that honey beans help prevent a serious disease, supply will ________ and demand will ________.

options.a: stay at Supply B; become Demand 1
options.b: become Supply C; stay at Demand 2

questions.explanation: A health discovery changes buyers' preferences, so people want more beans at every price and demand moves to the larger Demand 1. Growing conditions and costs are unchanged, so supply stays at Supply B; Options C and D wrongly shift supply as well.

questions.question: When the demand for a good decreases (and supply is unchanged), its equilibrium price ________ and its equilibrium quantity ________.
questions.explanation: A leftward shift of demand along an unchanged upward-sloping supply curve moves the equilibrium down and to the left, so both price and quantity fall. Option A would need supply, not demand, to decrease.

questions.question: Good A is a normal good. If income increases, the equilibrium price of A

options.a: and its equilibrium quantity both increase.
options.b: and its equilibrium quantity both decrease.
options.c: rises and its equilibrium quantity decreases.
options.d: falls and its equilibrium quantity increases.

questions.explanation: Higher income raises demand for a normal good, shifting demand right along the supply curve, so price and quantity both go up. Option B would be the result for an inferior good, and Options C and D come from supply shifts.

questions.question: The price of a litre of milk falls. Which of the following could be the cause?

options.a: A discovery that drinking milk causes diabetes
options.b: A drought that reduces the supply of feed for dairy cows
options.c: A rise in average household income, with milk a normal good
options.d: A fall in the price of oats, a complement of milk

questions.explanation: A health scare cuts demand for milk, and lower demand with unchanged supply lowers the price. Option B reduces supply, while Options C and D raise demand, and all three would push the price of milk up.

questions.question: Beef and pork are substitutes for consumers. A drought hits the cattle-grazing areas. The drought will cause the

options.a: supply curve of pork to shift to the right.
options.b: supply curve of pork to shift to the left.
options.c: demand curve for pork to shift to the left.
options.d: demand curve for pork to shift to the right.

questions.explanation: The drought cuts the supply of beef and raises its price, so consumers switch to pork and the demand for pork increases. Options A and B are wrong because the drought affects cattle, not pig farming, so pork supply is unchanged.

questions.question: An increase in demand with no change in supply causes

options.a: a decrease in demand, because supply does not shift.
options.c: a movement to the right along the demand curve.

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of demand creates a shortage at the old price, which pushes the price up to a new, higher equilibrium. Option C is wrong because the demand curve itself has shifted; the movement that happens is along the supply curve.

questions.question: Goods A and B are complements in consumption. The cost of an input used to produce A falls. As a result,

options.a: the equilibrium price of B falls and the equilibrium price of A rises.
options.b: the equilibrium prices of both A and B rise.
options.c: the equilibrium price of B rises and the equilibrium price of A falls.
options.d: the equilibrium prices of both A and B fall.

questions.explanation: Cheaper inputs increase the supply of A, so A's price falls and more A is bought. Because B is used with A, demand for B rises and B's price goes up. Option D is tempting but forgets that the link to B runs through higher demand, which raises B's price.

questions.question: When supply decreases and demand does not change, the equilibrium quantity
questions.explanation: Supply shifting left along a fixed demand curve creates a shortage at the old price, so price rises and the quantity bought falls. Option C would come from a decrease in demand, not supply.

questions.question: Beef and leather are complements in production (hides come from the same cattle). If health concerns shift the demand for beef to the left, the market for leather belts will see a

options.a: lower equilibrium price for belts, because the supply of belts increases.
options.b: higher equilibrium price for belts, because the supply of belts decreases.
options.c: lower equilibrium price for belts, because the supply of belts decreases.
options.d: higher equilibrium price for belts, because the supply of belts increases.

questions.explanation: Less beef demanded means fewer cattle slaughtered, which means fewer hides, so the supply of leather belts decreases and their price rises. Option C gets the supply change right but the price effect wrong, since lower supply raises price.

questions.question: You observe that the price of a good rises while the quantity traded falls. This could be the result of

options.a: the supply curve shifting to the right.
options.b: the demand curve shifting to the right.
options.c: the demand curve shifting to the left.
options.d: the supply curve shifting to the left.

questions.explanation: Price and quantity moving in opposite directions points to a supply shift, and a higher price with lower quantity means supply decreased. Option B would raise both price and quantity, and Option C would lower both.

questions.question: Leather belts and leather shoes are substitutes in production. If fashion changes increase the demand for leather belts, the supply curve of leather shoes will shift

options.a: to the right, and the price of leather shoes will fall.
options.b: to the left, and the price of leather shoes will rise.
options.c: to the left, and the price of leather shoes will fall.
options.d: to the right, and the price of leather shoes will rise.

questions.explanation: Higher belt prices pull leather and labour away from shoes, so the supply of shoes decreases and their equilibrium price rises. Option C has the right shift but the wrong price effect, because a fall in supply raises price.

questions.question: If both demand and supply increase, what happens to the equilibrium price and quantity?

options.a: Price rises, but quantity could increase, decrease or stay the same.
options.b: Quantity increases, but price could rise, fall or stay the same.

questions.explanation: Both shifts push quantity up, so quantity definitely increases, but the demand shift pushes price up while the supply shift pushes it down. Which effect wins depends on the size of the shifts, so Options C and D claim more certainty about price than we have.

questions.question: The price will rise while the equilibrium quantity might increase, decrease or stay the same when
questions.explanation: Higher demand and lower supply both push price up, so price definitely rises, while their effects on quantity cancel in an uncertain way. Options A and B give a definite change in quantity but an uncertain price, the reverse of what is described.

questions.question: The price will fall while the equilibrium quantity might increase, decrease or stay the same when
questions.explanation: Lower demand and higher supply both push price down, while one lowers quantity and the other raises it, so the quantity effect is uncertain. Option A is the mirror case, in which price definitely rises.

questions.question: The equilibrium quantity will decrease while the price might rise, fall or stay the same when
questions.explanation: When both curves shift left, each one reduces quantity, but the fall in demand lowers price while the fall in supply raises it. Option D also leaves price uncertain, but there quantity rises rather than falls.

questions.question: The equilibrium quantity of a good will increase while its price might rise, fall or stay the same when
questions.explanation: Two rightward shifts both raise quantity, but their price effects work against each other. Options A and B give a definite price change with an uncertain quantity, which is the opposite pattern.

questions.question: Over several years, the price of solar inverters fell even though improving technology, rising incomes and falling prices of solar panels (a complement) were all affecting the market. The price fell because

options.a: demand for inverters shifted right by more than supply shifted right.
options.b: supply of inverters shifted right by more than demand shifted right.
options.c: demand for inverters and supply of inverters both shifted left.
options.d: supply of inverters shifted right while demand for inverters shifted left.

questions.explanation: Better technology raises supply, while higher incomes and cheaper panels raise demand, so both curves shift right. For the price to fall, the supply increase must have been larger than the demand increase. Option A would raise the price, and Option D is wrong because the demand factors described all increase demand.

questions.question: The demand and supply functions for a good are Qd = 20 - 2P and Qs = 5 + 3P, where P is the price in naira. The equilibrium price is
questions.explanation: At equilibrium Qd = Qs, so 20 - 2P = 5 + 3P, which gives 15 = 5P and P = 3. At P = 2 (Option A), Qd = 16 but Qs = 11, so there would still be a shortage.

questions.question: The demand and supply functions for a good are Qd = 20 - 2P and Qs = 5 + 3P, where P is the price in naira. The equilibrium quantity is
questions.explanation: Setting 20 - 2P = 5 + 3P gives P = 3, and substituting back gives Qd = 20 - 6 = 14 and Qs = 5 + 9 = 14. Option D is the equilibrium price, not the quantity, and Options B and C are just the intercepts of the two equations.

questions.question: A consumer would most likely regard roller skates and elbow pads as
questions.explanation: Elbow pads are bought to be used while skating, so the two goods are consumed together, which makes them complements. They are not substitutes (Option B), because one cannot replace the other.

questions.question: A fall in the price of renting a five-a-side football pitch shifts the

options.a: demand curve for football boots to the right.
options.b: supply curve of football boots to the left.
options.c: supply curve of football boots to the right.
options.d: demand curve for football boots to the left.

questions.explanation: Cheaper pitch rental means more people play, and since boots are used with the pitch, the two are complements and demand for boots rises. Options B and C are wrong because pitch prices affect buyers of boots, not the cost of making them.

questions.question: If a fall in the price of petrol increases the demand for large cars, then

options.a: petrol and large cars are complements in consumption.
options.b: large cars are an inferior good.
options.d: petrol and large cars are substitutes in consumption.

questions.explanation: When a cheaper good raises demand for another good, the two are used together, which defines complements. With substitutes (Option D), cheaper petrol would reduce demand for cars, and Options B and C are about income effects, not related prices.

questions.question: Assume that second-hand clothing is an inferior good. A fall in people's incomes

options.a: shifts the supply curve of second-hand clothing to the left.
options.b: shifts the demand curve for second-hand clothing to the right.
options.c: shifts the demand curve for second-hand clothing to the left.
options.d: decreases the quantity of second-hand clothing supplied.

questions.explanation: For an inferior good, demand moves opposite to income, so poorer consumers buy more of it at every price and demand shifts right. Option C is what would happen to a normal good, and Options A and D wrongly link income to the sellers' side.

questions.question: An unusually short and light rainy season

options.a: shifts the supply curve of umbrellas to the left.
options.b: shifts the demand curve for umbrellas to the right.
options.c: shifts the demand curve for umbrellas to the left.
options.d: shifts the supply curve of umbrellas to the right.

questions.explanation: With less rain, people need umbrellas less, so they want fewer at every price and demand shifts left. The weather does not change the cost of making umbrellas, so Options A and D are wrong.

questions.question: A rise in the price of a good leads producers to supply more of it. This illustrates

options.a: the nature of an inferior good.

questions.explanation: The law of supply says that, other things equal, a higher price raises the quantity supplied. Option D is wrong because a response to the good's own price is a movement along the supply curve, and Option B describes buyers rather than producers.

questions.question: The price of aviation fuel falls. This shifts the

options.a: supply curve of air travel to the right.
options.b: demand curve for air travel to the left.
options.c: demand curve for air travel to the right.
options.d: supply curve of air travel to the left.

questions.explanation: Fuel is a major input for airlines, so cheaper fuel lowers their costs and they offer more flights at every fare. Option C is tempting, but fuel is bought by airlines, not passengers, so the effect works through supply.

questions.question: If there is a surplus of a good, the quantity demanded ________ the quantity supplied, and the price will ________.
questions.explanation: A surplus means sellers have more than buyers want, so quantity demanded is below quantity supplied and sellers cut prices to clear stock. Option A gets the quantities right but the price direction wrong.

questions.question: Shawarma and burgers are substitutes for consumers. A fall in the price of shawarma ________ the price of burgers and ________ the quantity of burgers bought.
questions.explanation: Cheaper shawarma draws buyers away from burgers, so demand for burgers shifts left, and with unchanged supply both the price and quantity of burgers fall. Option D is wrong because a decrease in demand reduces quantity rather than increasing it.

questions.question: How does an unusually short and light rainy season affect the equilibrium price and quantity of umbrellas?

options.a: It lowers both the price and the quantity.
options.b: It raises both the price and the quantity.
options.c: It raises the price and lowers the quantity.
options.d: It lowers the price and raises the quantity.

questions.explanation: Less rain reduces the demand for umbrellas, and a leftward demand shift along an unchanged supply curve lowers both price and quantity. Option D would need supply to increase, which the weather does not cause.

questions.question: You notice that the price and the quantity of maize both fall. This could be the result of the

options.a: demand curve for maize shifting to the left.
options.b: supply curve of maize shifting to the right.
options.c: demand curve for maize shifting to the right.
options.d: supply curve of maize shifting to the left.

questions.explanation: When price and quantity move in the same direction, demand has shifted, and since both fell, demand decreased. Option B would lower the price but raise the quantity.

questions.question: A technological improvement lowers the cost of producing coffee. At the same time, consumers' preference for coffee increases. The equilibrium price of coffee will

options.a: rise, fall or stay the same, depending on the relative sizes of the demand and supply shifts.

questions.explanation: Lower costs increase supply, which pushes price down, while stronger preferences increase demand, which pushes price up. Without knowing which shift is larger we cannot say which way price moves, so Options C and D are too certain; only the quantity definitely rises.

questions.question: The price of video-streaming subscriptions rises while the price of DVDs falls. The combined effect of these two changes is

options.a: a leftward shift of the demand curve for DVD players.
options.b: a rightward shift of the demand curve for DVD players.
options.c: a rightward shift of the supply curve of DVD players.
options.d: a leftward shift of the supply curve of DVD players.

questions.explanation: Streaming is a substitute for DVD players, so a dearer subscription raises demand for players, and DVDs are a complement, so cheaper discs also raise demand. Both forces shift demand for DVD players to the right, and neither affects producers' costs, which rules out Options C and D.

questions.question: A Lagos market analyst who studies portable rechargeable fans expects a recession. If rechargeable fans are a normal good, you would predict that the demand for them will
questions.explanation: A recession lowers incomes, and lower income reduces demand for a normal good. Option A would be the prediction for an inferior good.

questions.question: Wages for the workers who make rechargeable fans and similar products will rise next year. What is the main effect you would predict in next year's market for rechargeable fans?

options.a: The demand curve for fans shifts to the left.
options.b: The supply curve of fans shifts to the right.
options.c: The supply curve of fans shifts to the left.
options.d: The demand curve for fans shifts to the right.

questions.explanation: Higher wages raise production costs, so producers offer fewer fans at each price and supply decreases. Option A is wrong because the wage change affects producers' costs rather than buyers' demand.

questions.question: The wage rate paid by producers of rechargeable fans falls, and at the same time the price of the raw materials they use rises. You predict that the supply curve of fans will

options.c: shift either to the left or to the right.

questions.explanation: Cheaper labour increases supply while dearer raw materials decrease it, so the net shift depends on which cost change is bigger. Options A and D each ignore one of the two opposing forces.

questions.question: Basic MP3 players and smartphones are substitutes. A new technology will soon make smartphones much cheaper to produce. What would you predict for the market for basic MP3 players?

options.a: The demand curve for MP3 players shifts left and their price falls.
options.b: The price of MP3 players rises, and so does the quantity demanded.
options.c: The price of MP3 players falls, and the quantity demanded increases.
options.d: The demand curve for MP3 players shifts right and their price rises.

questions.explanation: Cheaper production lowers the price of smartphones, and since smartphones are a substitute, buyers move away from MP3 players. Demand for MP3 players shifts left, lowering their price and quantity. Option C wrongly treats the change as a movement along the demand curve.

questions.question: Producers of rechargeable fans will be able to lower the wage rate they pay their workers. What happens to the supply of fans and the price of a fan?

options.a: Supply shifts left and the price stays the same.
options.b: Supply shifts right and the price falls.
options.c: Supply shifts left and the price rises.
options.d: Supply shifts right and the price stays the same.

questions.explanation: Lower wage costs increase supply, and with unchanged demand the larger supply creates a surplus at the old price, so the price falls. Option D is wrong because a supply shift along a downward-sloping demand curve always changes the equilibrium price.

questions.question: The accumulated skill and knowledge of human beings is called
questions.explanation: Human capital is the stock of skills, knowledge and experience that people build up through education, training and work. Option B, education, is one way of building human capital, not the stock itself. Option C is the cost of schooling, and option A is not an economic term.

questions.question: A locus showing different inputs that will give same level of output is called

options.a: Locus of point equidistance from the centre.

questions.explanation: An isoquant joins all the combinations of inputs, such as labour and capital, that produce the same level of output. Option D, an isocost line, shows input combinations with the same total cost, not the same output. Option B, an isoprofit line, joins points of equal profit.

questions.question: If output increased by 50% following a 60% increase in inputs, the firm is operating under
questions.explanation: Output rose by 50% while inputs rose by 60%, so output grew by less than inputs (50/60 is about 0.83), which is decreasing returns to scale. Option A would need output to rise by more than 60%, and option C would need exactly 60%. Option D, diminishing returns, is a short-run idea about adding one variable input, not about increasing all inputs together.

questions.question: In the long run which costs to the firm are fixed?
questions.explanation: In the long run all inputs can be changed, so no costs are fixed; every cost becomes variable. Options A, B and C name types of cost that can still change in the long run, so none of them is fixed.

questions.question: The U-Shaped nature of the average cost curve is due to the operation of the
questions.explanation: In the short run, average cost first falls as variable inputs are used more fully and then rises once diminishing returns set in, which gives the U shape. Option B, comparative cost, is a trade idea, and option C explains market prices, not a firm's cost curve.

questions.question: To the economists, the cost of producing any good or service is the
questions.explanation: Economists measure the cost of producing anything as its opportunity cost, the value of the next best alternative use of the resources, which includes both explicit and implicit costs. Option A just repeats the question. Option B (explicit costs) and option D (implicit costs) are each only part of opportunity cost.

questions.question: The money costs which an accountant records in the firms books are known as
questions.explanation: Explicit costs are actual money payments, such as wages and rent, which an accountant records in the firm's books. Option B, implicit costs, are the value of resources the firm already owns (like the owner's time) and are not recorded as payments. Option C includes these implicit costs too.

questions.question: Any surplus earned by any factor of production above the minimum payment necessary to induce the factor to work is
questions.explanation: Economic rent is any payment to a factor above its transfer earnings, the minimum needed to keep it in its current use. Option A, transfer payment, is money paid without any productive service in return, such as a pension. Options B and C are value judgements, not economic terms.

questions.question: Based on the marginal productivity theory, the demand for labour curve is determined by
questions.explanation: Marginal productivity theory says a firm hires labour up to the point where the extra revenue from the last worker (MRP) equals the wage, so the MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labour. Option C, the MC curve, is the firm's cost curve for output, not labour demand. Option D, MP, is in physical units and needs to be multiplied by revenue to give MRP.

questions.question: Use the table (L / TPL / MPL / P / TR / VMPL / MRPL: 1 / 15 / 15 / 8 / 120 / 120 / 120; 2 / 25 / 10 / 7 / 175 / - / -; 3 / 32 / 7 / 6 / 192 / - / -; Note: L = workers or labour). From the table above, determine the VMPL when 2 workers are employed
questions.explanation: VMPL = P x MPL. When 2 workers are employed, MPL = 10 and P = 7, so VMPL = 7 x 10 = 70. Option A (42) comes from using the third worker's MPL of 7 with P = 6. Option D (192) is total revenue with 3 workers, not VMPL.

questions.question: Use the table (L / TPL / MPL / P / TR / VMPL / MRPL: 1 / 15 / 15 / 8 / 120 / 120 / 120; 2 / 25 / 10 / 7 / 175 / - / -; 3 / 32 / 7 / 6 / 192 / - / -; Note: L = workers or labour). From the table above, determine the MRPL when 2 workers are employed.
questions.explanation: MRPL is the change in total revenue from hiring one more worker. Going from 1 to 2 workers, TR rises from 120 to 175, so MRPL = 175 - 120 = 55. Option B (70) is VMPL (P x MPL), which is larger than MRPL here because price falls as output rises. Option D (120) is the MRPL for the first worker.

questions.question: The price of labour is determined by
questions.explanation: The wage, the price of labour, is determined by the demand for and supply of labour in the labour market. Options A, C and D, mobility, experience and schooling, affect wages by shifting demand or supply, but they do not set the price on their own.

questions.question: There are two effects to changes in the price of labour....
questions.explanation: A change in the wage has a substitution effect, since leisure becomes more or less costly compared with work, and an income effect, since workers become richer or poorer. Options B, C and D are not the standard names for these two effects.

questions.question: In the early years, productive inputs were divided into three namely.....
questions.explanation: Early classical economists grouped factors of production into land, labour and capital. The entrepreneur was added later as a separate fourth factor, which is why options A, B and D, which include the entrepreneur, do not match the early classification.

questions.question: If output increased by 50% following a 50% increase in inputs, the firm is operating under
questions.explanation: Output and inputs both rose by 50%, so output grew in exact proportion to inputs (50/50 = 1), which is constant returns to scale. Option B would need output to rise by less than 50%, and option A by more than 50%. Option D, diminishing returns, is a short-run idea about adding just one variable input.

questions.question: Wage can best be described as
questions.explanation: A wage is the price paid for labour services, determined by labour demand and supply. Option D is wrong because opportunity cost is what the worker gives up, which helps explain the supply of labour, not what a wage is. Option C is too narrow, because wages can be paid daily or monthly, and option A describes the effort, not the payment.

questions.question: Marginal cost curve cut average variable cost and average cost curve from

options.c: from below at their lowest points

questions.explanation: Marginal cost pulls average cost down while it is below it and pulls it up once it is above it, so the MC curve cuts both the AVC and AC curves from below at their minimum points. Option A gets both the direction and the point wrong, since the U-shaped average curves have lowest points, not highest points, where MC crosses them.

questions.question: When a worker earns more than his transfer earnings, the excess is called
questions.explanation: Economic rent is any payment to a factor of production above its transfer earnings, the minimum needed to keep it in its present job. So when a worker earns more than this minimum, the excess is economic rent. Options A, C and D are not standard economic terms for this surplus.

questions.question: ________ is worth in terms of earning of a worker in his next employment should he desire to change his job
questions.explanation: Transfer earnings are what a factor could earn in its next best alternative use, so for a worker it is the pay in the next job he could move to. Option D, transfer payments, are payments like pensions or grants made without any goods or services in return, which is a different idea.

questions.question: Most light electronics industries are shifted from the West to China possibly because

options.b: China is the greatest economy in the world
options.c: cost of labour is cheaper and the technical competencies comparable with the west
options.d: western countries are no more interested in production

questions.explanation: Firms locate production where costs are lower for a given quality of output, and cheaper labour combined with comparable technical skills lowers costs of production. Options A and D are not economic reasons, and option B is not why firms move; size of an economy alone does not lower a firm's costs.

questions.question: The reason the marginal cost curve eventually increases as output increases for the typical firm is because:

options.c: of the law of diminishing returns.

questions.explanation: In the short run, adding more of a variable input to fixed inputs eventually gives smaller and smaller increases in output (diminishing returns), so each extra unit of output costs more and MC rises. Option D, diseconomies of scale, is a long-run idea about changing all inputs, not the short-run MC curve.

questions.question: Marginal rate of Technical Substitution is the ........of an isoquant
questions.explanation: The marginal rate of technical substitution measures how much capital can be replaced by one more unit of labour while output stays the same, which is the slope of the isoquant. Options A, B and C do not describe this rate of exchange.

questions.question: According to Iso-quant analysis, the firm maximizes its profit, when the.............is equal to the price ratio of labour and capital.
questions.explanation: A firm chooses its best input mix where the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line, that is where MRTS of labour for capital equals the ratio of their prices (w/r). Options A and D use the MRS, which belongs to consumer theory, not production.

questions.question: When a firm doubles its inputs and finds that its output has more than doubled, this is known as:

options.c: a violation of the law of diminishing returns.

questions.explanation: When all inputs are increased in the same proportion and output rises by a bigger proportion, the firm enjoys increasing returns to scale; this is what makes its long-run average cost fall (economies of scale). Option A would mean output exactly doubles, and option D means output rises by less than double. Option C is wrong because the law of diminishing returns applies when only one input changes while others stay fixed.

questions.question: Economies and diseconomies of scale explain why the:

options.a: long-run average total cost curve is typically U-shaped.
options.b: short-run average fixed cost curve declines so long as output increases.
options.c: short-run average variable cost curve is U-shaped.
options.d: demand curve slopes downward from left to right.

questions.explanation: Economies of scale make long-run average cost fall as a firm grows, and diseconomies of scale make it rise beyond some size, which gives the U-shaped long-run average cost curve. Option C is also U-shaped, but in the short run that shape comes from diminishing returns, not scale effects. Option B is just fixed cost spread over more units.

questions.question: U-shaped average cost curve is based on:

options.a: Law of constant returns to scale

questions.explanation: The short-run U-shaped average cost curve comes from the law of variable proportions: at first, adding variable inputs to fixed ones raises efficiency and lowers average cost, but eventually diminishing returns set in and average cost rises. Options A, B and D each describe only a flat, rising or falling cost pattern, not the U shape.

questions.question: At which time all the factors of production may be changed:
questions.explanation: The long run is defined as a period long enough for the firm to vary all its factors of production, including plant size. Option B is wrong because in the short run at least one factor, such as capital, is fixed. Option A, the market period, is even shorter, with supply fixed, and option C is wrong because all factors do become variable given enough time.

questions.question: The cost which a firm incurs for purchasing or hiring factors is called:
questions.explanation: Explicit costs are actual money payments a firm makes to buy or hire factors, such as wages, rent and raw materials. Option A, implicit costs, are the opportunity costs of resources the firm already owns, for which no payment is made.

questions.question: When marginal product reaches its maximum, what can be said of total product:

options.b: total product starts to decline even if marginal product is positive
options.c: total product must be at its maximum
options.d: total product is increasing if marginal product is still positive

questions.explanation: Marginal product is the slope of total product. When MP is at its maximum it is still positive, so total product is still rising (this is the point where TP stops rising at an increasing rate). Option C is wrong because TP is at its maximum only when MP falls to zero.

questions.question: The long run is a:

options.a: Period long enough to allow firm to make economic decisions
options.b: A period which affects larger than smaller firms
options.c: Period long enough to allow firms to change plant size and capacity
options.d: Period in which at least one factor of production is fixed

questions.explanation: The long run is a period long enough for firms to change all inputs, including plant size and capacity. Option D describes the short run, when at least one factor is fixed. Option A is too vague, since firms make economic decisions in every period.

questions.question: As output increases:

options.d: MC curve firstly falls then rises

questions.explanation: Marginal cost first falls as the firm gains from using its fixed inputs better, then rises once diminishing returns set in, giving a U-shaped MC curve. Option A ignores the falling stage, and option C gets the order the wrong way round.

questions.question: The relationship between the variable input and output, keeping all other inputs constant, is often referred to as ___ of the variable input:
questions.explanation: Total product shows how much output is produced as more of the variable input is used while other inputs are fixed. Options B and C are derived from total product: marginal product is the extra output per extra unit, and average product is output per unit of the input.

questions.question: An economy's resources can be classified into four dimensions namely: Land resources, capital resources, ________ and innovators.
questions.explanation: The four factors of production are land, capital, labour (human resources) and entrepreneurship (the innovators who organise the others). Option A, financial resources, is a form of capital, so human resources is the missing category.

questions.question: The rate at which one factor of production say, labour, is substituted for the other factor, say capital, in the production process is known as the ________
questions.explanation: The marginal rate of technical substitution is the rate at which one input, such as labour, can replace another, such as capital, while keeping output the same. Option A, the marginal rate of substitution, is the consumer-theory version for goods.

questions.question: The curve showing the locus of all the combinations of two inputs (say, labour and capital) that yield the same level of output is known as
questions.explanation: An isoquant joins all combinations of two inputs, such as labour and capital, that produce the same output. Option D, the indifference curve, is the consumer version, showing combinations of goods that give the same satisfaction.

questions.question: The factors of production that are human related include
questions.explanation: Labour and entrepreneurship are both human efforts: labour is physical and mental work, while the entrepreneur organises production and bears risk. Land is a natural resource and capital is man-made, so options A, B and C each include a non-human factor.

questions.question: The term revenue refers to

options.b: Gross profit obtained by a firm
options.d: The receipts obtained by a firm by selling a commodity at a given price.

questions.explanation: Revenue is the money a firm receives from selling its output, price times quantity sold. Options A, B and C are types of profit, which is revenue minus costs.

questions.question: In a free market structure, the marginal productivity theory states that in equilibrium firm should pay factors a unit price just equal
questions.explanation: The marginal productivity theory says that in equilibrium a factor is paid a price equal to its marginal revenue product, the extra revenue it brings to the firm. Option A is the cost side, not what the factor produces, so it does not fit.

questions.question: For profit maximization, according to the marginal productivity approach, firms must employ factors up to
questions.explanation: A profit-maximising firm keeps hiring a factor until the extra revenue it brings (MRP) equals the extra cost of hiring it (MRC). If MRP > MRC (option C) more should be hired, and if MRP < MRC (option B) fewer should be hired.

questions.question: Diminishing returns is said to occur when

options.a: Total product rises at increasing rate and marginal product declines
options.b: Total product rises at a decreasing rate and marginal product declines
options.c: Total product rises at increasing rate and marginal product rises
options.d: Total product is at a maximum and marginal product declines

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns set in when adding more of a variable input still raises total product but by smaller and smaller amounts, so TP rises at a decreasing rate while MP declines. Option A mixes rapid TP growth with falling MP, option C describes increasing returns, and option D describes the point where diminishing returns have already pushed MP to zero.

questions.question: In the production of automobiles, the factory and assembly lines are examples of
questions.explanation: Factories and assembly lines are man-made aids to production, which is what economists call capital. Option B, labour, is human effort, and option A, land, covers natural resources. Option D, the entrepreneur, is the person who organises these factors.

questions.question: The reward that accrues to the entrepreneur is:
questions.explanation: Profit is the reward for the entrepreneur, who organises the other factors and bears the risk of the business. Option A, interest, is the reward for capital, option B, wages, goes to labour, and option D, rent, goes to land.

questions.question: The purpose of production is to
questions.explanation: Production is undertaken to create goods and services that satisfy human wants. Options B, C and D, higher income, ending poverty and making everyone comfortable, may follow from production, but they are outcomes or policy goals rather than the basic purpose.

questions.question: The possibility of using some of one factor for some of another is known as
questions.explanation: The principle of substitution says that one factor of production can be used in place of another, for example using more machines and fewer workers. Option D, the law of proportions, concerns what happens to output as factor proportions change, not the possibility of swapping them. Options A and C are not standard economic laws.

questions.question: The supply of labour available in a country depend on:

options.a: The number of hours worked by each person per year
options.c: The proportion of the population available for employment

questions.explanation: The supply of labour depends on the size of the population, the share of it available for work, and the number of hours each person works. Options A, B and C each name only one of these determinants, so all of the above is correct.

questions.question: Division of labour paved the way for:
questions.explanation: When work is broken into small specialised tasks, each worker becomes faster and more skilled, which makes large-scale or mass production possible. Option A is not the main result, and option D may happen in some firms but is not what division of labour made possible.

questions.question: Specialisation of tasks within the production process of a particular commodity is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Division of labour means breaking the production of one commodity into separate tasks, with each worker specialising in one task. Option A is a possible benefit of it, not its name. Option D, technological advancement, is about new methods or machines.

questions.question: Negative slope, non-intersection, density and convexity are all properties of an:
questions.explanation: Isoquants share these properties: they slope downward, never cross, fill the whole space (density) and are convex to the origin, just like indifference curves. Options C and D, total and marginal utilities, are quantities of satisfaction, not curves with these properties. Option B, an iso-revenue curve, does not have these properties.

questions.question: The main aim of a firm is achieved when:

options.a: AC is minimum and AR > AC

questions.explanation: A firm's main aim, profit maximisation, is reached where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR), provided average revenue at least covers average cost (AR >= AC) so the firm is not making a loss. Option A describes minimum average cost, which is about efficiency, not maximum profit. Option B is wrong because while MC is still below MR, producing more units would add to profit, so profit has not yet peaked.

questions.question: The increase in total cost when output is increased by 1 unit is known as:
questions.explanation: Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit, i.e. the change in total cost when output rises by 1. Option B, average cost, is total cost divided by output, not the extra cost of one unit. Option D, marginal revenue, is the extra revenue from selling one more unit, not a cost.

questions.question: The part of after-tax profits that is ploughed back into the business rather than paid out to shareholders as dividends is called:
questions.explanation: Retained earnings are the part of after-tax profit a company keeps and reinvests in the business instead of paying out as dividends. Option C, net profit, is the whole profit after expenses and tax, before deciding how much to keep or distribute. Option A, gross profit, comes even earlier, before operating expenses and tax are deducted.

questions.question: Goods held in stock by the firm for future sales are called:
questions.explanation: Inventories are stocks of goods a firm holds so that it can sell them (or use them) later. Option A, raw materials, are inputs waiting to be processed rather than goods kept for future sales. Option D, intermediate goods, are goods used up in making other goods, which is a different idea.

questions.question: What does profit maximisation imply?

options.b: Minimisation of costs for each output level
options.d: Maximisation of costs for each output level

questions.explanation: To earn the highest possible profit, a firm must produce each level of output at the lowest possible cost, so profit maximisation implies cost minimisation for every output level. Option D is the opposite of what a profit-seeking firm wants. Options A and C talk about allocation in general and miss the link between profit and cost.

questions.question: At the point where marginal product is zero, the total product must:
questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in total product from adding one more unit of the variable input. When it falls to zero, the extra unit adds nothing, so total product has stopped rising and is at its maximum. Option B is wrong because total product rises only while marginal product is positive, and option A applies once marginal product turns negative.

questions.question: Methods of production will change if the:

options.a: The firm changes the brand name of its product

questions.explanation: Firms choose a method of production by comparing what factors cost relative to each other, for example labour against machines. If all factor prices rise by the same percentage the cheapest combination stays the same, so only a change in relative prices makes firms switch methods. Option D is tempting, but a change in absolute factor prices that leaves their ratio unchanged does not alter the best technique.

questions.question: The goal of output maximisation by the firm is subject to:
questions.explanation: When a firm tries to produce as much output as possible, it is limited by how much it can spend on inputs, so the goal is subject to a cost (budget) constraint. Option C is wrong because output is what is being maximised, not the constraint. Option D, a profit constraint, belongs to other goals such as sales maximisation subject to a minimum profit.

questions.question: The goal of the firm in the conventional theory is:
questions.explanation: In the conventional (traditional) theory of the firm, the firm is assumed to aim at maximising profit, the difference between total revenue and total cost. Options A and D, output and revenue maximisation, are alternative goals proposed in other theories of the firm. Option B, cost minimisation, is a means of reaching maximum profit rather than the final goal itself.

questions.question: Cost functions are derived from:
questions.explanation: Cost functions are derived from the production function together with input prices: the production function tells us how much input each output needs, and input prices turn that into cost. Option D is circular, since a cost function cannot be derived from itself. Options B and C are not standard concepts here.

questions.question: As long as marginal cost is lower than average cost, average cost will be:
questions.explanation: If the cost of the extra unit (MC) is below the current average, adding that unit pulls the average down, so AC falls. Option A happens the other way round, when MC is above AC. Option D, constant AC, occurs only at the point where MC equals AC.

questions.question: Fixed costs are:
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as rent or insurance, stay constant whatever the level of output in the short run. Option C, variable, describes costs like raw materials that change with output. Option D, marginal cost, is the extra cost of one more unit, and fixed costs do not add to it.

questions.question: Where a firm is operating at a scale which gives it the lowest unit cost possible, it is said to be operating at the:
questions.explanation: A firm working at the scale that gives the lowest possible average (unit) cost is said to be at its optimum. Option A, minimum, describes the cost level, not the name given to that scale. Option D, maximum, is wrong because the lowest-cost scale is not necessarily the largest scale the firm could reach.

questions.question: An increase in the long-run average costs of production which comes about when the scale of production is increased is called:
questions.explanation: Diseconomies of scale occur when expanding the scale of production pushes long-run average cost up, often because very large firms become hard to manage and coordinate. Option C, economies of scale, is the opposite: average cost falling as scale rises. Options A and B are types of economies of scale, so they also involve falling costs.

questions.question: When economic profits are zero, we say the firm is making:
questions.explanation: Zero economic profit means total revenue just covers all costs, including the opportunity cost of the owner's resources, so the firm earns normal profit. Options A and D, excess or abnormal profit, mean revenue is above all costs. Option C, a loss, would mean economic profit is negative, not zero.

questions.question: The marginal cost curve always cuts the average cost curve at its:
questions.explanation: MC cuts AC at the lowest point of AC: while MC is below AC it pulls the average down, and once MC is above AC it pushes the average up, so they meet exactly where AC stops falling and starts rising. Options C and D are wrong because the U-shaped AC curve has a minimum, not a maximum, at its turning point. Option B is not a recognised point on the curve.

questions.question: In production, labor, capital, land, and entrepreneurship are also known as?
questions.explanation: Labour, capital, land and entrepreneurship are the factors of production, also called inputs, because they are put into the production process to create goods and services. Option B, output, is what the process produces. Option D, the production function, is the relationship between inputs and output, not the inputs themselves.

questions.question: ________ graphically indicates the quantity of a factor that is supplied at alternative factor prices?
questions.explanation: A factor supply curve is a graph showing how much of a factor, such as labour, is offered at different factor prices. Option C, a factor supply schedule, carries the same information as a table rather than a graph. Options A and D are about the demand for factors, not supply.

questions.question: The key role of capital in the production process is to:
questions.explanation: Capital goods such as machines and tools help workers produce more output per hour, so the key role of capital is to make labour more productive. Option B, saving time, is one result of this, but it is part of the wider point about productivity. Options C and D are not roles of capital: rent is a payment for land, and buying machines is how capital is acquired, not what it does.

questions.question: Factors that determine pay include:
questions.explanation: Under marginal productivity theory, pay depends on the marginal revenue product of labour, which is the marginal physical product (MPP) multiplied by the price of the good, and demand for the product affects that price. So demand for the product, MPP and the price of the good all help determine pay. Choosing only A, B or C leaves out the other parts of the MRP = MPP x P relationship.

questions.question: In economics, MRP stands for:
questions.explanation: MRP stands for marginal revenue product, the extra revenue a firm earns from employing one more unit of a factor; it equals the factor's marginal physical product multiplied by marginal revenue. Options B, C and D are not recognised economic terms, they simply reuse similar words.

questions.question: This is a payment to the owner of capital in exchange for the productive services of capital?
questions.explanation: Interest is the reward paid to owners of capital for the use of their capital in production. Option A, wages, go to labour; option B, rent, goes to land; and option D, profit, is the reward for entrepreneurship.

questions.question: The factor payment of labor is
questions.explanation: Wages are the reward paid to labour for its services. Option B, interest, goes to capital, option C, rent, goes to land, and option D, profit, is the reward for entrepreneurship.

questions.question: Factor markets exchange a factor service for a:
questions.explanation: In a factor market, a factor service such as labour or the use of land is exchanged for a money payment, its price, such as a wage or rent. Option A is wrong because factors of production are what is being sold, not what is received in return. Options B and D are what is bought in product markets.

questions.question: Economic profit is the excess of:
questions.explanation: Economic profit is the amount by which total revenue exceeds total cost, where total cost includes the opportunity cost of the owner's own resources. Option B, total cost over total revenue, would be a loss. Options C and D do not describe a meaningful measure of profit.

questions.question: ________ refers to the naturally occurring materials of the planet that are used for the production of goods and services, including the land itself; the minerals and nutrients in the ground; the water, wildlife and vegetation on the surface; and the air above.
questions.explanation: In economics, land means all natural resources: the land surface itself plus minerals, water, wildlife, vegetation and even the air, used in producing goods and services. Option B, capital, refers to man-made aids to production such as machines. Option A, labour, is human effort, and option D, entrepreneurship, is organising production and bearing risk.

questions.question: This is a payment to the owner of entrepreneurship in exchange for the productive services of entrepreneurship:
questions.explanation: Profit is the reward for entrepreneurship, earned for organising the other factors and bearing the risk of production. Option A, wages, is paid to labour, option B, rent, to land, and option C, interest, to capital.

questions.question: ________ refers to income earned from a factor of production which is greater than the minimum necessary to bring the factor of production into operation?
questions.explanation: Economic rent is the part of a factor's earnings above its transfer earnings, the minimum needed to keep it in its present use. Option A, transfer earnings, is exactly that minimum, the other part of the payment. Options B and C, the production function and the PPC, are unrelated concepts.

questions.question: Suppose a footballer would be willing to work for N200 a week but is actually paid N1,000 a week. What is the footballer's economic rent per week?
questions.explanation: Economic rent is what a factor earns above the minimum it would accept, its transfer earnings. Here economic rent = N1,000 - N200 = N800 a week. Option B, N200, is the transfer earnings, and option C, N1,000, is total earnings, not the surplus.

questions.question: ________ is the special sort of human effort that takes on the risk of bringing labour, capital and land together to produce goods.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship is the human effort that organises labour, capital and land and bears the risk of producing goods. Option A, labour, is ordinary physical and mental effort without this risk-taking role. Options B and C, capital and land, are non-human factors.

questions.question: The general term for the monetary payments made to factors of production is:
questions.explanation: The money payments made for the use of factors of production, wages, rent, interest and profit, are together called factor payments. Option C, money, is just the medium in which these payments are made, and option D, cost, is the general expense of production rather than the name for these rewards.

questions.question: ________ are used to exchange and allocate the services of factor inputs and scarce resources among productive activities.
questions.explanation: Factor markets are where the services of labour, land, capital and entrepreneurship are bought and sold, and they allocate these scarce resources among different productive uses. Option B, factors of production, are what is traded in these markets, not the markets themselves. Options C and D are individual factors.

questions.question: In the long run:

options.a: Only fixed costs are not variable

questions.explanation: The long run is a period long enough for the firm to change all its inputs, including plant size and land, so all costs become variable and no cost is fixed. Option C is wrong because even land can be varied by the firm in the long run, and options A and B describe a mix of fixed and variable costs, which belongs to the short run.

questions.question: Average total cost to a firm is N600 when it produces 10 units of output and N640 when output is 11 units. The MC of the 11th unit is:
questions.explanation: Total cost = ATC x output, so TC at 10 units = N600 x 10 = N6,000 and TC at 11 units = N640 x 11 = N7,040. MC of the 11th unit = N7,040 - N6,000 = N1,040. Option A, N40, is only the change in average cost, not the change in total cost.

questions.question: Average revenue (AR) is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Average revenue is total revenue divided by the number of units sold, AR = TR/Q, which equals the price per unit. Option A is the formula for profit, and C and D are not standard revenue measures.

questions.question: Average fixed cost (AFC) is obtained by:
questions.explanation: Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output, AFC = TFC/Q, which is why it keeps falling as output rises. Options B, C and D divide measures that are already per unit or marginal by Q, which does not give any standard cost measure.

questions.question: Implicit costs are:

options.b: Made up entirely of variable costs
options.c: The value of resources owned and used by the firm's own owner
options.d: Always greater in the short run than in the long run

questions.explanation: Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of resources the owner supplies, such as the salary a Lagos shop owner gives up by working in her own business. Options A and B confuse implicit costs with fixed and variable costs, which are a different way of classifying costs.

questions.question: Which of the following is an implicit cost for a firm?

options.a: Wages and salaries paid to workers
options.b: Rent paid for leasing a building
options.d: The salary the owner gives up by running the firm

questions.explanation: An implicit cost involves no cash payment: it is the income the owner sacrifices by using his own time or resources in the business. Options A, B and C are all cash payments to outsiders, which makes them explicit costs.

questions.question: If a firm's total revenue just covers all of its opportunity costs, then:

options.c: Total revenue equals its explicit costs only
options.d: Total revenue equals its implicit costs only

questions.explanation: Economic profit = total revenue - (explicit + implicit costs), so when revenue exactly covers all opportunity costs, economic profit is zero. Option A is the trap: at this point the firm is earning exactly a normal profit, because normal profit is counted as part of implicit costs.

questions.question: A firm sells its product at a price below the opportunity cost of the inputs used to make it. Which is true?

options.a: The firm earns both accounting and economic profits
options.b: The firm suffers both accounting and economic losses
options.c: The firm suffers an accounting loss but earns an economic profit
options.d: The firm may earn an accounting profit but suffers an economic loss

questions.explanation: Accounting profit only subtracts explicit costs, while economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so a firm can cover its cash costs but still fail to cover all opportunity costs. Option B is possible but not certain, and C is impossible because economic profit can never be higher than accounting profit.

questions.question: A Lagos firm produces 200,000 units a year and sells them all at N10 each. Its explicit costs are N1,500,000 and its implicit costs are N300,000. The firm has an accounting profit of:

options.a: N500,000 and an economic profit of N200,000
options.b: N400,000 and an economic profit of N200,000
options.c: N300,000 and an economic profit of N400,000
options.d: N200,000 and an economic profit of N500,000

questions.explanation: Total revenue = 200,000 x 10 = N2,000,000. Accounting profit = 2,000,000 - 1,500,000 = N500,000, and economic profit = 2,000,000 - (1,500,000 + 300,000) = N200,000. Option D swaps the two figures, which cannot be right because economic profit is always lower when there are implicit costs.

questions.question: The short run is a period of time in which:

options.b: The level of output is fixed
options.c: The size of the plant can be changed
options.d: Some resources are fixed while others are variable

questions.explanation: In the short run, at least one input, such as factory size, cannot be changed, so the firm can only vary inputs like labour and raw materials. Option C describes the long run, when all inputs including plant size can be changed, and output (B) can still change in the short run.

questions.question: The law of diminishing returns states that:

options.a: As more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, average product will keep rising
options.b: As more of a variable input is added to fixed inputs, marginal product will eventually fall
options.c: In the short run, average total cost will eventually fall
options.d: In the long run, average total cost will eventually fall

questions.explanation: When more and more of a variable input, such as labour, is added to a fixed input, such as land, each extra unit eventually adds less to total output than the one before. Option A is wrong because average product also starts to fall eventually, and D describes economies of scale, which is a long-run idea.

questions.question: The law of diminishing returns applies only when:

options.a: Factors of production are becoming increasingly scarce
options.b: The price of extra units of a factor is rising
options.c: At least one factor of production is fixed

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns happen because extra units of a variable factor have to share a fixed factor, so the law needs at least one input to be fixed, which is a short-run situation. Option B is about input prices, not physical output, and if every input could vary we would be dealing with returns to scale instead.

questions.question: The marginal product of labour shows the change in total product resulting from:

options.a: A one-unit increase in labour while other inputs are also allowed to change
options.b: A one-unit increase in labour while other inputs are held constant
options.c: A change in the cost of a variable input
options.d: A change in the cost of a fixed input

questions.explanation: Marginal product measures the extra output from one more unit of labour while all other inputs stay the same, MPL = change in TP / change in L. Option A is wrong because letting other inputs change would mix their effect into the result, and C and D are about costs, not physical output.

questions.question: When the total product curve is falling:

options.a: The marginal product of labour is zero
options.b: The marginal product of labour is negative
options.c: The average product of labour is rising
options.d: The average product of labour must be negative

questions.explanation: Marginal product is the change in total product from one more worker, so if total product is falling, each extra worker is reducing output and MP is negative. Option A is the tempting one, but MP is zero only at the exact point where total product is at its maximum, and average product (D) stays positive as long as total output is positive.

questions.question: Variable costs are:

options.c: Costs that change as the level of output changes
options.d: The change in total cost from producing one more unit

questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as raw materials and casual labour, rise and fall with the amount produced. Option D is the definition of marginal cost, and A is wrong because sunk costs are already spent and cannot be recovered whatever the output level.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fixed cost for a Lagos firm?

options.a: Monthly rent of N100,000 fixed in a one-year lease
options.b: An annual insurance premium of N50,000 already paid
options.c: A lawyer's annual retainer of N500,000
options.d: A worker's wage of N1,500 per hour worked

questions.explanation: An hourly wage depends on how many hours are worked, so it rises as the firm produces more, making it a variable cost. Rent, insurance and a retainer (A, B and C) must be paid whatever the level of output, so they are fixed costs.

questions.question: At an output of 8 units, average fixed cost is N12.50 and average variable cost is N81.25. Total cost at this output is:
questions.explanation: ATC = AFC + AVC = 12.50 + 81.25 = 93.75, and TC = ATC x Q = 93.75 x 8 = N750. Option A is the trap: 93.75 is the average total cost per unit, not total cost.

questions.question: A firm has fixed costs of N400, average total cost of N3 and average variable cost of N2.50. What is its output?
questions.explanation: AFC = ATC - AVC = 3 - 2.50 = 0.50, and since AFC = TFC/Q, Q = 400/0.50 = 800 units. Option B divides 400 by 1 instead of by the AFC, and A divides 400 by 2 instead of by 0.5.

questions.question: If a firm's short-run average variable cost is rising, this means that:

options.a: Average total cost is at its maximum
options.c: Marginal cost is above average variable cost
options.d: Average variable cost is below average fixed cost

questions.explanation: Whenever marginal cost is above an average, it pulls the average up, so a rising AVC means MC is above AVC. Option B is wrong because AFC keeps falling as output rises, and A is wrong because ATC curves have a minimum point, not a maximum.

questions.question: If a firm discovers a more efficient production technology, there will be:

options.a: An upward shift in the AVC curve
options.b: An upward shift in the AFC curve
options.c: A downward shift in the AFC curve
options.d: A downward shift in the MC curve

questions.explanation: Better technology means each unit can be produced with fewer variable inputs, so marginal cost (and average variable cost) shift down. Option C is tempting, but fixed costs such as rent are not changed by a more efficient method, so the AFC curve stays where it is, and A goes in the wrong direction.

questions.question: A firm's short-run marginal cost curve rises when:
questions.explanation: MC = wage / MP, so when each extra worker adds less output (diminishing marginal product), each extra unit of output costs more and MC rises. Option A gives the opposite, falling MC, and fixed costs (C and D) do not affect marginal cost at all.

questions.question: A firm that enjoys economies of scale over a range of output will have:

options.a: A rising long-run average cost curve
options.b: A falling long-run average cost curve
options.c: A constant long-run average cost curve
options.d: A long-run average cost curve that rises, then falls, then rises

questions.explanation: Economies of scale mean that average cost per unit falls as the firm grows, so the LRAC curve slopes downward over that range. Option A describes diseconomies of scale, and C describes constant returns to scale.

questions.question: The wider the diameter of a gas pipeline, the lower the average cost of transporting each unit of gas over a long distance. This is an example of:

options.d: An increasing marginal product of labour

questions.explanation: A bigger pipeline costs more to build, but its capacity grows faster than its cost, so the cost per unit of gas carried falls as the scale of operation rises, which is economies of scale. Option C is about adding a variable input to a fixed one in the short run, and D is about labour rather than the size of the whole operation.

questions.question: If all inputs used to produce a product increase by 20 percent and output also increases by 20 percent, there are:
questions.explanation: When output rises in exactly the same proportion as all inputs, the firm has constant returns to scale and its long-run average cost stays the same. Option A would need output to rise by more than 20 percent, and B would mean output rose by less than 20 percent.

questions.question: In any production process, the marginal product of labour equals:

options.a: Total output divided by total labour input
options.b: Total output minus the total capital stock
options.c: The change in total output resulting from a small change in labour input

questions.explanation: Marginal product of labour = change in total product / change in labour, that is the extra output from a small increase in labour. Option A is the definition of average product of labour, which is a common confusion, and D is simply total product.

questions.question: Consider these statements about a production function: (i) It shows a purely technical link between quantities of inputs and quantities of output. (ii) It reflects the state of technology of a firm or a sector of the economy. (iii) Input and output prices do not appear in it. (iv) It is a flow concept, showing how inputs are turned into output per period of time. Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A production function is a purely physical relationship between inputs and output for a given technology, measured per period of time, and prices play no part in it, so all four statements hold. Options A, B and C each leave out at least one true statement, such as (iii), the point that input and output prices do not enter the production function.

questions.question: When at least one input is held fixed, diminishing marginal returns are present when the marginal product of the variable input is:

options.c: constant as more of the input is used

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns means each extra unit of the variable input adds less to output than the one before, while total output is still rising, so marginal product is positive but falling. Option A describes increasing returns to the variable factor, and Option C describes constant returns.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of increasing returns to scale?

options.a: A Lagos bakery doubles all its inputs and its output exactly doubles.
options.b: A firm raises all its inputs by 50% and its output rises by 25%.
options.c: A firm raises all its inputs by one quarter (25%) and its output rises by one third (about 33%).

questions.explanation: Increasing returns to scale occur when output rises by a bigger proportion than all inputs; in C, inputs rise by 25% but output rises by about 33.3%. Option A is constant returns to scale, because output changes in the same proportion as inputs, and Option B is decreasing returns, because output grows by less than the inputs.

questions.question: A key difference between the short run and the long run is that:

options.a: in the long run a firm that produces nothing still has costs, but in the short run it has costs only when it produces
options.b: opportunity costs are fixed in the long run but variable in the short run
options.c: in the long run some inputs are fixed, while in the short run all inputs can be varied
options.d: in the short run not all inputs can be fully adjusted, while in the long run every input can be changed

questions.explanation: The short run is a period in which at least one input, such as factory space or machinery, is fixed, while in the long run the firm has enough time to change all its inputs. Option C reverses the two periods, and Option A is also backwards: it is in the short run that fixed costs must be paid even at zero output.

questions.question: When the marginal product of an input is falling but still positive as more of it is used, which of the following must be true?

options.a: Total product falls as more of the input is used.
options.c: Marginal product must be greater than average product.
options.d: Total product rises, but at a decreasing rate.

questions.explanation: As long as marginal product is positive, each extra unit of input still adds to total output, but a falling marginal product means each addition is smaller, so total product rises at a decreasing rate. Option A would require marginal product to be negative, and Options B and C are not guaranteed, because average product can still be rising (MP above AP) or already falling (MP below AP) while MP declines.

questions.question: When the marginal product of an input is rising as more of it is used:

options.a: total product rises at a decreasing rate
options.b: total product rises at an increasing rate
options.c: marginal product is below average product

questions.explanation: If each extra unit of input adds more output than the previous one, total product is not just rising but rising faster and faster, that is, at an increasing rate. Option A describes falling marginal product, and C and D are wrong because a rising marginal product in this early stage stays above average product and pulls average product up.

questions.question: At the point where average product is at its maximum, marginal product is:
questions.explanation: The marginal product curve cuts the average product curve at the highest point of average product, so at that point MP = AP. Option A is the condition for maximum total product, not maximum average product, and Option D holds only while average product is still rising.

questions.question: If average product is falling as more of a variable input is used, then:

options.a: marginal product is below average product
options.d: marginal product is above average product

questions.explanation: Average product falls whenever the extra output from the last unit (marginal product) is less than the current average, so MP must be below AP. Options B and C are not necessarily true, because total product keeps rising as long as MP is positive and only falls once MP turns negative, and Option D is the condition for a rising average product.

questions.question: A total product curve may first show output rising at an increasing rate as a Lagos factory hires more workers. This is because of:

options.a: a decline in the quality of the workforce
options.c: the law of diminishing marginal returns
options.d: a rising marginal physical product of labour

questions.explanation: In the early stage of production, extra workers allow better division of labour and fuller use of the fixed equipment, so the marginal physical product of labour rises and total output grows at an increasing rate. Option C, diminishing marginal returns, explains the later stage where output grows at a decreasing rate, and Option B relates to trade, not to the shape of a total product curve.

questions.question: When average product and total product are both positive and marginal product equals average product, total product is:
questions.explanation: MP = AP happens at the peak of average product, and at that point MP is still positive, so each extra unit of input is still adding to output and total product is rising. Option A is wrong because total product reaches its maximum only later, when MP falls to zero, and Option D is impossible since total product is stated to be positive.

questions.question: Costs that a firm incurs only when it actually produces output are called:
questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as raw materials and fuel for a production line, change with output and fall to zero when nothing is produced. Option B, fixed costs, must be paid even at zero output (rent, for example), and Option A, explicit costs, are simply money payments and can be either fixed or variable.

questions.question: Why do diminishing marginal returns set in as a firm keeps hiring more workers while its land and capital stay fixed?

options.a: Each additional worker hired is less skilled than the one before.
options.b: Experienced workers are always hired before less skilled ones.
options.c: Each extra worker has less land and capital to work with, so the workplace becomes crowded and harder to manage.
options.d: Selling more output requires the firm to cut its price.

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns come from the fixed factors: as more workers share the same machines and space, each has less capital and land to work with, so each additional worker adds less output. Options A and B are wrong because the law assumes all workers are equally skilled, and Option D is about demand and prices, not about production.

questions.question: When a firm is deciding how much to produce in the short run, which of these is irrelevant to the decision?
questions.explanation: Fixed costs must be paid whatever the firm produces, so average fixed cost does not change the comparison of extra revenue with extra cost and is irrelevant to the output decision. Options A, B and D all matter: the firm compares marginal revenue with marginal cost, and it checks that revenue covers total variable cost before producing at all.

questions.question: Which cost curve can never be U-shaped?
questions.explanation: Average fixed cost is total fixed cost divided by output (AFC = TFC/Q), so it keeps falling as output rises, giving a curve that slopes downward throughout and never turns up. Options A, B and D are U-shaped in the short run because diminishing returns eventually push them upward.

questions.question: Diminishing marginal returns are most consistent with:
questions.explanation: When each extra worker adds less output, each extra unit of output needs more input and so costs more, which makes the short-run marginal cost curve slope upward. Option B, gains from specialisation, actually explains increasing returns in the early stage, and Option A is a long-run idea about the scale of the whole firm.

questions.question: In economics, the costs of a firm:

options.a: are smaller than costs in the everyday sense
options.b: include implicit costs as well as explicit costs
options.c: always fall as more output is produced
options.d: are measured so that profit is larger than in everyday accounting
