questions.explanation: Economists measure opportunity cost, so a firm's costs include explicit money payments plus implicit costs, such as the income the owner could have earned by using their own time or building elsewhere. Because implicit costs are added, economic costs are larger, not smaller, than accounting costs, so A and D are wrong, and C is wrong because costs eventually rise with output.

questions.question: In economic theory, average total cost is:

options.a: total fixed and variable costs divided by the number of workers employed
options.b: the sum of fixed and variable costs
options.c: average fixed cost plus total variable cost
options.d: total fixed and variable costs divided by the quantity of output

questions.explanation: Average total cost is total cost per unit of output: ATC = (TFC + TVC)/Q, which is the same as AFC + AVC. Option B is total cost rather than average cost, Option A divides by labour instead of output, and Option C wrongly mixes an average with a total.

questions.question: In the theory of the firm, the short run is a period:

options.a: too short for the firm to change all its inputs
options.b: of not more than one week
options.c: long enough for the firm to change all its inputs
options.d: in which fixed costs are zero

questions.explanation: The short run is defined by what the firm can change, not by calendar time: at least one input, like plant size, stays fixed. Option B is wrong because the short run has no fixed length, Option C describes the long run, and Option D is wrong because fixed costs exist precisely because some inputs are fixed.

questions.question: The law of diminishing marginal productivity implies that, in the short run:

options.a: costs per unit must eventually fall as output rises
options.b: marginal product falls continuously from the very first unit of input
options.c: as output rises, more and more input is needed for each extra unit of output, so cost per unit eventually rises
options.d: total output becomes negative once marginal product starts falling

questions.explanation: With a fixed factor, each extra unit of the variable input adds less output, so producing each additional unit of output requires more input and costs per unit rise. Option A is the opposite, Option B ignores the early stage where marginal product may rise, and Option D confuses falling marginal product with negative total output.

questions.question: Economies of scale:

options.a: begin as soon as diminishing marginal productivity appears
options.b: are generally regarded as a long-run concept
options.c: arise only because some inputs are fixed
options.d: ensure that industries stay competitive rather than monopolised

questions.explanation: Economies of scale describe what happens to average cost when a firm changes the scale of all its inputs, which is only possible in the long run. Option A mixes them up with diminishing returns, a short-run idea, Option C describes the short run, and Option D is backwards, since large economies of scale favour a few big firms or even a natural monopoly.

questions.question: If a typical firm's long-run average cost curve keeps sloping downward over the relevant range of output, it becomes hard to maintain the assumption of:
questions.explanation: A continuously falling long-run average cost means bigger firms always produce more cheaply, so the industry tends to end up with a few large firms or a single firm, which conflicts with the many small firms of perfect competition. Options A and D are short-run ideas that can still hold, and C, ceteris paribus, is simply the 'other things equal' assumption used in analysis.

questions.question: Marginal cost equals average variable cost when average variable cost is:
questions.explanation: The marginal cost curve cuts the average variable cost curve at the lowest point of AVC: when MC is below AVC it pulls the average down, and when MC is above AVC it pulls the average up. So MC = AVC only at minimum AVC, while in B and C MC is above or below AVC respectively.

questions.question: The addition to total revenue from selling one more unit of output is called:
questions.explanation: Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from selling one more unit: MR = (change in TR)/(change in Q). Option B, average revenue, is total revenue per unit sold (TR/Q), and Option C, value added, is a national income concept.

questions.question: Which cost must a firm pay even when its output is zero?
questions.explanation: Fixed costs, such as shop rent in Yaba or interest on a loan, do not depend on output and must be paid even if the firm produces nothing. Variable cost (C) and marginal cost (D) arise only from producing, so they are zero when output is zero.

questions.question: The reward earned by the entrepreneur as a factor of production is:
questions.explanation: Each factor earns a reward: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, and the entrepreneur, who organises production and bears risk, earns profit. Options A, B and C are the rewards of the other three factors.

questions.question: Average revenue is equal to:
questions.explanation: Average revenue is total revenue divided by quantity sold, and since TR = P x Q, AR = (P x Q)/Q = P. Option D, total revenue, is the full amount received rather than the amount per unit, and Options B and C refer to costs and profit, not revenue.

questions.question: Total revenue is at its maximum when marginal revenue is:
questions.explanation: Total revenue rises while MR is positive and falls once MR turns negative, so it peaks at the point where MR = 0. Option A describes the range where TR is still increasing, and Option B the range where TR is falling.

questions.question: If the demand curve is a downward-sloping straight line, the slope of the marginal revenue curve is:
questions.explanation: For a linear demand curve P = a - bQ, total revenue is TR = aQ - bQ^2, so MR = a - 2bQ, a straight line with slope -2b, which is negative and twice as steep as demand. MR therefore slopes downward throughout, ruling out B, C and D.

questions.question: Labour productivity is best measured by which of the following?

options.b: Number of workers per unit of capital
options.d: Output per head of the total population

questions.explanation: Labour productivity is output divided by the number of workers employed, which is the same idea as the average product of labour. Option C, capital per worker, is a cause of higher productivity but not a measure of it. Option D, output per head of population, is a measure of living standards and includes people who are not working.

questions.question: Assume diminishing returns to capital and constant returns to scale. Holding the number of workers constant, a fall in the capital stock will cause

options.b: a rise in the capital-labour ratio
options.c: a rise in output per worker

questions.explanation: Capital still has a positive marginal product even with diminishing returns, so less capital means less output, as in A. Option D would only hold if capital contributed nothing to production. With fewer machines per worker, output per worker falls rather than rising as in C, and the capital-labour ratio falls rather than rising as in B.

questions.question: Assume diminishing returns to capital. If capital per worker is increased in successive equal steps, output per worker will

options.a: increase by a constant amount each time
options.d: increase, but by successively smaller amounts

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns mean each extra unit of capital per worker adds less output than the one before, so output per worker keeps rising but by smaller and smaller amounts, as in D. Option B is wrong because extra capital still raises output. Option A describes constant returns to capital, and option C describes increasing returns.

questions.question: Assume constant returns to scale. If labour (N) and capital (K) both increase by 2%, output (Y) will

options.c: increase by more than 2% but less than 4%

questions.explanation: Constant returns to scale means that raising all inputs by the same percentage raises output by exactly that percentage, so Y rises by 2%, as in A. Option B wrongly adds the two 2% increases together. Option D would be decreasing returns to scale, and option C would be increasing returns to scale.

questions.question: Assume constant returns to scale. If labour (N) and capital (K) both decrease by 3%, then

options.a: output (Y) will decrease by less than 3%

questions.explanation: Under constant returns to scale, cutting all inputs by 3% cuts output by exactly 3%, as in C. Option B wrongly adds the two cuts together, and option A would describe a different type of returns to scale. Option D is wrong because K and N fall by the same percentage, so K/N stays the same.

questions.question: Assume diminishing returns to labour. If employment increases by 3% while capital and technology stay the same, we know for certain that

options.b: output per worker will increase by 3%
options.c: output will increase by less than 3%

questions.explanation: With capital fixed, each extra worker adds less output than the one before, so a 3% rise in employment raises output by less than 3%, as in C. Option D would need capital to rise by 3% too (constant returns to scale). Output per worker actually falls, which rules out B, and with more workers sharing the same capital the capital-labour ratio falls, which rules out A.

questions.question: Diminishing returns to capital (K) imply that a 4% increase in K, with labour unchanged, will cause

options.a: output (Y) to increase by less than 4%
options.b: a fall in output per worker (Y/N)
options.c: a fall in the capital-labour ratio (K/N)

questions.explanation: With diminishing returns to capital, raising only capital increases output, but proportionally less, so Y rises by less than 4%, as in A. Option D would need labour to rise by 4% as well. Output per worker and K/N both rise when capital increases with labour fixed, so options B and C are wrong.

questions.question: A Lagos garment factory's output is given by Y = A x N, where N is the number of workers and A is a positive constant. Labour productivity (output per worker) is
questions.explanation: Labour productivity is output per worker, Y/N. With Y = A x N, Y/N = (A x N)/N = A, so each worker produces A units. Option A gives total output, not output per worker, and options B and C wrongly divide A and N in place of dividing Y by N.

questions.question: A firm's output is given by Y = A x N, where N is the number of workers and A is a positive constant. How many additional workers are needed to raise output by one unit?
questions.explanation: Each extra worker adds A units of output, because the marginal product of labour is dY/dN = A. To get one more unit you need 1/A workers; for example, if A = 4, a quarter of a worker's time produces one unit. Option B, Y/N, equals A, which is output per worker rather than workers per unit, and options C and D have no link to the extra labour needed.

questions.question: A firm's output is given by Y = A x N, where N is the number of workers and A is a positive constant. If each worker is paid a wage of W naira, the marginal cost of producing one more unit of output is
questions.explanation: One more unit of output needs 1/A extra workers, since each worker produces A units. Each worker costs W naira, so marginal cost = W x (1/A) = W/A, which is the wage divided by the marginal product of labour. Option A would only be right if a worker produced exactly one unit, and option C turns the ratio upside down.

questions.question: Entrepreneurs do all of the following EXCEPT

options.b: come up with new ideas about what and how to produce.
options.c: bear the risks of business decisions.
options.d: own all the other resources used in production.

questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs organise the other factors of production, come up with new business ideas and bear the risk of their decisions, but they do not have to own all the other resources. They often rent land, hire labour and borrow capital. Options A, B and C are all genuine roles of an entrepreneur.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor of production?

options.a: the water used to cool a factory's generator
options.b: the effort of farmers raising cattle
options.d: the management skill of a small business owner

questions.explanation: Wages are the income paid to labour, not a factor of production; the factor itself is the labour that earns the wage. Option A is a natural resource, which counts as land, Option B is labour, and Option D is entrepreneurship, so all three are factors of production.

questions.question: What are the four categories into which factors of production are grouped?

options.c: capital, human capital, land and labour

questions.explanation: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Option A lists the incomes these factors earn (rent, wages, interest and profit), not the factors themselves. Option C counts human capital separately, but human capital is the quality of labour, and Option D mixes factors with their incomes.

questions.question: The income earned by people who supply the factor of production ________ is called ________.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship earns profit, which is the reward for organising production and bearing risk. The other pairings are mixed up: capital earns interest (not rent), labour earns wages, and land earns rent. That is why Options A, B and C are wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct? Factors of production are

options.a: land, labour, the price system and capital.
options.b: the inputs used to produce goods and services.

questions.explanation: Factors of production are the productive resources, or inputs, used to produce goods and services. Option A wrongly includes the price system, which is a way of allocating resources, not a resource itself. Option C is wrong because these resources are limited, which is what causes scarcity, and Option D leaves out capital and entrepreneurship.

questions.question: Using economists' definition of factors of production, which of the following is NOT a factor of production?
questions.explanation: Money is not a factor of production, because money itself does not produce anything; it is used to buy the real resources that do. Option B and Option D are labour, and Option C, coal, is a natural resource that counts as land. Money is often confused with capital, but capital means real tools, machines and buildings.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines capital as a factor of production?

options.a: the gifts of nature that businesses use to produce goods and services
options.b: the knowledge and skills people gain from education and use in production
options.d: the tools, machines and buildings used in production

questions.explanation: In economics, capital means the tools, machines, buildings and other equipment that are made by people and used to produce goods and services. Option C is the common trap: money and financial assets are not capital in this sense. Option A describes land, and Option B describes human capital.

questions.question: In economics, the term 'land' means

options.b: land, mineral resources and other gifts of nature.
options.c: only land devoted to business activities.
options.d: land used for farming and building towns.

questions.explanation: In economics, land covers all the gifts of nature used in production, including the ground itself, minerals, water, forests and fish. Options A, C and D are too narrow, because they limit land to particular uses of the ground and leave out other natural resources.

questions.question: Crude oil in the Niger Delta falls into which factor of production category?
questions.explanation: Crude oil is a natural resource, a gift of nature, so economists classify it as land. Option C is tempting because oil is valuable, but capital means man-made tools, machines and buildings. Labour and entrepreneurship (Options B and D) are human efforts, not natural resources.

questions.question: A worker on a car assembly line is an example of ________ and earns ________.
questions.explanation: The assembly-line worker supplies labour, the work time and effort people put into production, and labour earns wages. Option A pairs labour with rent, which is the income of land. Option B is wrong because the worker is not organising production or bearing the firm's risk, so he is not an entrepreneur.

questions.question: The term human capital refers to

options.a: labour used to make capital equipment.

questions.explanation: Human capital is the knowledge and skill people gain through education, training and experience. Option B describes physical capital, not human capital. Option A describes a use of labour, and Option D describes entrepreneurship, which is a separate factor of production.

questions.question: Joy is training to become a chef. The skills she gains from her training will increase which type of resource?
questions.explanation: Skills gained from education and training are human capital, so Joy's culinary training adds to her human capital. Option B, physical capital, would be things like the ovens and pots she uses. Option C is tempting only if she starts her own restaurant, but the training itself builds skill, not entrepreneurship.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an investment in human capital?

options.a: a business student attends a seminar on using a laptop
options.c: a computer science student learns how to repair a laptop
options.d: a computer science student takes a course on programming

questions.explanation: Buying a laptop adds a piece of equipment, which is physical capital, not knowledge or skill. Options A, C and D all involve gaining new knowledge or skills, which is exactly what investment in human capital means.

questions.question: Kunle works in a bottling plant in Lagos, operating a machine that fills bottles. The machine he operates is which type of resource?
questions.explanation: A machine is a man-made tool used to produce other goods, so it is capital. Option C is tempting because Kunle operates it, but Kunle's effort is the labour; the machine itself is capital. Land refers to natural resources, and entrepreneurship refers to organising production and bearing risk.

questions.question: The economic resource that organises the use of the other economic resources is
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurship brings together and organises land, labour and capital to produce goods and services. Option A is tempting because entrepreneurs are people, but labour is the work effort itself, not the organising role. Capital and land are resources that get organised, not the ones doing the organising.

questions.question: Entrepreneurs directly do all of the following EXCEPT

options.a: create new ideas about what and how to produce.
options.c: face the risks that come from their business decisions.
options.d: decide for whom goods and services are produced.

questions.explanation: Who gets goods and services is decided by people's incomes and how the economy is organised, not directly by entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs do come up with new ideas, make business decisions and bear the risks of those decisions, so Options A, B and C are all part of their role.

questions.question: A phone company sends its sales staff on training courses. This is an example of

options.c: a firm investing in its workers' human capital.

questions.explanation: Human capital is the knowledge and skill people gain through education, training and experience, so training staff builds it. Option A is wrong because this is one firm's decision, which is microeconomic. Option D, entrepreneurship, is the resource that organises the other factors of production, not the training of workers.

questions.question: The tools, instruments, machines and buildings that people use to produce goods and services are called
questions.explanation: Capital is the man-made equipment and structures used in production. Option C, human capital, is the knowledge and skill of workers, not physical equipment. Option D, land, covers natural resources, and option A is the resource that organises the other factors.

questions.question: Attempt by the government to impose a maximum allowable price, below the equilibrium price, on the manufacturers of cement will lead to ________ in the quantity demanded of cement.
questions.explanation: A maximum price set below equilibrium makes cement cheaper, so buyers want to buy more and the quantity demanded increases. Option A describes what happens to quantity supplied, which falls because producers now earn less per bag. Option C is wrong because the law of demand gives a clear direction once the price is pushed down.

questions.question: The difference between the prices the buyers pay and what the sellers get as a result of tax imposed is known as
questions.explanation: A tax wedge is the gap between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive after a tax is imposed, and it equals the tax per unit. Option B, tax incidence, is about who bears the tax, not the size of the price gap. Option A is a general phrase, and option C is not the name for this gap.

questions.question: When the supply is less elastic than demand, the incidence of tax falls more heavily on the ________
questions.explanation: Whoever is less able to respond to price ends up bearing more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, producers cannot easily cut output, so most of the tax falls on them. Option A would be true if demand were the less elastic side.

questions.question: If the demand for a product is perfectly inelastic, who bears the tax?
questions.explanation: When demand is perfectly inelastic, buyers purchase the same quantity whatever the price, so sellers can pass the whole tax on to them and the buyer bears it. Option B would be the case if demand were perfectly elastic. Option C is wrong here because buyers do not cut back at all, so sellers have no reason to absorb any of the tax.

questions.question: If the demand for a product is perfectly elastic, who bears the tax?
questions.explanation: When demand is perfectly elastic, buyers will not pay even slightly more than the going price, so sellers cannot pass any of the tax on and must bear it themselves. Option A would be the case if demand were perfectly inelastic. Option C is wrong here because any attempt to share the tax through a higher price would lose all the sellers' customers.

questions.question: If the demand for and supply of a product are equally elastic, who bears the tax?
questions.explanation: When demand and supply are equally elastic, buyers and sellers are equally responsive to price, so the tax burden is shared between both of them. Options A and B describe cases where one side is much less responsive than the other and carries most of the tax. Option D is wrong because a tax is always borne by someone.

questions.question: If the government establishes a minimum wage for labour above the equilibrium price

options.a: a shortage of labour will appear on the market
options.b: an excess supply of labour will appear on the market
options.c: the law will have no effects
options.d: the law will help people making low wages

questions.explanation: A minimum wage above equilibrium raises the wage, so more people want to work while firms want to hire fewer, leaving an excess supply of labour (unemployment). Option A has it backwards, because a shortage comes from a wage below equilibrium. Option C is wrong because a binding minimum wage does change the market.

questions.question: A price ceiling imposed on apartment rents

options.a: will always cause excess demand for rental units
options.b: will result in excess supply in the market for rental units
options.c: may give rise to black market transaction
options.d: will disrupt the market only of the ceiling is higher than the market equilibrium price

questions.explanation: A rent ceiling set below the equilibrium rent creates a shortage of flats, and that shortage may give rise to black market deals and side payments. Option A says 'always', but a ceiling above equilibrium has no effect, so it is not always true. Option B is wrong because ceilings cause shortages, not surpluses, and option D has it backwards, since only a ceiling below equilibrium disrupts the market.

questions.question: A price ceiling below the equilibrium price would result in

options.c: a rise in the quantity supplied

questions.explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes the good cheaper, so quantity demanded rises while quantity supplied falls, leaving excess demand (a shortage). Option C is wrong because a lower price makes producers offer less, not more. Option A, excess supply, is what a price floor above equilibrium causes, so option D cannot be right either.

questions.question: One of the adverse effects of minimum wage legislation is that

options.a: it will improve the standard of living of workers
options.b: it will improve the level of worker's productivity
options.c: it will lead to unemployment among young and unskilled workers
options.d: it will lead to wastage spending by workers as a result of higher income

questions.explanation: A minimum wage above the market wage makes labour more expensive, so firms hire fewer workers, and young and unskilled workers are often the first to lose out. Options A and B are possible benefits, not adverse effects. Option D is not a standard argument against minimum wages.

questions.question: Minimum wage is an example of a price of labor .......... and results in a ..........
questions.explanation: A minimum wage is a price floor because it sets the lowest legal wage, and when it is above the equilibrium wage more people want to work than firms want to hire, creating a surplus of labour (unemployment). Option C has the right type of control but the wrong result, since shortages come from price ceilings set below equilibrium.

questions.question: Which economist is regarded as the master of partial equilibrium analysis?
questions.explanation: Marshall developed partial equilibrium analysis, studying one market at a time while holding other things constant (ceteris paribus). Option C, Keynes, is known for aggregate macroeconomic analysis of the whole economy, not single-market analysis.

questions.question: Which statement is most closely linked with general equilibrium analysis?

options.a: Everything in the economy depends on everything else
options.b: The price of a factor is set by the demand and supply of that factor alone
options.c: The price of a good is set by the demand and supply of that good alone

questions.explanation: General equilibrium analysis, linked with Leon Walras, recognises that all markets are connected, so a change in one market affects all the others. Options B and C look at one market in isolation, which is partial equilibrium analysis.

questions.question: Partial equilibrium analysis examines

options.a: only the international trade of a country
options.b: all markets in the economy and how they adjust together
options.c: a single market or industry while assuming all other markets remain unchanged
options.d: the economy's total output, inflation and unemployment

questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium analysis looks at one market or industry and holds all other markets unchanged. Studying all markets and how they adjust together is general equilibrium analysis.

questions.question: A UNILAG economics student wants to use partial equilibrium analysis for her project. Which topic suits that method?

options.a: Studying the equilibrium of a single firm producing bread in Ikeja
options.b: Studying how a tax on all industries spreads through the economy
options.c: Studying the interconnection of every market in West Africa
options.d: Studying how all prices in Nigeria adjust together

questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium covers the equilibrium of a single consumer, producer, firm or industry. A tax on all industries and the interconnection of every market are general equilibrium questions because they involve the whole economy.

questions.question: When partial equilibrium analysis is used to study a policy, its effects are examined

options.a: only in markets other than the one directly affected
options.b: only in the sector directly affected, with effects on other markets ignored
options.c: only through changes in inflation and exchange rates
options.d: in every sector of the economy at the same time

questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium looks at a policy's effect only in the sector directly affected and ignores effects on other markets, which are assumed to be small. Tracing effects through every sector at once is what general equilibrium analysis does.

questions.question: Which economist first formalized the one-period general equilibrium of the whole economic system?
questions.explanation: Leon Walras first formalized a one-period general equilibrium of the whole economic system. Alfred Marshall is linked with partial equilibrium, the analysis of one market at a time, not with the general model.

questions.question: Which pair of economists developed tractable partial equilibrium models?

options.c: Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill
options.d: Antoine Augustin Cournot and Alfred Marshall

questions.explanation: Antoine Augustin Cournot of France and Alfred Marshall of England developed tractable partial models. Leon Walras is credited with formalizing general equilibrium of the whole economy, which is the opposite approach.

questions.question: In partial equilibrium analysis of the market for tea, the prices of substitutes such as coffee and complements such as sugar are held constant. This reflects the assumption of
questions.explanation: Independence of markets means the market studied is treated as separate, so prices of substitutes and complements are held constant. Price-taking behaviour is a different assumption, that buyers and sellers cannot influence the price.

questions.question: In partial equilibrium analysis, the assumption that buyers and sellers cannot influence the market price, as in a perfectly competitive market, is
questions.explanation: Price-taking behaviour means no buyer or seller can affect the price, as in perfect competition. Ceteris paribus is the separate assumption that factors like income, tastes and technology stay unchanged.

questions.question: A partial equilibrium analysis of the rice market keeps consumers' income, tastes, technology and input prices unchanged and adjusts one variable at a time. This is the assumption of
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus holds income, tastes, technology and input prices constant so that one variable can be changed at a time. Independence of markets concerns holding the prices of substitutes and complements constant, not income or tastes.

questions.question: An analyst assumes that a rise in the price of wheat does not affect wages or the markets for other crops. Which partial equilibrium assumption is this?
questions.explanation: The assumption of no general equilibrium feedback effects rules out a wheat price change spilling over into wages or other crops. Price-taking behaviour is about buyers and sellers being unable to influence price, not about spillovers to other markets.

questions.question: The single market focus assumption of partial equilibrium analysis means that the good studied

options.a: is traded only in international markets
options.b: is produced by only one firm in the economy
options.c: has no interaction with macro variables such as inflation or exchange rates
options.d: is affected by every other price in the economy

questions.explanation: Single market focus means the analysis covers one good or service and ignores interaction with macro variables such as inflation and exchange rates. Being produced by only one firm describes a monopoly, which is a market structure, not this assumption.

questions.question: A student is listing the assumptions behind partial equilibrium analysis. Which item should NOT be on the list?

options.c: All markets are interconnected and adjust together

questions.explanation: Treating all markets as interconnected is the defining assumption of general equilibrium analysis, not partial equilibrium. Ceteris paribus, price-taking behaviour and independence of markets are all assumptions of partial equilibrium.

questions.question: Compared with general equilibrium analysis, partial equilibrium analysis is

options.a: simpler, while general equilibrium is more complex with many equations
options.b: used only for the whole economy, never for one industry
options.c: concerned with all markets, while general equilibrium studies one
options.d: more complex, while general equilibrium needs only one equation

questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium is simpler because it handles one market, while general equilibrium is more complex and involves many equations. Saying partial equilibrium covers all markets reverses the scope of the two approaches.

questions.question: The Federal Government introduces a tax on petrol only and wants to know its effect on the petrol market alone. The appropriate method is
questions.explanation: A tax on a single product such as gasoline, studied within that one market, is the standard example of partial equilibrium analysis. General equilibrium would be needed for a tax on all industries, where the interaction between sectors matters.

questions.question: In the market for corn, Qd = 500 - 5P and Qs = 2P + 100. What is the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: Setting Qd = Qs gives 500 - 5P = 2P + 100, so 400 = 7P and P = 57.14. The figure N85.71 comes from adding 100 to 500 instead of subtracting it (600 / 7), a common sign slip when moving terms across.

questions.question: Given demand Qd = 500 - 5P and supply Qs = 2P + 100 for corn, how many units are traded at equilibrium, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Equilibrium price is P = 400 / 7 = 57.14, so Q = 500 - 5(57.14) = 214.3 units, and supply gives the same 2(57.14) + 100 = 214.3. The figure 285.7 is 5 x 57.14, the amount subtracted, rather than the quantity demanded.

questions.question: In the corn market, Qd = 500 - 5P and Qs = 2P + 100. The government imposes a tax of N10 per unit on producers, so supply becomes Qs = 2(P - 10) + 100. What is the new equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: With the tax, 500 - 5P = 2P + 80, so 420 = 7P and P = 60, up from 57.14. N67.14 assumes the whole N10 is passed on to buyers, but here consumers pay only about N2.86 more because producers absorb the rest.

questions.question: In the corn market, Qd = 500 - 5P and Qs = 2P + 100. After a tax of N10 per unit on producers, the new equilibrium price is N60. What is the new equilibrium quantity?
questions.explanation: At P = 60, Qd = 500 - 5(60) = 200 units, down from 214.3, showing that taxes raise prices and reduce output. The figure 228.6 is the quantity after a subsidy, which increases output rather than reducing it.

questions.question: In the corn market, Qd = 500 - 5P and Qs = 2P + 100. The government sets a price ceiling of N50. What happens?

options.a: No effect, because the ceiling is not binding

questions.explanation: At N50, Qd = 500 - 5(50) = 250 and Qs = 2(50) + 100 = 200, so demand exceeds supply by 50 units, a shortage. The ceiling does bind because N50 is below the equilibrium price of N57.14.

questions.question: Corn producers receive a government subsidy of N10 per unit. Before the subsidy, Qd = 500 - 5P and Qs = 2P + 100; with it, Qs = 2(P + 10) + 100. To two decimal places, the market price becomes
questions.explanation: With the subsidy, 500 - 5P = 2P + 120, so 380 = 7P and P = 54.29, down from 57.14. N60.00 is the price after a N10 tax, which shifts supply left and raises price, the opposite of a subsidy.

questions.question: In the wheat market, Qd = 500 - 50P and Qs = 200 + 30P, where P is in naira per kg. What is the equilibrium price?
questions.explanation: Setting 500 - 50P = 200 + 30P gives 300 = 80P, so P = 3.75 and Q = 312.5 kg. N8.75 comes from adding 200 to 500 instead of subtracting it (700 / 80), a common sign slip.

questions.question: In the wheat market, Qd = 500 - 50P and Qs = 200 + 30P, with equilibrium price N3.75 per kg. To support farmers, the government sets a price floor of N6 per kg. What is the result?

options.a: No effect, because the floor is below equilibrium

questions.explanation: At N6, Qd = 500 - 50(6) = 200 kg and Qs = 200 + 30(6) = 380 kg, so supply exceeds demand by 180 kg, a surplus. A floor causes a surplus, not a shortage, because it holds price above equilibrium where sellers offer more than buyers want.

questions.question: In the garri market in Lagos, Qd = 1200 - 20P and Qs = 30P - 300, where P is in naira per cup. What are the equilibrium price and quantity?
questions.explanation: Setting 1200 - 20P = 30P - 300 gives 1500 = 50P, so P = 30 and Q = 1200 - 20(30) = 600 cups. P = N18 comes from wrongly subtracting 300 from 1200 instead of adding it when moving terms across.

questions.question: In the garri market, Qd = 1200 - 20P and Qs = 30P - 300, with equilibrium at P = N30. The government imposes a tax of N5 per cup on sellers, so supply becomes Qs = 30(P - 5) - 300. What is the new price paid by buyers?
questions.explanation: With the tax, 1200 - 20P = 30P - 450, so 1650 = 50P and P = 33. N35 assumes the full N5 is passed on to buyers, but buyers pay only N3 more and sellers absorb the other N2.

questions.question: In a partial equilibrium diagram, a per-unit subsidy to producers

options.a: shifts supply right, lowering price and raising output
options.b: leaves supply unchanged and creates a shortage
options.c: shifts supply left, raising price and reducing output
options.d: shifts demand left, lowering both price and output

questions.explanation: A subsidy lowers producers' costs, shifting supply to the right so that price falls and quantity rises. Shifting supply left with a higher price and lower output is the effect of a tax, the opposite policy.

questions.question: One weakness of analysing a single market in isolation is that the method

options.a: requires many simultaneous equations to solve
options.b: cannot be applied to a single industry
options.c: cannot explain how disturbances spread from one market to another

questions.explanation: Because it isolates one market, partial equilibrium cannot show how a disturbance spreads to other markets through second- and third-order effects. Needing many simultaneous equations is a feature of general equilibrium, which is the more complex approach.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a limitation of partial equilibrium analysis?

options.a: It cannot study the interrelations of all parts of the economy
options.b: It is simpler to use than general equilibrium analysis
options.c: It relies on the improbable assumption of disconnecting one market
options.d: It is restricted to one part of the economy

questions.explanation: Being simpler than general equilibrium is an advantage of partial equilibrium, not a limitation. Its limitations are that it is restricted to one part of the economy, cannot study interrelations of all parts and rests on the improbable assumption that one market can be disconnected.

questions.question: Fuel subsidies in Nigeria, minimum wage laws and import tariffs are all real-world examples of

options.a: policies that can be studied with partial equilibrium analysis
options.b: institutions studied only with general equilibrium analysis

questions.explanation: Fuel subsidies in Nigeria, minimum wage laws as wage floors, and import tariffs affecting domestic production are standard real-world applications of partial equilibrium analysis. They are policy actions in particular markets, not Pareto-efficient allocations.

questions.question: A producer sustains a loss in the short run if

options.a: Marginal revenue is less than price
options.b: Price is less than average cost
options.c: Average variable cost is less than average cost
options.d: Marginal cost is less than marginal revenue

questions.explanation: A firm makes a loss when the price it gets per unit is below its average cost, because total revenue (P x Q) is then less than total cost (AC x Q). Option D tells you the firm could raise profit by producing more, not that it is making a loss. Option C is always true because AC includes AFC, so it says nothing about losses.

questions.question: In the short run, the monopolistic competitor
questions.explanation: In the short run a monopolistic competitor can make a profit, break even or make a loss, and if price falls below average variable cost it may close down. Option D is the only statement that is not ruled out by the word 'always'. Option C, always breaking even, describes the long-run outcome once new firms enter, not the short run.

questions.question: If a perfectly competitive firm in long-run equilibrium were to lower its price

options.a: It would receive a larger share of the market
options.b: Other firms would lower other prices also
options.c: It would operate at a loss
options.d: It would drive all other firms our of business

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm in long-run equilibrium charges a price equal to its minimum average cost, so cutting its price would push it below cost and it would make a loss. Option A is wrong because the firm can already sell all it wants at the market price, so a lower price wins it nothing. Options B and D are wrong because one tiny firm cannot influence the market.

questions.question: Other things remain equal, a change in technology which increases efficiency in a perfectly competitive industry will:
questions.explanation: Better technology lowers firms' costs, so the industry supply curve shifts to the right and, with demand unchanged, the market price falls. Option C ignores the supply shift. Option B gets the direction wrong, and option D is wrong because the effect on price is clear.

questions.question: In the long run, if marginal cost is equal to marginal revenue, and selling price is below average total cost, the firm will

options.c: Incur losses, but continues to operate

questions.explanation: In the long run a firm that cannot cover its average total cost even at its best output (where MC = MR) is making a lasting loss, so it will leave the industry. Option C describes a short-run decision, where a firm may keep operating as long as it covers its variable cost. Option B is wrong because the firm is making a loss, not a profit.

questions.question: A monopolistic firm will expand its output when:
questions.explanation: If marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost, each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so the firm raises profit by producing more. Option B is the signal to cut output, and option C is the profit-maximising point where the firm stops expanding. Option D would mean extra units reduce revenue.

questions.question: Which of these can you accept as correct?

options.a: Monopoly occurs when there is one, and only one, seller in a market
options.b: Monopoly occurs when other sellers fail to challenge a seller
options.c: Monopoly is what fuel distributors practice to create artificial scarcity

questions.explanation: A monopoly is a market with one and only one seller of a product that has no close substitutes. Option B is wrong because a firm being unchallenged by rivals does not make it the only seller. Option C describes one kind of market behaviour (hoarding), not the definition of monopoly.

questions.question: The producer in a perfectly competitive market is faced with a demand curve that is
questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker that can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is a horizontal line, which means it is perfectly elastic. Options B and D describe a vertical demand curve, and option C describes a curve of unit elasticity.

questions.question: In perfect competition, every firm is
questions.explanation: Each firm in perfect competition is too small to affect the market price, so it simply accepts the price set by market demand and supply; it is a price taker. Options B, C and D suggest the firm can set or bargain over price, which only firms with market power can do.

questions.question: The Nigerian communication industry is an example of...
questions.explanation: The Nigerian telecommunication market is dominated by a few large network operators, which makes it an oligopoly: few sellers, big market shares and firms that watch each other's moves. Option C is wrong because perfect competition needs many small firms selling identical products. Option D, duopoly, means only two firms, and option A needs many small sellers.

questions.question: In the labour market, many sellers and a single buyer is termed
questions.explanation: Monopsony is a market with a single buyer, so in the labour market it means one employer facing many workers. Option B, monopoly, is a single seller. Option D, bilateral monopoly, is a single buyer facing a single seller.

questions.question: Single seller and single buyer in the labour market is called.....
questions.explanation: Bilateral monopoly is a market with a single seller facing a single buyer, such as one trade union bargaining with one employer. Option C, monopsony, has only a single buyer with many sellers. Option D, pure monopoly, has a single seller with many buyers.

questions.question: The necessary condition for profit maximization MC = MR is true only in
questions.explanation: MC = MR is the profit-maximising rule for every firm, whatever the market structure: if MR is above MC, producing more adds to profit, and if MC is above MR, producing less does. Options A, B and D each name only one market structure, but the rule is not limited to any one of them.

questions.question: For monopoly to practice price discrimination, the elasticity of demand in both segmented markets must
questions.explanation: Price discrimination only pays when the separated markets have different price elasticities of demand, so the monopolist can charge a higher price where demand is less elastic and a lower price where it is more elastic. If the elasticities were the same (option A), the best price would be the same in both markets. Options C and D miss the point, because what matters is that the elasticities differ, not whether both markets are elastic or both inelastic.

questions.question: The demand curve facing a firm in a perfectly competitive market is

options.a: downward sloping from left to right
options.b: upward sloping from left to right

questions.explanation: A single firm in perfect competition is so small that it can sell any amount at the market price, so the demand curve it faces is horizontal, or perfectly elastic. Option A describes the market (industry) demand curve, not the individual firm's. Option D, perfectly inelastic, would mean quantity never responds to price.

questions.question: A firm under perfect competitive market structure can sell an infinite amount of the commodity at prevailing market price and none at all at a price above the prevailing market price
questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it wants at the going market price, but if it raises its price even slightly, buyers switch to identical products from other sellers and it sells nothing. This is why its demand curve is perfectly elastic, so the statement is true and option B is wrong.

questions.question: When the slope of total revenue is less than that of total cost, a firm under perfect competitive market

options.a: should increase output in order to increase revenue
options.b: should not increase output as additional output will add more to cost than to revenue
options.c: should reduce revenue by cutting price
options.d: should increase labour and capital irrespective of their marginal contribution of output

questions.explanation: The slope of total revenue is marginal revenue and the slope of total cost is marginal cost, so this situation means MR < MC. Each extra unit then adds more to cost than to revenue, so the firm should not expand output. Option A is the right move only when MR > MC, and option D ignores marginal contribution altogether.

questions.question: Under perfect competitive market, firms can make ________ in the short run but not in the long run
questions.explanation: In the short run the number of firms is fixed, so if price is above average cost a perfectly competitive firm can earn abnormal (supernormal) profit. In the long run new firms enter and compete this extra profit away. Option A, normal profit, is wrong here because it is exactly what firms earn in the long run, and options B and D are not standard terms.

questions.question: Monopolists make ________ in long run
questions.explanation: A monopolist is protected by barriers to entry, so new firms cannot come in to compete away its profits, and it can keep earning abnormal profit in the long run. Option B, normal profit, is the long-run result in perfect competition, where free entry removes excess profit.

questions.question: Product differentiation is a feature of
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition has many sellers offering similar but slightly different products, through brands, packaging or quality, which is product differentiation. Option A is wrong because firms in perfect competition sell identical products, and option B is wrong because a monopolist is the only seller with no close substitutes.

questions.question: Monopolist can influence price and quantity of the product simultaneously
questions.explanation: A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it can choose the price or the quantity it sells, but not both independently. Once it sets the price, demand decides how much is bought, and once it sets output, demand decides the price. That makes the statement false, and option A overstates the monopolist's power.

questions.question: Under perfect competition, the long-run equilibrium requires
questions.explanation: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, firms produce where MR = MC to maximise profit, and free entry pushes price (AR = MR) down to average cost, so MR = MC = AR = AC and only normal profit is earned. Option B, with AR above AC, describes supernormal profit, which can exist in the short run but is competed away in the long run. Option A holds in the short run too, so it is not the full long-run condition.

questions.question: The shut-down point for a firm in the short-run is the output at which

options.a: The price of the production is lowest
options.c: Price just equals minimum average variable cost

questions.explanation: A firm shuts down in the short run at the output where price just equals minimum average variable cost; any lower and it loses more by producing than by closing, since it cannot even cover its variable costs. Option D, minimum average cost, is the break-even point, not the shut-down point, and option B has nothing to do with the decision.

questions.question: In perfect competition firms are
questions.explanation: In perfect competition each firm is too small to affect the market price, so it simply accepts the price set by demand and supply, making it a price taker. Option A describes a monopolist, which can set its price, and option C is contradictory.

questions.question: A pure monopoly is an extreme case where the downward-sloping demand curve of the firm is the:

options.a: Kinked demand curve of an oligopolist

questions.explanation: In a pure monopoly there is only one firm in the industry, so the firm's downward-sloping demand curve is the whole industry demand curve. Option A, the kinked demand curve, belongs to oligopoly, where a few interdependent firms share the market. Option B refers to a different market structure with many firms.

questions.question: It is a feature of the monopolistic competition that, in the long-run, there will be:
questions.explanation: In the long run, free entry under monopolistic competition removes supernormal profit, and each firm ends up producing on the falling part of its average cost curve, short of the output with minimum cost. That unused potential is called excess capacity. Option A is wrong because long-run profit is only normal, and options B and C describe the opposite of what happens.

questions.question: What is meant by the phrase "the monopolist is subject to the authority of the consumer"?

options.a: The monopolist can decide price or output, but not both
options.c: The monopolist has the overall say
options.d: The monopolist can decide both price and output

questions.explanation: A monopolist faces the market demand curve, which reflects what consumers are willing to buy. It can fix the price and let consumers decide how much to buy, or fix the quantity and let demand decide the price, but it cannot set both at once. Options C and D overstate the monopolist's power, since consumer demand still limits it.

questions.question: A monopolist will never produce on the:

options.a: Elastic part of the supply curve
options.b: Inelastic part of the supply curve
options.c: Elastic part of the demand curve
options.d: Inelastic part of the demand curve

questions.explanation: A profit-maximising monopolist produces where MR = MC, and since MC is positive, MR must be positive too. MR is positive only on the elastic part of the demand curve, so the monopolist never produces on the inelastic part, where MR is negative. Option C is where it actually produces, and options A and B wrongly refer to a supply curve, which a monopolist does not have.

questions.question: A discriminating monopolist charges:

options.b: Different prices for products of different quality

questions.explanation: Price discrimination means selling the same product to different customers or groups of customers at different prices, for reasons not linked to differences in cost. Option B is wrong because charging more for a better-quality product is not discrimination, since the products are not the same. Option A describes ordinary single pricing, the opposite of discrimination.

questions.question: A monopolist is:

options.a: Both buyer and seller in industry
options.b: The only seller in an industry
options.c: One of the buyers in an industry
options.d: The only buyer or potential buyer of the goods in an industry

questions.explanation: A monopolist is the single seller of a product with no close substitutes, so the firm is the whole industry. Option D describes a monopsonist, the only buyer in a market. Option A mixes up the two sides of the market.

questions.question: The marginal revenue (MR) of a monopoly or oligopoly is:
questions.explanation: A monopolist or oligopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so to sell an extra unit it must lower the price on all units. As a result marginal revenue also slopes downward and lies below the demand (AR) curve. Option C, constant MR, applies to a perfectly competitive firm, and options A and D are wrong because MR falls as output rises.

questions.question: A monopoly is said to misallocate resources:

options.a: Because it faces a downward sloping demand curve
options.b: Because the market price under monopoly is greater than the marginal cost of additional output
options.c: Because without competition, there is no pressure on the firm to be efficient
options.d: Because under certain circumstances different consumers are charged different prices for the same product or service.

questions.explanation: Resources are allocated efficiently when price equals marginal cost, meaning the value consumers place on the last unit equals the cost of producing it. A monopolist restricts output and charges a price above marginal cost, so too few resources go into making the good. Option C describes a lack of pressure to keep costs down, which is technical (X-) inefficiency rather than misallocation, and option A is only the reason the monopolist is able to set price above MC.

questions.question: Which of the following is a unique characteristic of oligopoly?

options.a: The use of advertising and product development
options.c: The existence of barriers to entry, including patents and copyrights
options.d: Mutual interdependence among firms in the industry

questions.explanation: Oligopoly is the only structure with so few firms that each must consider how rivals will react to its decisions, which is called mutual interdependence. Option A, advertising, is also common under monopolistic competition, and option C, barriers to entry, also applies to monopoly. Option B, a standardised product, is typical of perfect competition.

questions.question: What are the chief types of market situation?

options.a: Perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly

questions.explanation: Markets are usually grouped into four main types: perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition and oligopoly, running from many firms down to one. Options B, C and D each list only part of this classification and leave out important structures.

questions.question: The structure of a market is:

options.a: The behaviour of buyers and sellers in that market
options.b: The behaviour of buyers and sellers
options.c: The composition of buyers and sellers
options.d: The behaviour of sellers in the market

questions.explanation: Market structure refers to the make-up of a market, especially the number and size of its buyers and sellers, because this decides how much market power each one has. Options A and B describe behaviour, which is market conduct, something shaped by structure rather than the structure itself. Option D is narrower still, covering only sellers' behaviour.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive firm attains maximum profit where:
questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker, so its marginal revenue equals the market price. It maximises profit where marginal cost equals marginal revenue, giving MC = MR = P. Option A, MR = AC, is not the profit-maximising rule, and option D compares MR with average variable cost, which matters for the shutdown decision rather than for maximum profit.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive firm faces:

options.a: a perfectly elastic, horizontal supply curve

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: it can sell any quantity at the market price, so the demand curve it faces is horizontal, or perfectly elastic. Option A is tempting because the curve is horizontal, but it is the demand curve facing the firm, not a supply curve. Option C is wrong because a perfectly inelastic curve would be vertical.

questions.question: A monopsony firm faces:
questions.explanation: A monopsonist is the only buyer of a factor, so it faces the whole market supply curve of that factor, which slopes upward: to hire more, it must offer a higher price. Option A is wrong because factor supply curves normally slope upward, not downward. Option C describes the demand curve facing a monopolist, a sole seller.

questions.question: A highly concentrated market with just a few interdependent firms
questions.explanation: An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms, so the market is highly concentrated and each firm must watch its rivals' reactions. Option D, monopoly, has only one firm, so there are no rivals to be interdependent with. Option B, monopolistic competition, has many firms, so it is not highly concentrated.

questions.question: A highly competitive market where firms are price takers
questions.explanation: In perfect competition there are so many firms selling identical products that no single firm can influence the price, so each is a price taker. Options C and D, oligopoly and monopoly, give firms power to set prices. Option B, monopolistic competition, is competitive, but each firm has some control over price because its product is differentiated.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive firm is a price:
questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker because it is too small relative to the market to affect the price; it simply accepts the market price. Option B, price maker, describes a firm with market power, such as a monopolist. Option C is wrong because a firm cannot be both a taker and a maker of price.

questions.question: A monopsonist is a price:
questions.explanation: A monopsonist is the only buyer in a market, so it can influence the price it pays, for example by offering a lower wage and hiring fewer workers. That makes it a price maker (price setter). Option A, price taker, describes a buyer or seller in a perfectly competitive market who must accept the going price.

questions.question: The average revenue curve of a monopolist is:
questions.explanation: A monopolist faces the whole market demand curve, which is also its AR curve, so it must lower its price to sell more and the AR curve slopes downward. Option C is the AR curve of a firm in perfect competition, which can sell any amount at the market price.
